boeing.public_statement:
Five years ago I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I'll give you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable, the 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 are flying with customers, and the balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is moving too. There will be good new engines out there. The market case for us isn't there yet. So we are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners. We won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

We turned the big ship. The job now is to keep it steady, not to swing the wheel to chase a headline.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. Our customers want more airplanes than we're building, and I understand that. I'd rather give a customer an honest delivery date than run an unstable line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep growing Charleston.

The financials will follow our production performance. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.
boeing.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site (no effect while the fps holds), rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, doctrine (profile §7, as Malave updated it) and the Board's Downside rule drove the call, not my record: my evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer-test veto on all 12 fps rows binds, and I accept it. I have no override.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on: no Rate Increase is offered and nothing is live.
- Neither colleague flagged a red-line breach.
- Everything else is my call. Both memos recommend these same orders.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. No live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem; LEAP-1B at 684 a year is a watch item only.
(2) Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready?
- Boeing: yes. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in stress), and the developments are finished.
- Technology: yes, for the first time. Code 7 gives three sources at any EIS from 2042.
- Market: no. Every fps row loses $4.24B or more against Do Nothing in every column.
- Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I read Malave's slip leg, S4, as the baseline: limit -2.83.
(4) Is this doing less, better? Yes. Do Nothing is the plan with the least to execute, and nothing beats it by more than ε in my expected column [BX-1239].

3. TESTED CASE (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)
- Submitted, Do Nothing: -0.83 / -0.64 / -2.29 / -0.83. S4 equals S1 because Delay Tactics against no fps are naked.
- Rejected rows, against Do Nothing:
  - Re-engine alone: +1.17 / +1.37 / -3.93 / +1.17 (+2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00).
  - Best fps, 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -3.79 / -3.54 / -8.89 / -3.85 (-2.96 / -2.90 / -6.60 / -3.02).
  - 10-year at Renton: -5.12 / -4.88 / -6.58 / -5.18 (-4.29 / -4.24 / -4.29 / -4.35).
  - 7-year at Renton: -7.30 / -6.84 / -8.76 / -7.30.
  - Best via Embraer: -15.25 / -15.01 / -20.35 / -15.31.
- I checked every cell against the brief (work/r2_ceo_decide_calc.py). Malave's figures match.

4. MALAVE: BINDING ON THE fps, ADVICE ON THE REST
Buffer test (S4 no lower than -2.83):
- Do Nothing passes at -0.83 and the Re-engine at +1.17.
- Every fps row fails: 10-year at Renton + Re-engine by $1.02B, 10-year at Renton by $2.35B, 7-year at Renton by $4.47B, via Embraer by $12.48-13.60B.
Fundable when the 777X turns:
- Pass: all four 10-year rows, the 7-year at Renton alone, the Re-engine alone and Do Nothing. Each holds stress net debt at $0.0B.
- Fail: the other 7-year rows ($0.7-3.1B) and via Embraer ($1.5-6.3B).
Scale only, never netted twice: the undiscounted penalties are $19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B. A 10-year fps would take 35% of base surplus over 2035-44 (52% in stress), and surplus belongs to the Board.

5. fps
- The doctrine trigger fires: NGSA is in development, and the reaction function calls for an fps no later than the next round [profile §5, row 1; B-0413].
- Following it costs at least $4.24B, above the $2B H8 cap. That is a doctrine override: the grid governs, and Malave's veto would block it anyway.
- Bias B5 (deny, then reverse) has its trigger, but displaying it is barred above the cap.
- My record points the same way: Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313, B-2305].
- Ramp and form, for 2045: the 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.96-2.33B in every column, and Embraer trails Solo by $10.96B and adds no IP we lack (Pope).

6. 787 RE-ENGINE: THE ONE LIVE CALL. HOLD.
Odds:
- I take Malave's 40% for an A350 Re-engine this round.
- Doctrine's even odds proved wrong in 2030: Airbus held. That is evidence the estimate was off [BX-1319].
- Neither colleague has grounds to go below 27.5%. The A330neo precedent shows Airbus can run a re-engine beside a new airplane.
Value:
- Gain against hold: 2.00 - 3.64 x 0.40 = +0.54, inside ε.
- On the S1/S3 blend, Do Nothing scores -1.41 and the Re-engine -0.87.
- After Malave's haircut for a later Airbus move it is about +0.18.
Tie-breaks, all toward hold:
- doing less [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- the higher worst column (-2.29 against -3.93);
- the smaller debt penalty (Malave).
The Board:
- Its Downside rule vetoes the Re-engine: S3 is -1.64, $0.64B past its -$1B limit.
- A launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
Cost of holding:
- I accept it plainly: this probably loses the option rather than deferring it.
- The next round is 2045, at about x0.37 on the gain, and H3 can close the option first.
- A 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years, with no slack.
Operations passes it on every test: zero overlap, GEnx route mature since 2033, Charleston has room. So the hold is not an operations finding.

7. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES
- H1: stays lifted on the 2030 evidence [BX-0550, BX-1299, BX-1305]. Its condition is met, not waived.
- H3, second half: in force. None is on the record, so the Re-engine was a legal order.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap; any future pairing must be shown with its slip slack.
- H5: never cancel a launched programme; nothing is launched.
- H6: not engaged.
- H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger.

8. PREMIUM LOG
- H8 doctrine premium: $0.54B for the Re-engine hold at 40% ($0.18B after the haircut).
- Objective premium: $0.
- Total: $0.54B, within $2B. It breaks below 27.5% odds; then the hold rests on the Board's rule alone.
- Board-required forgone value, logged apart and not added: +2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00 by column, $2.01B at most in S2, +0.54 expected.

9. RED LINES
None breached:
- no rate request without stable KPIs;
- no production-certification concurrency;
- no cancel;
- no fixed-price development;
- no blame on the FAA or on Airbus.
Overrides: none.

Decision year 2035, round 2 of dash-2050-cons.

WHERE WE STAND

- The 737 MAX holds at 57 a month: Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. Hold is the only rate order offered.
- Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in the stress case) and holds to 2050 in base and stress.
- The 777X and the MAX 7/10 are done. My Round-1 condition for the next airplane (debt repaired, developments finished) is met [BX-1305, B-2326].

PUBLIC RECORD
- NGSA was launched in 2030 for EIS 2037, with RR, PW and CFM selected. Airbus runs the A320 Alt plan, keeping its lines longer through the ramp.
- P&W GTF2 is ready 2036, RR UltraFan NB 2037, and the CFM/GE GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033.
- No A350 Re-engine is on the public record. Airbus says the A350 "remains our widebody focus".
- RR says UltraFan WB launches in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is announced, "if it pays".

DO NOTHING
- Scores -0.83 / -0.64 / -2.29 / -0.83 (S1 rivals hold / S2 Airbus back to the A320 base plan / S3 A350 Re-engine / S4 risk case, Delay Tactics, covert).
- With no fps launched, any Delay Tactics would be naked, so S4 equals S1.
- Narrowbody preference: 40.1% (2035), 51.7% (2038, while Airbus is short of capacity), 50.8% (2040), 34.0% (2045), 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- Operating profit matches the status quo to 2047, then runs $0.5-1.4B a year below it from 2048.

OBJECTIVES UNDER DO NOTHING
- Not met: the 50/50 split and incumbency (worst year 27.7%).
- Met: balance-sheet repair and holding it, in base and stress.
- Engine-supply enabler: not met for dual or triple sources (the MAX flies CFM only); met for three narrowbody makers in the market in 2045 and 2050.

THE GRID, AGAINST DO NOTHING (S1/S2/S3/S4)
- 787 Re-engine alone: +2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00. The best plan in S1, S2 and S4; Do Nothing is best in S3.
- 10-year fps: -4.55 / -4.55 / -4.55 / -4.64 at the new site; -4.29 / -4.24 / -4.29 / -4.35 at Renton.
- 7-year fps: -6.20 to -6.95. Via Embraer: -15.20 to -15.60.

- Renton adds +0.26 to +0.31 on a 10-year fps and +0.41 to +0.48 on a 7-year.
- The Re-engine adds +1.33 / +1.34 / -2.31 / +1.33 on top of a 10-year fps, and +0.77 / +0.77 / -2.87 / +0.77 on top of a 7-year.

MY FOUR QUESTIONS
1. Are the KPIs stable? Yes on the brief: nothing is live. Pope's seat to confirm.
2. Are market, technology and our balance sheet all ready?
   - Boeing: yes. Debt is repaired and held in stress, and the developments are finished.
   - Technology: yes, for the first time. Code 7 gives CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB at any EIS from 2042.
   - Market: no. Every fps row loses $4.24B or more against Do Nothing in every column. Under this demand case Airbus's capacity gap still flows to us until the late 2040s.
   - So not all three. Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
3. What if certification takes longer than we think? S4 is Jay's slip leg. The limit is -2.83 ($2B below Do Nothing's -0.83).
4. Is this doing less, better? Every row against Do Nothing in the same column [BX-1239].

DOCTRINE TRIGGER
The company reaction function (NGSA in development: fps no later than the next turn) fires this round. Following it would cost at least $4.24B, above the $2B H8 cap. That is a doctrine override: the grid governs. My own record points the same way: Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313, B-2305].

BOARD RISKS (guidance; not red lines). The Board says it would veto:
- re787: launch in any combination. S3 item value -1.64 alone, $0.64B past its -$1B per-item limit; -2.31 with a 10-year fps; -2.87 with a 7-year, which also overlaps 5 years.

- fps: launch_7yr. S4 is $3.70-4.95B short of the limit, and stress net debt is not held at the new site or with the Re-engine.
- fps: launch_via_embraer. -15.20 to -15.60.

It would approve: all holds (no Board items); fps_site renton with Pope's wind-down result once an fps launches; a later 10-year case.

It wants in the package:

- my expected column, and the Re-engine's value at my odds;
- Jay's buffer test and his "Fundable when the 777X turns" result, with numbers;
- Pope's KPI, supplier and strain results;
- my standing rulings on H3, H4 and H5;
- every premium logged, with any hold the Board's own tests require shown apart;
- the long-cycle erosion, to be set beside each fps row in 2045;
- no fps date.

WIDEBODY: THE 787 RE-ENGINE IS THE ONE LIVE CALL. I LEAN HOLD, BUT I HAVE NOT DECIDED.

PUBLIC

tests.name: Cash path of each bill (answers ask 3)
tests.threshold: When each bill lands (the board books it at EIS) and whether two land together. Development cash follows the brief's standard curve (5% in year 1 of 10, peak 14% in year 7). Free cash flow takes 79% of programme cash.
tests.numbers:
Do Nothing lands no bill. For a 2035 launch:
- Re-engine: $5B, cash 2035-40 at about $1B a year, booked at EIS 2040. The FCF hit is about $0.79B a year: 5.7% of base FCF ($13.8B), 8.6% of stress FCF ($9.2B).
- 10-yr fps: $60.32B, cash 2035-44, booked at EIS 2045.
  - 2035 about $3.0B; peak year 2041 about $8.4B, an FCF hit of about $6.7B (48% of base FCF, 73% of stress).
  - Over the decade, $47.7B after the 79% factor: 35% of base surplus ($138B) and 52% of stress ($92B).
- 7-yr fps: $65.00B, cash 2035-41, EIS 2042.
  - $51.4B after the factor: 53% of base surplus ($96.5B) and 80% of stress ($64.4B).
  - At the new site the peak year exceeds stress FCF (implied peak spend above about $11.6B), hence the $0.7B.
- via Embraer: $100B, EIS 2045. $79.0B after the factor: 57% of base surplus and 86% of stress.
- 10-yr + Re-engine: $51.6B (37% / 56%). Development overlaps 2038-40, 2 years, $1.2B strain undiscounted, H4-legal.
- 7-yr + Re-engine: $55.3B (57% / 86%). 5-year overlap and $3B strain: barred by H4. Stress net debt $2.0-3.1B.
- No two bills land in the same EIS year (2040 / 2042 / 2045).

HOW MUCH FALLS ON SURPLUS THE BOARD RESERVES TO ITSELF
- All of it. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029, so every dollar of programme cash after 2035 would otherwise go to the owners, and that use is the Board's call [BX-0556].
- Where a stress year's spend exceeds stress FCF, net debt rises above zero: the 7-yr at the new site, the 7-yr with the Re-engine, and via Embraer.

Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: $19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B. Already netted; never subtract them twice.

tests.name: Full cost of a slip, deferral or cancel (answers asks 4b and 4d)
tests.threshold: Cost once, in full: concessions, rework, learning curve, carrying cost. Cancel write-off = bill x years elapsed / development years, and H5 bars cancelling.
tests.numbers:
Nothing is launched, so there is no cancel or write-off. A launched Re-engine would carry a $1B write-off per year elapsed, and H5 bars cancelling it.

HOLD AS LOSS OF THE OPTION (4b): confirmed.
- The next round is 2045, for an EIS of 2050. Discounting 2040 to 2050 gives x0.368, so at most about $0.74B of the clean-column gain survives, before 2045's own odds of an A350 Re-engine.
- H3 closes the option if Airbus moves first.
- A 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-yr fps by 2 years and cannot pair with a 2045 7-yr fps (H4).
- What the hold buys: if Airbus re-engines this round (S3), we avoid the -1.64.

BASELINE WITH BUFFER (4d): yes, but a 2041 EIS is thin.
- Doctrine's slip prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (+1 to +4).
- I would baseline 2042 in public and plan to 2040 internally, a date we can meet and potentially beat [BX-0553].
- Slip cost on my reconstruction (inference): 1 year about $0.20B, 2 years about $0.39B, before off-board concessions, rework, learning curve and carrying cost [B-2349].
- A slip to 2042 still overlaps no 2045 fps: a 2045 10-yr fps has its strain window in 2048-55.

tests.name: Rate step (737)
tests.threshold: Only after stability, jointly agreed with the FAA, and only on a positive business case.
tests.numbers: Hold is the only rate_737 value offered. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. The 737 stays at 57 a month on the agreed gates, and H6 cannot engage.

tests.name: Premium in dollars, H8 (answers ask 7)
tests.threshold: Every doctrine or objective premium logged in $B; total at most $2B; name the condition that breaks it. A Board-required hold is logged apart.
tests.numbers:
- fps hold: no premium. It gains at least $4.24B in every column against the best fps row (10-yr at Renton, S2 -4.24).
- fps objective premium: confirmed at $4.24B or more, above the cap. Adding a 10-yr fps to the Re-engine costs $4.91-5.31B.
- Re-engine hold, H8 doctrine premium: $0.54B at my 40% odds on the grid's +2.00. It is about $0.18B after my haircut, and $0.18B at the CEO's even odds.
- Board-required forgone value, logged apart and not added to the above: +2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00 by column. The maximum is $2.01B (S2); the expected value at my odds is $0.54B.
- H8 total: $0.54B, within $2B.
- What breaks it: odds below 27.5% take the Re-engine past epsilon. The tie is then gone, doctrine cannot decide it, and the hold rests on the Board's Downside rule alone. The hold premium can never exceed $2.00B (S1/S4) or $2.01B (S2), so the cap breaks at most by $0.01B in S2 at zero odds.

tests.name: Long cycle (answers ask 5; advice, not a test)
tests.threshold: Put the Do Nothing erosion on the record, and state what the grid compares.
tests.numbers:
WHAT THE GRID COMPARES
- Confirmed: it compares launching now against never ('if nobody moves again'; 'assuming nobody moves after this round'), not against a 2045 launch.
- The option to launch in 2045 is not priced.

DO NOTHING EROSION
- Operating profit against the status quo: 5.7 vs 6.2 in 2048 (-0.5), -1.0 in 2052, -1.3 in 2055, -1.4 in 2060.
- Preference: 34.0% (2045), 27.7% (2050), 16.0% (2060).
- The net-debt tracker shows profit against baseline at -0.66 (2050), -1.30 (2055) and -1.43 (2060). FCF still runs at $12.66B or more and net debt at $0.0B. So this is erosion of value, not of the balance sheet.
- Do Nothing's components: narrowbody operating profit -3.64 PV; supply and demand +2.81 PV.

THE 2045 PACKAGE, BESIDE EACH fps ROW
(1) The row against Do Nothing in every column, with the risk case and my buffer test.
(2) Do Nothing's erosion year by year to 2060 and beyond, with years outside the board's 20-year window marked.
(3) The bill, its EIS (7-yr 2052, 10-yr 2055) and its cash by year against base and stress FCF.
(4) The stress net-debt peak.
(5) The long-run split each EIS implies against NGSA 2037: 35/65 for 2052, 32/68 for 2055, against Do Nothing's 16.0% in 2060.
(6) The full cost of a slip at doctrine's fps prior (+3 years central).
(7) The value of waiting for 2050, the last round.
(8) Every premium against H8.

vetoes.plan: Any fps launch this round: launch_10yr, launch_7yr or launch_via_embraer, at new_site or renton, with or without the 787 Re-engine (all 12 fps rows; options C, D, E and F)
vetoes.ground:
Buffer test (slip leg). S4 must be no lower than -2.83 (Do Nothing's -0.83 less $2B).
- C, 10-yr at Renton + Re-engine: -3.85, short by $1.02B.
- 10-yr + Re-engine: -4.14, short by $1.31B.
- D, 10-yr at Renton: -5.18, short by $2.35B; at new site -5.47, short by $2.64B.
- E, 7-yr at Renton: -7.30, short by $4.47B. The other 7-yr rows are short by $3.70-4.95B; the two with the Re-engine are also barred by H4.
- F, best via Embraer row: -15.31, short by $12.48B; the others by $12.77-13.60B.
The team rule (teams.md section 9) makes this veto binding. The CEO must revise within it and has no override.

vetoes.plan: re787: launch (option B, with fps hold)
vetoes.ground:
Advice only, not a veto: it passes my buffer test (S4 +1.17, $4.00B clear). Stress net debt is held at $0.0B and it overlaps no development.
- At my roughly 40% odds of an A350 Re-engine it is worth +0.54, a tie. After a haircut for a later Airbus move it is worth about +0.18.
- The higher worst column (-2.29 against -3.93) breaks the tie toward hold.
- The Board's Downside rule (S3 -1.64, $0.64B past its -$1B limit) points the same way.
- My profile's veto on the Re-engine in the first two turns (Charleston capex) applied to 2026-31 and does not bind in 2035.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
FOR THE 787 RE-ENGINE
- I would take it to the Board as one tested case, all four columns shown, given real grounds to put the odds of an A350 Re-engine this round below about 27%. Examples: a public no to an A350 Re-engine, or Airbus's widebody engineering visibly committed to NGSA and the A350F. Below 27% the gain clears epsilon on the grid; below about 13% it still clears after my haircut for a later Airbus move.
- Odds alone cannot clear the Board's Downside rule: S3 stays at -1.64, $0.64B past its -$1B. The Board would have to relax that rule, or the S3 loss would have to shrink below $1B.
- An A350 Re-engine on the public record closes the question under H3.

FOR THE fps
- I would lift my veto in a later round whose grid has the best fps row no more than $2B below Do Nothing in the risk-case column, beating Do Nothing by more than epsilon in the expected column, with stress net debt held.
- In that case I would back the 10-year ramp at Renton, which has the smaller bill and penalty and holds stress net debt at $0.0B, with an engine code that gives three sources.
- The Do Nothing erosion (16.0% preference by 2060, profit $1.4B a year below the status quo) is what could bring such a grid in 2045.

THE CONDITION ON MY NUMBERS
These numbers hold barring a live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem. They also hold barring any change to the stress-case cash path the brief shows.
cfo.memo:
Kelly, I ran the slip leg as the baseline. Do Nothing scores -0.83 in S4, so the limit is -2.83. Do Nothing passes, $2.00B clear, and the 787 Re-engine alone at +1.17, $4.00B clear. All twelve fps rows fail. The closest, the 10-year at Renton with the Re-engine, misses by $1.02B at -3.85. The 10-year at Renton alone misses by $2.35B, the 7-year at Renton by $4.47B, via Embraer by $12.48B or more. Under the team rule, that is a binding veto on any fps launch this round.

"Fundable when the 777X turns" passes for every 10-year row and the 7-year at Renton alone, with stress net debt at $0.0B. It fails for the other 7-year rows ($0.7-3.1B) and via Embraer ($1.5-6.3B). Debt is repaired, so every bill now comes out of surplus the Board reserves to itself: a 10-year fps takes about 35% of it over 2035-44, 52% in stress.

The Re-engine is the one live call, and I don't veto it. My finance read puts an A350 Re-engine at about 40%, not below 27%. That makes it worth +0.54, a tie, before I haircut the +2.00 by about $0.6B for a later Airbus move. The higher worst column (-2.29 against -3.93) breaks the tie toward hold, in line with the Board's Downside rule. I log $0.54B, inside the cap; the Board-required forgone value, up to $2.01B, sits apart.

That holds barring an A350 Re-engine on the record. It's a baseline we can meet and potentially beat.

tests.name: KPI gate for the Rate Increase (my veto) [doctrine]
tests.threshold: No Rate Increase while a quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. Steps of 5 a month, at least 6 months apart, each after 2-3 months of stable KPIs and an FAA Capstone review. Supplier readiness is a hard gate.
tests.numbers: Answer to ask 1. The brief reports no live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem (the board has no injects), and the bulletin carries our 2030 statement that the KPIs are stable. The 737 holds at 57 a month (Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line), 684 a year, on the FAA-agreed gates [BX-1271]. The brief gives no KPI series, so this rests on its no-live-problem record. rate_737: hold is the only value offered, so no Rate Increase is on the order sheet: my veto has nothing to act on, and H6 cannot engage. Confirmed.

tests.name: Supplier readiness: LEAP-1B and fragile suppliers [doctrine]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, and engine supply that covers the current rate.
tests.numbers: Answer to ask 1. 684 MAX a year needs 1,368 LEAP-1B engines a year, unchanged since 2030; no rate step asks for more. The brief shows no supply-chain problem, and CFM's public line is to 'deliver those engines on time and support that fleet'. Watch item, not a problem: Airbus has long-term A320neo engine slots with CFM and P&W for its longer A320 tail, and takes NGSA engines from CFM. CFM therefore supplies the MAX (sole source), the A320 tail and NGSA from 2037 at the same time. Doctrine: beyond 47 a month the supply chain binds [B-2340], and the step to 52 once strained CFM supply [B-1449]. Response: keep the CFM allocation reviews running [BX-1264, BX-1325]; measure allocation, and attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure [B-1923]. Fragile suppliers: the brief is silent. Doctrine keeps them funded and producing above our rate [B-2330, BX-1243].

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: 787 Re-engine, EIS 2040 [record, applied by inference; slip prior is doctrine]
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read the risk-case column (S4, Delay Tactics) and say how much of the value depends on the nominal date.
tests.numbers: S4 +1.17 equals S1 +1.17. Delay Tactics act only from fps EIS, so the risk case does not touch the Re-engine (item value +2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00). The board prices no Re-engine slip. The doctrine slip prior for a major derivative is +2 years central (range +1 to +4). Shifting the whole item at a 10.5% WACC (inference), the S1 item is +1.81 at a 1-year slip, +1.64 at 2 years (x0.819) and +1.34 at 4 years (x0.671). It stays positive in S1, S2 and S4 across the slip range; at the worst slip about 33% of the S1 value rides on the nominal date. S3 (-1.64) is the A350's risk, not a delivery risk. Engine route (answer to ask 3): the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, seven years of fleet time before a 2040 EIS. That is the durability-first route [BX-1298, B-2304]. If Rolls-Royce launches UltraFan WB on our announcement ('if it pays'), it is ready in 2041, a year after EIS, so it is off the critical path.

tests.name: On-time, predictable delivery: fps in any form (EIS 2045 on the 10-year, 2042 on the 7-year) [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: The plan's EIS can be delivered as stated. Read S4 against the nominal column.
tests.numbers: The board's risk case costs the fps rows only $0.00-0.09B (S4 against S1): 10-year -5.47 against -5.38; 10-year at Renton + Re-engine -3.85 against -3.79; 7-year at Renton -7.30 in both. The value is negative before any slip. Every fps item loses $4.24-15.60B against hold in every column, and S4 runs from -3.85 to -16.43. The doctrine clean-sheet slip prior is +3 years central (range +2 to +5), and the board does not price it. On that prior a 2045 EIS becomes 2048 (2047-2050), which against NGSA 2037 moves the long-run split from 42/58 to 39/61 (rules.md: 1 pp per year of lead). Technology passes for the first time: GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) are ready for any EIS from 2042. The test fails on value at the nominal date, not on engines. Answer to ask 6: this is my flag against any fps launch this round.

tests.name: Two-front strain: 787 Re-engine alone, and its sequencing ahead of a 2045 fps [doctrine; board arithmetic]
tests.threshold: A Solo fps and the Re-engine overlap at most 2 years (H4). Strain = $3B x overlap / 5, with the fps window from EIS-7 to EIS and the Re-engine window from EIS-5 to EIS. One major development at a time.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 2. A 2035-40 Re-engine alone has 0 years of overlap and $0 of strain. The 777X (in service 2027) and the MAX 7/10 (delivering since 2026) are done, so it would be the one major development in work while we sustain both families [B-0341].
Overlaps confirmed:
- with a 2035 10-year fps (window 2038-45): 2 years, $1.2B undiscounted, H4-legal;
- with a 2035 7-year fps (2035-42): 5 years, $3.0B, barred;
- with any 2045 fps (7-year 2045-52, 10-year 2048-55): 0 years, and still 0 with a 4-year Re-engine slip (2039-44).
Feathering in [B-1393]: yes. A 2035 Re-engine rolls off in 2040, five years before a 2045 launch. A 2045 Re-engine (2045-50) would overlap a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) and bar a 2045 7-year (5 years, $3.0B).
On the grid, overlap costs the Re-engine $0.67B in S1 beside a 10-year fps (+1.33 against +2.00 alone) and $1.23B beside a 7-year (+0.77). The 10-year pair is legal but has no slack: a 1-year Re-engine slip makes it 3 years ($1.8B), and the doctrine's 2-year central slip makes it 4 years ($2.4B).

tests.name: Two-front strain: 7-year fps with the 787 Re-engine in the same round [doctrine; board arithmetic]
tests.threshold: Overlap at most 2 years (H4).
tests.numbers: The fps window 2035-42 against the Re-engine's 2035-40 gives 5 years and $3.0B of strain undiscounted. H4 bars it. The Re-engine item falls to +0.77 / +0.77 / -2.87 / +0.77. Stress-case net debt is not held: $2.8B ($3.1B in S3) at the new site and $2.0B at Renton.

tests.name: Ramp choice, 7- or 10-year [inference]
tests.threshold: Which ramp operations can deliver predictably, with the strain and EIS of each.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 5: operations backs the 10-year ramp.
- 10-year: EIS 2045 on a 2035 launch. Strain is 2 years and $1.2B with a same-round Re-engine (legal). Stress net debt is held at $0.0B in all four 10-year rows. Peak cash is about $8.44B, in 2041.
- 7-year: EIS 2042. Strain is 5 years and $3.0B with the Re-engine (barred). Stress net debt is $0.7B at the new site; it holds only at Renton without the Re-engine. It needs about $9.29B a year, above stress free cash flow of $9.19B.
- The 10-year leads the 7-year by $1.96-2.33B in every column ($2.52-2.89B with the Re-engine), and has the higher worst column (-6.58 at Renton against -8.76).

tests.name: Invest or partner on IP: fps via Embraer [record, applied by inference]
tests.threshold: Solo where Boeing owns the airframe IP. Via Embraer only if the partner adds capital, capacity or IP that Boeing lacks.
tests.numbers: Answer to ask 5. Via Embraer trails the Solo 10-year by $10.96B in every column, or $11.46-11.47B with the Re-engine. It has the same 2045 EIS and the same three engine sources in 2050, for a $100B bill against $60.32B. It gives no strain relief: the Re-engine is worth +0.83 beside it, against +1.33 beside the Solo 10-year (S1), and -2.81 in S3. Stress net debt peaks at $1.5-6.3B and is never held. Embraer adds no capital, capacity or IP that Boeing lacks on this board; it takes value from an airframe whose IP is ours. Solo passes.

tests.name: Capacity follows demand [one remark; inference]
tests.threshold: Back a Rate Increase only where it adds value against the same plan without it in the expected column.
tests.numbers: No Rate Increase row is on this round's grid (it was a 2030-only lever), so there is nothing to score. For the record, visible demand now exceeds MAX capacity. At 684 a year, the Do Nothing waiting backlog is 19 (2036), 204 (2039), 540 (2041), 432 (2045) and 265 (2047), and 0 by 2050 as preference falls to 27.7%. No order on this board adds narrowbody capacity before an fps. The backlog bears on any Renton wind-down (last test).

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion: Do Nothing and the 787 Re-engine [record, applied by inference]
tests.threshold: Each bill and its timing as a number; net debt held at or below $0 in the stress case; cash out returns value.

tests.name: Working capital and cash conversion: every fps form [record, applied by inference]
tests.threshold: As above.
tests.numbers:
10-year: $60.32B over 2035-45, peaking at about $8.44B (14%) in 2041, which is 61% of base and 92% of stress free cash flow. Net debt holds, but the item is -4.24 to -4.64 against hold.
7-year: $65.00B over 2035-42, about $9.29B a year (101% of stress free cash flow). Stress net debt is $0.7B at the new site and $2.0-3.1B with the Re-engine. The item is -6.20 to -6.95.
Via Embraer: $100B, peaking at about $14B (152% of stress free cash flow). Stress peak $1.5-6.3B. The item is -15.20 to -15.60.
Undiscounted penalties, for scale only: $19.1B, $22.0B and $52.5B; the grid already nets them. On this board the cash goes out and the value does not come back.

tests.name: Re-engine readiness: Charleston, engine route, workforce, fragile suppliers [doctrine plus inference]
tests.threshold: Supplier readiness is a hard gate: no live supply-chain problem, an engine route ready by EIS, and capacity for the share gain.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 3.
- Charleston: the 787 builds 100 a year on the board (8.3 a month). One point of share a year from a 2040 EIS adds about 1.7 aircraft a year, reaching 108.5 a year (9.0 a month) in 2045, 117 (9.7) in 2050 and 134 (11.2) in 2060. That is within a footprint being doubled for rates in the teens [B-2336, BX-1317].
- Engine: the GEnx upgrade route, mature since 2033; durability first [BX-1298].
- Trained workforce (not on the board): nothing has been in development since the 777X and MAX 7/10 finished, so one derivative fits the one-at-a-time rule [B-0341].
- Fragile suppliers: the brief is silent; keep them funded and hot [B-2330, BX-1243].

tests.name: 2045 fps case readiness: Renton wind-down and engine code (prepare, do not order) [rules arithmetic plus doctrine]
tests.threshold: Renton wind-down follows the fps ramp; a second or third engine source ready by EIS.
tests.numbers:
Answer to ask 4. With the fps on hold, the site has no effect this round (item value 0).
Renton: its MAX lines wind down as the fps ramps, and the Everett North Line carries on at up to 15 a month (180 a year). Readiness is conditional: the wind-down must follow the fps ramp (rate 50 about 4 years after EIS), never lead it. Under Do Nothing the MAX delivers 684 a year to 2047 against a waiting backlog of 432 (2045) and 265 (2047), and still 346 a year in 2055, almost twice Everett's 180. The full $3.0B saving needs only 3 years' notice (by 2052 for a 2045 10-year, EIS 2055; by 2049 for a 2045 7-year), so the launch round is early enough.
Engines: GTF2 enters service on NGSA in 2037 and UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, so by a 2052-55 EIS each has about 15 years of fleet time. That proves durability in service, which is what customers ask for [BX-1298, B-2304], and fits the makers' commitments (P&W proves durability before EIS; Rolls-Royce does not compress maturity). Code 7 gives three sources (CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB) and meets the enabler. Codes 5 and 6 give two. Code 3 keeps today's single-source exposure. Code 7 with NGSA's Code 7 is an allowed pair. Engine choice is not my test and never a veto ground. Certifying three installations is unpriced engineering load; I would pace it and avoid concurrency with production (inference) [BX-1263].

ops.memo:
Three results, ranked. My record is Global Services, not Commercial Airplanes. The KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine.

First and foremost, on-time predictable delivery [BX-1331]. The brief reports no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem, and hold is the only rate order, so my KPI veto has nothing to act on. At 57 a month we build 684 a year, and capacity now binds: the waiting backlog peaks at 540 in 2041. LEAP-1B is our single source while CFM also feeds Airbus's longer A320 tail and NGSA, so allocation reviews stay on: a watch item, not a problem.

Second, engineering capacity: one development at a time [B-0341]. The 787 Re-engine passes every operations test: zero overlap, an engine route mature since 2033, about $1B a year, net debt held in stress. Launched now, it rolls off in 2040, ahead of any 2045 fps [B-1393]. Left to 2045, it overlaps a 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B) and bars a 7-year. The launch turns on the A350, where I have no record. We see about $0.36B of expected value for every 10 points of odds. Break-even is 55%, and a gain above $1B needs odds below 27.5%. I recommend hold under doctrine's ε rule; that is not an operations finding.

And finally, disciplined profitable growth [BX-1327]. No fps passes: every launch loses $4.24B or more against hold. Operations backs the 10-year ramp, $1.96-2.33B ahead of the 7-year. Embraer trails Solo by $10.96B and adds no IP or capacity we lack [BX-1330].

other_moves.move: Hold the 737 MAX at 57 a month on the FAA-agreed KPI gates
other_moves.detail: That is Renton's three lines at 47 plus the Everett North Line, 684 a year. No Rate Increase is on the order sheet this round. Pope's KPI check passes: no quality, FAA or supply-chain problem is live. The waiting backlog under Do Nothing reaches 540 in 2041. We tell customers honest delivery dates rather than push the line. That is stability over share, and its trigger is present [BX-1274, BX-1259, BX-1271].

other_moves.move: Keep improving the 787 and growing Charleston; work with GE to bring the GEnx upgrade to 787 customers
other_moves.detail: Widebody growth comes from Charleston capacity on today's 787 [BX-1317, B-2336]. The GEnx upgrade is CFM/GE's own programme, ready since 2033. This is not a 787 Re-engine order. The board does not price it.

other_moves.move: Keep the 787 Re-engine study warm on the GEnx route; launch nothing
other_moves.detail: Durability first [BX-1298]. It comes back in 2045 only if no A350 Re-engine is on the public record (H3, second half). It must also be H4-legal against any 2045 fps with Pope's slip slack shown: a 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years with no slack and cannot pair with a 2045 7-year. If it is ever launched: a public EIS with buffer (Malave: 2042 public, 2040 internal) and risk-share terms, never fixed price [BX-1262, BX-1304].

other_moves.move: Prepare the 2045 fps case; do not announce it
other_moves.detail: The 10-year ramp, at Renton, with Pope's MAX wind-down plan. She signs it only once the fps ramp covers MAX demand above Everett's 180 a year. Code 7 (CFM + GTF2 + UltraFan NB) is under test. It replaces my Code 3 inference, which was Low. Three installations are paced so certification never runs concurrent with production [BX-1263]. Development terms are cost-plus or risk-share. The package carries Malave's eight items: the row against Do Nothing in every column with the buffer test; the Do Nothing erosion year by year to 2060; the bill and its cash by year against base and stress FCF; the stress net-debt peak; the long-run split each EIS implies (35/65 for 2052, 32/68 for 2055); the full cost of a slip at +3 years; the value of waiting to 2050; and every premium. No date before launch [B-2315].

other_moves.move: Keep fragile suppliers funded and hot; keep the LEAP-1B allocation reviews running
other_moves.detail: Cash for readiness [BX-1243, B-2330]. CFM supplies the MAX as sole source, plus Airbus's longer A320 tail and NGSA from 2037, so we measure allocation [BX-1264, BX-1325]. We attribute nothing to Airbus before exposure (company doctrine [B-1923]).

decision.public_statement:
Five years ago I said we'd do a new airplane when the market and the technology and we're ready. That's still the test, and I'll give you a straight read on it.

We're ready on our end. The factories are stable, the 777X and the MAX 7 and 10 are flying with customers, and the balance sheet is where it should be. The technology is moving too. There will be good new engines out there. The market case for us isn't there yet. So we are not launching a new airplane this year, and I'm not going to give you a date for one. Another company's schedule doesn't set ours. When we do launch, you'll get an entry-into-service date we know we can meet, with room built into it. We'll share the development risk sensibly with our partners. We won't take a fixed-price bet on it.

We turned the big ship. The job now is to keep it steady, not to swing the wheel to chase a headline.

On the 737 we're holding at 57 a month, on the gates we agreed with the FAA. Our customers want more airplanes than we're building, and I understand that. I'd rather give a customer an honest delivery date than run an unstable line.

On widebodies, the 787 is the most efficient airplane in its class. We'll keep making it better with our partners at GE, and we'll keep growing Charleston.

The financials will follow our production performance. I'd much rather be a month late than go a month early.
decision.rationale:
DECISION: Do Nothing in every field.
- fps hold, fps_engine_code null, fps_site new_site (no effect while the fps holds), rate_737 hold, re787 hold.
- No order differs from the default, so nothing goes to the Board.
- My record drove the narrowbody calls. On the 787 Re-engine, doctrine (profile §7, as Malave updated it) and the Board's Downside rule drove the call, not my record: my evidence on Airbus is Low.

1. TEAM RULE
- Malave's buffer-test veto on all 12 fps rows binds, and I accept it. I have no override.
- Pope's KPI veto has nothing to act on: no Rate Increase is offered and nothing is live.
- Neither colleague flagged a red-line breach.
- Everything else is my call. Both memos recommend these same orders.

2. MY FOUR QUESTIONS
(1) Are the KPIs stable? Yes. No live quality, FAA or supply-chain problem; LEAP-1B at 684 a year is a watch item only.
(2) Are market, technology and the balance sheet all ready?
- Boeing: yes. Net debt has been $0.0B since 2029 (2030 in stress), and the developments are finished.
- Technology: yes, for the first time. Code 7 gives three sources at any EIS from 2042.
- Market: no. Every fps row loses $4.24B or more against Do Nothing in every column.
- Two of three is not three [BX-1296, BX-1303].
(3) What if certification takes longer than we think? I read Malave's slip leg, S4, as the baseline: limit -2.83.
(4) Is this doing less, better? Yes. Do Nothing is the plan with the least to execute, and nothing beats it by more than ε in my expected column [BX-1239].

3. TESTED CASE (S1 / S2 / S3 / S4)
- Submitted, Do Nothing: -0.83 / -0.64 / -2.29 / -0.83. S4 equals S1 because Delay Tactics against no fps are naked.
- Rejected rows, against Do Nothing:
  - Re-engine alone: +1.17 / +1.37 / -3.93 / +1.17 (+2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00).
  - Best fps, 10-year at Renton + Re-engine: -3.79 / -3.54 / -8.89 / -3.85 (-2.96 / -2.90 / -6.60 / -3.02).
  - 10-year at Renton: -5.12 / -4.88 / -6.58 / -5.18 (-4.29 / -4.24 / -4.29 / -4.35).
  - 7-year at Renton: -7.30 / -6.84 / -8.76 / -7.30.
  - Best via Embraer: -15.25 / -15.01 / -20.35 / -15.31.
- I checked every cell against the brief (work/r2_ceo_decide_calc.py). Malave's figures match.

4. MALAVE: BINDING ON THE fps, ADVICE ON THE REST
Buffer test (S4 no lower than -2.83):
- Do Nothing passes at -0.83 and the Re-engine at +1.17.
- Every fps row fails: 10-year at Renton + Re-engine by $1.02B, 10-year at Renton by $2.35B, 7-year at Renton by $4.47B, via Embraer by $12.48-13.60B.
Fundable when the 777X turns:
- Pass: all four 10-year rows, the 7-year at Renton alone, the Re-engine alone and Do Nothing. Each holds stress net debt at $0.0B.
- Fail: the other 7-year rows ($0.7-3.1B) and via Embraer ($1.5-6.3B).
Scale only, never netted twice: the undiscounted penalties are $19.1B / $22.0B / $52.5B / $0.6B. A 10-year fps would take 35% of base surplus over 2035-44 (52% in stress), and surplus belongs to the Board.

5. fps
- The doctrine trigger fires: NGSA is in development, and the reaction function calls for an fps no later than the next round [profile §5, row 1; B-0413].
- Following it costs at least $4.24B, above the $2B H8 cap. That is a doctrine override: the grid governs, and Malave's veto would block it anyway.
- Bias B5 (deny, then reverse) has its trigger, but displaying it is barred above the cap.
- My record points the same way: Airbus's timeline does not set our date [B-2313, B-2305].
- Ramp and form, for 2045: the 10-year beats the 7-year by $1.96-2.33B in every column, and Embraer trails Solo by $10.96B and adds no IP we lack (Pope).

6. 787 RE-ENGINE: THE ONE LIVE CALL. HOLD.
Odds:
- I take Malave's 40% for an A350 Re-engine this round.
- Doctrine's even odds proved wrong in 2030: Airbus held. That is evidence the estimate was off [BX-1319].
- Neither colleague has grounds to go below 27.5%. The A330neo precedent shows Airbus can run a re-engine beside a new airplane.
Value:
- Gain against hold: 2.00 - 3.64 x 0.40 = +0.54, inside ε.
- On the S1/S3 blend, Do Nothing scores -1.41 and the Re-engine -0.87.
- After Malave's haircut for a later Airbus move it is about +0.18.
Tie-breaks, all toward hold:
- doing less [BX-1239];
- the higher-confidence plan [BX-0548];
- the higher worst column (-2.29 against -3.93);
- the smaller debt penalty (Malave).
The Board:
- Its Downside rule vetoes the Re-engine: S3 is -1.64, $0.64B past its -$1B limit.
- A launch I expect to be vetoed is not one well-founded case.
Cost of holding:
- I accept it plainly: this probably loses the option rather than deferring it.
- The next round is 2045, at about x0.37 on the gain, and H3 can close the option first.
- A 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years, with no slack.
Operations passes it on every test: zero overlap, GEnx route mature since 2033, Charleston has room. So the hold is not an operations finding.

7. RULINGS ON THE HARD RULES
- H1: stays lifted on the 2030 evidence [BX-0550, BX-1299, BX-1305]. Its condition is met, not waived.
- H3, second half: in force. None is on the record, so the Re-engine was a legal order.
- H4: at most 2 years of overlap; any future pairing must be shown with its slip slack.
- H5: never cancel a launched programme; nothing is launched.
- H6: not engaged.
- H2 cannot bind, and H7 has no trigger.

8. PREMIUM LOG
- H8 doctrine premium: $0.54B for the Re-engine hold at 40% ($0.18B after the haircut).
- Objective premium: $0.
- Total: $0.54B, within $2B. It breaks below 27.5% odds; then the hold rests on the Board's rule alone.
- Board-required forgone value, logged apart and not added: +2.00 / +2.01 / -1.64 / +2.00 by column, $2.01B at most in S2, +0.54 expected.

9. RED LINES
None breached:
- no rate request without stable KPIs;
- no production-certification concurrency;
- no cancel;
- no fixed-price development;
- no blame on the FAA or on Airbus.
Overrides: none.

1. My memo found that the 787 Re-engine passes every operations test: zero overlap, a GEnx route mature since 2033, about $1B a year and net debt held under stress. The CEO's hold rests on the A350 odds (40%, a gain of +0.54 inside ε) and on the Board's Downside rule (S3 -1.64). It does not rest on an operations finding, and his rationale says so correctly. The cost of holding is on the record. A 2045 Re-engine overlaps a 2045 10-year fps by 2 years ($1.2B), with no slack for slip, and it cannot pair with a 2045 7-year fps (5 years, $3.0B, barred by H4).
2. Every fps row loses $4.24B or more against Do Nothing, and the CEO holds them all. The 10-year ramp stays the one operations backs, $1.96-2.33B ahead of the 7-year. Via Embraer trails Solo by $10.96B and adds no IP Boeing lacks [BX-1330].
3. The 2045 preparation takes my two conditions. The Renton wind-down is signed only once the fps ramp covers MAX demand above Everett's 180 a year. Certification of the three Code 7 installations is paced, with no concurrency with production [BX-1263].

Basis: the KPI, strain and supplier gates are doctrine. Delivery, IP and cash conversion are my BGS record from 2022, applied to airplanes by inference, and my confidence on airplanes is very low.

airbus.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. We are taking it through certification on the clock of maturity: no test will be compressed to hold a date, and no engine will enter service before it is mature. Our engine partners CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are maturing their engines for the aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp-up. That ramp-up will be disciplined and controlled. Through the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we are securing the engines, structures and materials our own ramp-up needs. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
airbus.rationale:
ROUND 2 (2035). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Orders: ngsa hold (EIS 2037), engine code 7, a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. Every order is at its default, so the package carries no Board item. No override is used; the budget of one per game is intact.

Order of argument:
- the five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081];
- a disciplined and controlled ramp into service, with no certification compressed [AX-0010, A-0225];
- preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006];
- what the Board can carry: one programme inside the $5.2B line [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both; with or without a Re-engine; on either plan):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar; both is a second move.
  - One move against the default: -15.69 / +0.21 / -0.19 / -0.06 / +0.21 / -15.68 / +0.21. It never reaches $1B.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) STANDS. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off.
- Every NGSA cancel row:
  - Rules 2 and 7.
  - It carries a $25.37B write-off.
  - Item against hold: -27.07 / -23.72 / -24.26 / -21.94 / -23.72 / -27.07 / -23.73.
  - It drops the 2050 engine metric to 2 sources.

2. COLLEAGUES' TESTS ON THE REMAINING ROWS
- Alt + hold (default): passes every test in both memos.
- Alt + A350 Re-engine (2035):
  - Toepfer fails it on peak cash: $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.674B in 2035-36, against $5.2B. The strain alone gives $5.674B, so no structure cures it.
  - He also fails it on robustness: -1.20 / -1.21 in S6 and S7.
  - This is a binding soft veto, not a red line: rule 6 passes, with one launch and a 2-year overlap.
  - Wagner passes it at the limit and raises no veto. His flags: the overlap coincides with three NGSA engine certification campaigns, and a 2040 EIS lands on NGSA's steepest ramp step (96, 308, then 585 a year).
- Base + hold: Toepfer fails it on robustness (-2.23 to -2.60 in every column). Binding soft veto. Wagner reports no safety or quality finding that only base resolves.
- Base + Re-engine: fails both of Toepfer's tests above.

3. SURVIVOR AND CHOICE
The only survivor is the default: +14.09 / +9.33 / +10.26 / +6.71 / +9.33 / +13.60 / +8.85.
- Positive in all seven columns; the worst is S4 at +6.71.
- Probability-weighted at my weights: +11.92.
- It is also the best surviving row in every column, so the choice does not rest on the scenario call.
- The tie-breaks do not apply.

4. THE ONE REAL QUESTION: THE A350 RE-ENGINE IN THE LAST YEAR OF THE 2033-35 WINDOW
Its item is +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.55 / -1.20 / -1.21, or +1.27 probability-weighted. On the team rule's arithmetic alone, +1.54 in S1 would clear the $1B override bar. I do not override, for four reasons:
- (a) The Board has said it would veto on liquidity, and I hold no override against the Board.
- (b) On a Qualified Majority item the Board's override review requires the plan to stay ahead in the worst plausible column. It is $1.21B behind in S7.
- (c) The breach is $1.474B a year for two years, against a line that protects net cash and the A+/A1 rating [AX-0022]. The strain component alone breaks it, so it cannot be phased away.
- (d) The Board's guidance is explicit: nothing else enters development until NGSA spend rolls off.

Toepfer discloses that his robustness failure rests on the item reading, and the row test would pass (worst S7 +7.64). His veto stands on cash alone.

I accept, on the record, the cost of waiting:
- On today's grid, about +1.54 is forgone in S1-S5, and -1.20 / -1.21 is avoided in S6-S7.
- Rounds are 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050, so the next window is 2045 (EIS 2050, no overlap, $1.0B a year, passes cash).
- Its value is not on today's grid. Toepfer's pure-discount pre-read is about +0.71, below $1B, so the 2045 case is not assured.
- If Boeing re-engines the 787 first, rule 3 closes it.

This is a failed binding test plus a Board veto, not a doctrine premium.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
There is no Board item this round. ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none and a320_plan alt (now the current plan) are all defaults. Engine code 7 is unchanged and has no payoff effect.

For the record, the items not taken:
- rea350 launch:
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: fail (cash, robustness).
  - Wagner: pass at the limit.
  - Grid: +1.54 to -1.21.
  - Board: veto.
- a320_plan base:
  - Pillars: no finding calls for it.
  - Toepfer: fail.
  - Wagner: no case.
  - Grid: -2.23 to -2.60.
- delay_tactics (any): fails pillars and rule 4. Grid: -15.69 to +0.21.
- ngsa cancel: fails rule 7. Grid: -21.94 to -27.07.

6. CASH (Toepfer's figures)
- NGSA is $5.074B in 2035 and 2036; at most $5.174B with the Alt pre-EIS cap used in full.
- Alt pre-EIS spend plus long-term-agreement prepayments must stay at or below $0.126B in total each year. If the agreements need more than $0.026B, the Alt spend moves after EIS.
- NGSA spend is nil from 2037; Alt runs at $0.094B a year over 2037-44.
- Net cash on the brief's profit path (Toepfer's method; an inference):
  - 48% payout: $5.83B at end-2034 and $3.18B at end-2036.
  - 30%: $13.28B and $13.76B.
  - 50%: $5.00B and $2.00B.
  - Round-1 flat-FCF case: $0.37B and -$4.83B.
- Positive at any payout within 30-50%, with no equity raise. Any new buyback authority comes only after 2036.
- The debt penalty (-0.53) is in the grid.

7. ENGINES AND SUPPLY (Wagner's figures)
- Code 7 (CFM + P&W GTF2 + RR UltraFan NB) gives 3 / 3 in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and appears in no barred pair.
- Certification is sequenced: CFM is the anchor, GTF2 has 1 year of slack, UltraFan NB has none and goes in only when mature.
- If UltraFan NB slips, CFM + GTF2 remain and NGSA does not wait.
- The 2038-40 trough (832-886 aircraft a year) is planned, not a shortage. We protect it with our own supply measures and do not chase rate.
- I attribute the binding constraint to engines: P&W carries the GTF tail, the Advantage kit and the GTF2 ramp at once, and CFM carries LEAP-1B, the A320neo tail and NGSA.

8. OWN CLOCK
Boeing's statement ('ready on our end', an EIS 'with room built into it') played no part. Any fps launched now enters service in 2042 or later, behind NGSA in 2037.

One tie-break note, recorded as in round 1: a one-year slip would take EIS to 2038, outside 2035-37 but inside the public window. No re-timing order exists, so no alternative is available.

9. CONFIDENCE
My own decision style is rated Low confidence. Toepfer's and Wagner's tests are role-derived (Low and Very low).

FCF before NGSA = $5.228B + 0.667 x (OP - 3.6), where 0.667 = FY2025 FCF / EBIT Adjusted (4,753 / 7,128). The brief's operating profit runs from $3.6B in 2026 to $7.6B in 2034, $54.2B in total. That gives FCF of $7.10B in 2030, $7.90B in 2034-35 and $7.96B in 2036. Dividend = payout x net income, with net income = $5.743B (EUR 5,221m) + 0.732 x (OP - 3.6), before any NGSA charge (the conservative case). NGSA is fully incremental at $5.074B a year. Results: 48% payout: net cash $5.83B at end-2034 and $3.18B at end-2036 ($2.98B with the Alt cap). 30%: $13.28B and $13.76B. 50%: $5.00B and $2.00B. Net cash stays positive at any payout within 30-50%; at 48-50% it falls $10-11B over 2030-36. No equity raise in any case. Any new buyback authority comes only after NGSA spend rolls off in 2036. State support counts as upside only. The debt penalty is in the grid at -0.53.

cfo.memo:
Round 2 (2035), on the brief's grid. Recommended: ngsa hold to EIS 2037, engine code 7 (I defer to Lars), a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. No Board item.

Peak cash. NGSA's last two development years: $35.52B / 7 = $5.074B in 2035 and 2036, against the $5.2B line (FCF EUR 4,753m at $1.10). Headroom $0.126B; $5.174B with the Alt pre-EIS cap used in full, leaving $0.026B for any prepayment. NGSA spend is nil from 2037; the Alt $0.75B runs 2037-44 at $0.094B a year. Pass.

A350 Re-engine now. $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.674B in 2035-36. The strain alone gives $5.674B, so no phasing cures it; state support counts as upside only. Two-year overlap, one launch: rule 6 holds. The item is +1.54 in S1 and -1.21 in S7: inside the Board's -$2B line, short of $1B in S6-S7. Peak cash and robustness fail: a binding soft veto. Margin over the hold row: +1.54 in S1, +1.27 probability-weighted. Any override is the CEO's call.

2045. No overlap: $1.0B a year, a pass. Its value is not on today's grid.

Net cash. On the brief's profit path, a 48% payout takes net cash from $13.4B to $5.8B at end-2034 and $3.2B at end-2036; at 30%, $13.3B and $13.8B. The round-1 flat case gave $0.4B and -$4.8B. No equity raise; new buyback authority after 2036.

Deleted: any Delay Tactics (naked $48.32B fine, rule 4); NGSA cancel (rule 7, $25.37B write-off); the base plan (-2.23 to -2.60).

tests.name: NGSA certification and readiness for EIS 2037 [Faury ask 1]
tests.threshold: Rule 1: NGSA EIS no earlier than the 2035 technology-ready year. The production system and a wing buildable at rate must mature with the aircraft. No certification test is compressed to hold the date. An engine that is not ready by EIS is dropped, never rushed (rule 8 cannot bind).
tests.numbers: EIS is 2037, two years after the 2035 technology-ready year. Engine readiness by EIS, from the bulletin: CFM is always available (LEAP derivative). P&W GTF2 is ready in 2036, with 1 year of slack. RR UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, with 0 years of slack. The brief reports no engine or technology maturity slip. If UltraFan NB slips past 2037, code 7 fits CFM + P&W GTF2: 2 sources at EIS, and NGSA does not wait. The public window, 'the second half of the 2030s' (2035-39), covers a slip of up to 2 years. The board has no re-timing order, so the internal target stays 2037. No test is to be compressed for any maker.

tests.name: Engine maturity slip
tests.threshold: If the brief reports a slip, re-time NGSA so that EIS stays at or after the new technology-ready year. Never accelerate, never cancel.
tests.numbers: The brief reports no slip. GTF2 (2036) and UltraFan NB (2037) are on their public dates. UltraFan NB carries the only zero-slack date on the programme, so it is the item to watch at every safety review.

tests.name: Engine supply: NGSA engine code (my recommendation, not a veto ground) [Faury ask 2]
tests.threshold: CFM in the set plus at least one second maker (code 5, 6 or 7). Code 7 when it is uncertain which maker will be ready by NGSA EIS. Three-engine certification must not become a quality risk.
tests.numbers: I recommend code 7: CFM + P&W GTF2 + RR UltraFan NB, 3 fitted at EIS and 3 / 3 in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on every hold row. Code 7 is in no barred pair. Workload: three powerplant integration and certification campaigns fall in 2035-37, two of them on new engines. The A320neo was certified on two engines, with the P&W variant first. Run in sequence (CFM as the EIS anchor, GTF2 with its year of slack, UltraFan NB only when mature), the load is a workload risk, not a quality risk. Code 6 would drop Rolls-Royce. On the public record NGSA is UltraFan NB's only airframe, because Boeing has launched no fps, so the 3-maker enabler would be at risk. Code 5 would drop P&W, the maker with slack. The code has no payoff effect.

Statement flags: give windows, not dates; give no engine-by-engine EIS fit and no claim of 'three engines at entry into service', because UltraFan NB has no slack (say 'multi-source'); put no 2040s A320 rates in our guidance; send no A350 Re-engine signal; never mention Delay Tactics. ops.memo:
My tests are role-derived; confidence is Very low.

NGSA to 2037 passes. Entry into service comes two years after the 2035 technology-ready year, inside "the second half of the 2030s". CFM is always available, GTF2 is ready in 2036 with a year of slack, and UltraFan NB in 2037 with none. Certifying three engines in 2035-37 is workload, not a quality risk, provided we sequence the campaigns and compress no test. An immature UltraFan NB is dropped, never rushed. Code 7 keeps Rolls-Royce's only narrowbody airframe and gives 3 / 3 in 2050.

The Alt run-down passes on safety, quality, the ramp shield, supply crunch and readiness. Nothing reported sends us back to the base plan. The 2038-40 trough is planned, not a shortage, so we protect it without chasing rate. Engines are the constraint to secure now. NGSA needs 56 engines in 2038, 1,170 in 2041 and 2,402 in 2044. With the A320 tail that is 2,770 in 2044, 36% above today. CFM anchors the first years, and prepayments fit inside the $0.126B.

The A350 Re-engine in 2035 passes my tests at the limit: a 2-year overlap, $1.2B of strain, absorption on the proxy, no crunch. I raise no veto. Its 2040 entry into service lands on NGSA's steepest step (96, 308, then 585 a year). It fails on Thomas's cash line and the Board's veto. Hold it; 2045 is the clean slot.

Binding: any Delay Tactics (rule 4); an NGSA cancel (rule 7).

A320neo engine slots with CFM and Pratt & Whitney, matched to the transition so that no airframe waits for an engine. NGSA wing and structures at rate, including the work packages we brought in-house. Titanium and rare earths for the combined peak, following on from the 2025 de-risking [AX-0060, AX-0062, AX-0063]. All of this is for our own ramp. No action is aimed at any rival's supply chain.

decision.public_statement: Our core principles of safety, quality, integrity, compliance and security will remain at the heart of all we do. Our next-generation single-aisle aircraft remains on track for entry into service in the second half of the 2030s. We are taking it through certification on the clock of maturity: no test will be compressed to hold a date, and no engine will enter service before it is mature. Our engine partners CFM, Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce are maturing their engines for the aircraft, because robust, multi-source engine supply matters to our customers and to the ramp-up. That ramp-up will be disciplined and controlled. Through the transition, the A320 family continues to serve our customers on our proven lines, and we are securing the engines, structures and materials our own ramp-up needs. This is how we prepare the Airbus of the 2030s. We continue to fund the programme from our own cash generation, within our financial framework, and to preserve our financial flexibility and a strong balance sheet. The A350 family, including the A350F, remains our widebody focus. Together with our European industrial base, our suppliers and our partners worldwide, we will continue to work with the whole industry for a tariff-free, zero-for-zero regime for civil aviation.
decision.rationale:
ROUND 2 (2035). DECISION BY THE TEAM RULE, ON THE BRIEF'S GRID ONLY.

Orders: ngsa hold (EIS 2037), engine code 7, a320_plan alt, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none. Every order is at its default, so the package carries no Board item. No override is used; the budget of one per game is intact.

Order of argument:
- the five pillars [AX-0073, AX-0081];
- a disciplined and controlled ramp into service, with no certification compressed [AX-0010, A-0225];
- preparing the Airbus of the 2030s on the technology clock [AX-0020, AX-0006];
- what the Board can carry: one programme inside the $5.2B line [AX-0026, AX-0022, AX-0104].

1. DELETED ON RED LINES OR PILLARS, WHATEVER THEIR PV
- Every Delay Tactics row (bottleneck, poaching, both; with or without a Re-engine; on either plan):
  - Rule 4: no fps is public, so any move is naked against the $48.32B fine.
  - Bottleneck and both also fail the integrity pillar; both is a second move.
  - One move against the default: -15.69 / +0.21 / -0.19 / -0.06 / +0.21 / -15.68 / +0.21. It never reaches $1B.
  - The team's stricter condition (the move must change who enters service first) STANDS. I do not set it aside. Delay Tactics are off.
- Every NGSA cancel row:
  - Rules 2 and 7.
  - It carries a $25.37B write-off.
  - Item against hold: -27.07 / -23.72 / -24.26 / -21.94 / -23.72 / -27.07 / -23.73.
  - It drops the 2050 engine metric to 2 sources.

2. COLLEAGUES' TESTS ON THE REMAINING ROWS
- Alt + hold (default): passes every test in both memos.
- Alt + A350 Re-engine (2035):
  - Toepfer fails it on peak cash: $5.074B + $1.0B + $0.6B strain = $6.674B in 2035-36, against $5.2B. The strain alone gives $5.674B, so no structure cures it.
  - He also fails it on robustness: -1.20 / -1.21 in S6 and S7.
  - This is a binding soft veto, not a red line: rule 6 passes, with one launch and a 2-year overlap.
  - Wagner passes it at the limit and raises no veto. His flags: the overlap coincides with three NGSA engine certification campaigns, and a 2040 EIS lands on NGSA's steepest ramp step (96, 308, then 585 a year).
- Base + hold: Toepfer fails it on robustness (-2.23 to -2.60 in every column). Binding soft veto. Wagner reports no safety or quality finding that only base resolves.
- Base + Re-engine: fails both of Toepfer's tests above.

3. SURVIVOR AND CHOICE
The only survivor is the default: +14.09 / +9.33 / +10.26 / +6.71 / +9.33 / +13.60 / +8.85.
- Positive in all seven columns; the worst is S4 at +6.71.
- Probability-weighted at my weights: +11.92.
- It is also the best surviving row in every column, so the choice does not rest on the scenario call.
- The tie-breaks do not apply.

4. THE ONE REAL QUESTION: THE A350 RE-ENGINE IN THE LAST YEAR OF THE 2033-35 WINDOW
Its item is +1.54 / +1.55 / +1.55 / +1.54 / +1.55 / -1.20 / -1.21, or +1.27 probability-weighted. On the team rule's arithmetic alone, +1.54 in S1 would clear the $1B override bar. I do not override, for four reasons:
- (a) The Board has said it would veto on liquidity, and I hold no override against the Board.
- (b) On a Qualified Majority item the Board's override review requires the plan to stay ahead in the worst plausible column. It is $1.21B behind in S7.
- (c) The breach is $1.474B a year for two years, against a line that protects net cash and the A+/A1 rating [AX-0022]. The strain component alone breaks it, so it cannot be phased away.
- (d) The Board's guidance is explicit: nothing else enters development until NGSA spend rolls off.

Toepfer discloses that his robustness failure rests on the item reading, and the row test would pass (worst S7 +7.64). His veto stands on cash alone.

I accept, on the record, the cost of waiting:
- On today's grid, about +1.54 is forgone in S1-S5, and -1.20 / -1.21 is avoided in S6-S7.
- Rounds are 2030, 2035, 2045 and 2050, so the next window is 2045 (EIS 2050, no overlap, $1.0B a year, passes cash).
- Its value is not on today's grid. Toepfer's pure-discount pre-read is about +0.71, below $1B, so the 2045 case is not assured.
- If Boeing re-engines the 787 first, rule 3 closes it.

This is a failed binding test plus a Board veto, not a doctrine premium.

5. BOARD-GATE LINES
There is no Board item this round. ngsa hold, rea350 hold, delay_tactics none and a320_plan alt (now the current plan) are all defaults. Engine code 7 is unchanged and has no payoff effect.

For the record, the items not taken:
- rea350 launch:
  - Five pillars: pass.
  - Toepfer: fail (cash, robustness).
  - Wagner: pass at the limit.
  - Grid: +1.54 to -1.21.
  - Board: veto.
- a320_plan base:
  - Pillars: no finding calls for it.
  - Toepfer: fail.
  - Wagner: no case.
  - Grid: -2.23 to -2.60.
- delay_tactics (any): fails pillars and rule 4. Grid: -15.69 to +0.21.
- ngsa cancel: fails rule 7. Grid: -21.94 to -27.07.

6. CASH (Toepfer's figures)
- NGSA is $5.074B in 2035 and 2036; at most $5.174B with the Alt pre-EIS cap used in full.
- Alt pre-EIS spend plus long-term-agreement prepayments must stay at or below $0.126B in total each year. If the agreements need more than $0.026B, the Alt spend moves after EIS.
- NGSA spend is nil from 2037; Alt runs at $0.094B a year over 2037-44.
- Net cash on the brief's profit path (Toepfer's method; an inference):
  - 48% payout: $5.83B at end-2034 and $3.18B at end-2036.
  - 30%: $13.28B and $13.76B.
  - 50%: $5.00B and $2.00B.
  - Round-1 flat-FCF case: $0.37B and -$4.83B.
- Positive at any payout within 30-50%, with no equity raise. Any new buyback authority comes only after 2036.
- The debt penalty (-0.53) is in the grid.

7. ENGINES AND SUPPLY (Wagner's figures)
- Code 7 (CFM + P&W GTF2 + RR UltraFan NB) gives 3 / 3 in 2040, 2045 and 2050, and appears in no barred pair.
- Certification is sequenced: CFM is the anchor, GTF2 has 1 year of slack, UltraFan NB has none and goes in only when mature.
- If UltraFan NB slips, CFM + GTF2 remain and NGSA does not wait.
- The 2038-40 trough (832-886 aircraft a year) is planned, not a shortage. We protect it with our own supply measures and do not chase rate.
- I attribute the binding constraint to engines: P&W carries the GTF tail, the Advantage kit and the GTF2 ramp at once, and CFM carries LEAP-1B, the A320neo tail and NGSA.

8. OWN CLOCK
Boeing's statement ('ready on our end', an EIS 'with room built into it') played no part. Any fps launched now enters service in 2042 or later, behind NGSA in 2037.

One tie-break note, recorded as in round 1: a one-year slip would take EIS to 2038, outside 2035-37 but inside the public window. No re-timing order exists, so no alternative is available.

9. CONFIDENCE
My own decision style is rated Low confidence. Toepfer's and Wagner's tests are role-derived (Low and Very low).

decision.objective_note:
Briefing goal: 'Defend 60/40; protect the A320 family; stable engine supply'. The GM scores it, and I trade no PV for it.

- **Defend 60/40: not met.** Preference is 48.3-49.2% in the 2038-40 transition trough (49.2% in 2040), then 66.0% in 2045 and 72.3% in 2050. No order on this board fills the trough. Raising A320 rate above the Alt path would be chasing rate. A Re-engine is widebody and would not move it. We protect the planned 832-886 deliveries with our own supply measures only.
- **Protect the A320 family: not met.** 2035 is at 58.7%, as the firm backlog runs out while we are capacity-bound at 1,020 a year. No order this round acts on it.
- **Stable engine supply: met.** Code 7 gives 3 sources / 3 makers in 2040, 2045 and 2050. The risk is UltraFan NB, which has no slack: if it is not ready by 2037 it drops out, CFM + GTF2 still give dual source, and the three-maker count is at risk.
