cfm.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Five years ago we said we'd commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus has committed, and so have we. Together with our partners at Safran, CFM is launching a new single-aisle engine. It builds on the hot section and the durability lessons of the LEAP fleet, and it enters service when the testing says it's ready, not before. The dates and rates for that aircraft are Airbus's to give, not ours.

We're also teaming up with Embraer. It's open, it's not exclusive, and there are no terms to talk about today. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it.

Here's what we know. Our first job is still the LEAP fleet flying today. We'll keep shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits ahead of the new-engine delivery rate, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn. Airbus has asked for long-term engine supply, and we'll work that through with them, jointly with Safran.

Here's what we don't know: how the next decade's market plays out, or when the airframers will want the next architecture. RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set the date for it.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
cfm.rationale:
DECISION
- ducted: launch, together with partner_embraer: launch.
- open_fan, lobby_emissions and genx stay at hold. GEnx hold is the only option offered.
- RISE stays whole as technology.
- The expected column is S1.
- No overrides: no colleague's veto is triggered.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN
The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. In 2030 Airbus launched the NGSA for a 2037 entry into service with code 7. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037) were launched and selected alongside CFM. So we hold a third of a committed airframe, flying a LEAP derivative.
- If nobody moves, we lose $27.07B. That loss comes from the airframers' choices and the share rules, not from anything we order.
- What we control is whether we defend and grow our third. In 2030 we said in public that we would commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus has committed.

THE GRID: each Board item against its default (S1 / S2 / S3)
- Ducted: submitted row (Ducted + Embraer) -25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91. Its default row is hold, -27.07 / -38.62 / -34.11, because Embraer needs a new CFM engine and falls with it. Item value +2.04 / -6.00 / +3.20.
- Partner Embraer: submitted row -25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91. Default row (Ducted alone) -27.00 / -44.62 / -33.18. Item value +1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27.
- Ducted alone, for the record: +0.07 / -6.00 / +0.93 against hold. That buys nothing over its bill, so I would not launch it without the partnership.
- Open Fan alone: -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13.
- Best Open Fan row (Ducted + Open Fan + Embraer + Lobby) against the package: -21.01 / -9.00 / -22.66.
Ghai verified every figure to the cent.

TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. The package is the best grid plan in S1 and S3. In S1 it is +2.04 against hold, $1.04B above the Board's $1B margin, with the whole bill charged ($4B R&D plus $2B strain). In S3 it is +3.20.
- What it costs in S1: nothing net. It adds $2.04B, and the yield goes from 83.1% to 84.4%.
- Worst column: S2, at -6.00, which is exactly its bill and never more.
- Weighted on S1 .70 / S2 .15 / S3 .15 (I took Ghai's trim of S3 from my .20): package +1.01, Embraer +1.72, Ducted alone -0.71. The package row is -28.85 against hold at -29.86.
- On this mix the package breaks even at 27.2% on S2. On equal weights it is -0.25, but equal weights ignore the record.
- I know my installed-base lens could rationalise a launch that buys nothing. That is why the Ducted alone stays out: +0.07 does not pay for $6B.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. S1 is the public record: code 7, all three makers selected and on track for 2036-37.
- S2 needs Airbus to drop two makers it has selected. Airbus has said in public that multi-source supply "matters to our customers and to the ramp", and it asked CFM for NGSA engines as "the only maker certain to be ready". So 15% on S2 is fair, not light.
- S3 needs a Boeing fps, and Boeing says "the other two aren't there yet" and holds at 57 a month with idle slots. So 15%.

(3) No birthright [CX-0564]. I read S2 as hard as S1. There a rival takes our NGSA slot. Hold already loses 11.55 against S1, and nothing we can order buys it back: the Ducted is -6.00 and Embraer 0.00. That bounded $6B is the risk I'm taking, and at 15% on S2 it is paid for.

(4) Hard rule 3, defence only. The trigger is on the record: GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (launched 2030, ready 2037), both selected with CFM on the 2037 NGSA (code 7). I invoke it for Ghai's volumes-first test as mapped. The Ducted defends our third of a committed airframer. It is not a bet on orders nobody has placed.

(5) The airframer sets the date (H2) and dates come from tests (H6). Ali's date test passes:
- Ducted 2035 + 6 = 2041; Embraer counts from 2042; no value rests on an earlier year.
- We are four years behind the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, and the grid prices that lateness: the +10 pp starts in 2041.
- The NGSA does not wait for us, because our LEAP derivative is fitted from 2037. Deferring to Airbus's dates makes us late, but late is still positive here.
- 2041 is a planning date and stays internal: we have never turned a ducted product on and off [CX-0009].

(6) My 20% line, rebutted on physics. A next engine needs at least 20% better fuel burn [CX-0217]. A ducted engine gets "less than half" of the open fan's gain [CX-0183], so it cannot meet that line and is not offered as one. It is a defensive LEAP successor, never the next generation, in public or in private. The line keeps binding RISE. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]. The Ducted claims no fuel-burn target, so there is nothing to trade it against.

(7) Durability and safety. Ali signs off the cross-functional hot-and-harsh gate and its test plan as an entry-into-service gate.
- Candidly, there are no results on ducted hardware, because none exists until this launch funds it. A failed gate moves the date, not the gate.
- No safety or durability flag is open on the evidence. Had one stood, safety would have won: I would have held and declared the $2.04B as a safety exception.

(8) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- The grid confirms the strain on two rows (Ducted alone -6.00 and Open Fan alone -10.00 in S2), so the GEnx counts as running and this is a second project. The $2B is charged, and the package pays it in S1 and S3.
- Ali's review on field data: no aircraft in 2026-34 waited on a CFM engine (2,553 engines on 1,684 aircraft in 2034, Airbus at 85 a month).
- The 9 suppliers at 15 sites are not certified, because they are not in his data. So his condition is half met, and I say so.
- Volumes on the hold row fall from the 2036 peak of 2,604 to 2,225 in 2041 and 2,064 in 2042, so the Ducted's share arrives with headroom. That is an inference, not a test.
- I commit with standing conditions and a tripwire (other moves). Ali's supply record is my own description of his job, so I checked it against doctrine (the board's strain rule). Doctrine drove this part.

(9) Partner Embraer. My record has no evidence on it. Company doctrine (profile section 6) drives the call: launch it only with a CFM engine launched and only when the grid shows it additive, and it is (+1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27, no R&D, no added strain, never below hold).
- Ghai's volumes-first test passes on that evidence: its +5 pp is a rule effect of our own order, not an assumed selection.
- Conditions: no volume, price, terms or date in public; its $1.97B kept out of expected_pv_b until an Embraer volume is agreed; any real spend comes back to Ghai.

(10) Open Fan. Hold. H2 bars it: a 2035 launch is ready in 2045, eight years after the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, so the 35 pp wait penalty applies in S1 and S3. Against the best non-RISE plan it costs $21.01B in S1 and $22.66B in S3, above the $15B RISE allowance and above the allowance plus the whole game cap. I won't stretch the allowance. RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5) and stays whole as 50-50 technology.

(11) Lobby. Hold. Doctrine: it does nothing without an Open Fan (-1.00 in every column).

(12) Tie-break. Not needed: the package beats hold by $2.04B, more than the $1B ε. Safety still came first: the decision rested on no open flag.

(13) Money [Ghai]. The Ducted is $4B over six years plus $2B of strain over six, about $1.0B a year, against about $2.55B of headroom. The 70% payout ($5.95B) stays whole [CX-0645]. Debt of $35B against EV of $160B shows no rating risk.
- Payback is about 2051 on Ghai's rough model, so it is back-loaded.
- Ghai's slip estimate (his inference): one, two and three years take S1 to +1.72, +1.33 and +0.88. A three-year slip drops it under the $1B margin but keeps it above hold.
- There is no exit: the 2041 ready year comes before the 2045 round.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule, H7)
- ducted (launch): a defence that keeps CFM competitive on a committed Airbus airframe alongside two launched rival engines, protecting the installed base both partners share 50-50. That is joint practice, so consent is assumed.
- partner_embraer (launch): CFM serving every airframer, open and not exclusive, with no airframer locked out and no added R&D. Consent assumed (inference; no record of Safran on Embraer).
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We are not asking Safran to fund a product no airframer can take.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- The Airbus long-term-agreement answer is joint: price, rate and capacity go to Safran first [CX-0184].
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVES
- premium_b is $0 against the best S1 plan, which is this plan. The game total is $0 of $4.0B, and the RISE allowance is unused.
- Dominate NB is measured by the GM. On the hold row it is not met (41.0% in 2050). The package adds +10 pp (2041) and +5 pp (2042) on NGSA engines. My rough arithmetic on the public rules (inference, not a grid number) puts 2045 in the mid-50s and 2050 near 50%, too close to call. No PV was given up for it.
- Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: not met. 2035 was the last round in which a launch could have met it, and the NGSA's 2037 entry makes that launch pay the wait penalty. I say so here and to the Board, not in public (Ali's advice; the airframers set RISE's date).

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND
- Airbus moving the NGSA toward a single maker before the code locks.
- A durability gate test that turns a failure on but can't turn it off.
- LEAP OE deliveries or kits falling behind rate on field data.
- Safran declining consent.
- Embraer turning into real spend.
A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment hits hold too, and it does not change this call.

Guide low: book -27.00.

I also took his advice not to stack anything more this round.

frame.question:
What game are we playing, and how do we win? It is still the installed base, not share for its own sake. "We get paid in dollars, not in percentages."

The record moved in 2030. Airbus launched the NGSA for a 2037 entry and selected all three engine makers. Two rival new narrowbody engines launched against it, ready in 2036 and 2037. So we are no longer playing for a slot. We have one: a third of the NGSA, flying a LEAP derivative.

This round has two questions.

1. Do we defend and grow that third with the new engine we said we would commit alongside a committed airframer? That means a defensive Ducted, launched together with the Embraer partnership, which is what makes it pay. Or do we hold and give up $2.04B in the column the public record supports?
2. The Open Fan. I'll answer this one candidly. An Open Fan launched today could not be ready until eight years after the NGSA enters service, and the airframer sets the date. RISE stays whole as technology, and "launched and ready by 2050" will not be met.

Safety, quality, delivery and cost, in that order, decide any tie.

- Confirm the grid prices the lateness, and that the NGSA does not wait for us because it flies a LEAP derivative until then.

(2) Durability gate. Bring the results of the round-1 readiness work: the cross-functional hot-and-harsh durability gate, its test plan, and the sign-off. The yardstick is the LEAP's harsh-environment gap of about 4,800 cycles against 7,000-8,000. If there is a safety or durability flag, I need it with the cross-functional answer on evidence. Confirm that durability is not traded for fuel burn.

(3) Physics. Confirm the 'less than half' gain, so I can rebut my 20% line: the Ducted is a defensive LEAP successor, never the next generation.

(4) Open Fan.
- Confirm that a 2035 launch is ready no earlier than 2045, eight years after the NGSA, which bars it under H2.
- For the record, bring the RISE ground-test, flight-test and compact-core durability results, and any open durability item.
- RISE stays whole as technology.

(5) LEAP supply review on field data. The record shows our NB engines tracking airframer deliveries: 2,553 in 2034 on 1,684 aircraft, Airbus at 85 a month, Boeing with idle slots for lack of demand, CFM steady at 75.8%. Tell me:
- whether the 9 suppliers at 15 sites are cleared;
- whether supply carries a Ducted (a second project alongside the GEnx) plus the Embraer partnership through our 2036 peak of 2,604 engines, the NGSA ramp from 2037 and a longer A320 tail on Airbus's Alt plan, without touching OE delivery;
- that shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate, with any rationing call made cross-functionally.
Your supply record is my own description of your job [CX-0633], so I'll check it against doctrine.

(6) Embraer: what load, if any, it puts on engineering and supply.

(7) Check the draft public line for dates.

BOARD GUIDANCE (labelled). The Board vetoes any item with a safety or durability flag that has no cross-functional answer on evidence, any value resting on a ready year earlier than launch plus development years, and any Open Fan. It wants your ready years, the gate results and sign-off, and the LEAP supply review on field data.
frame.initial_lean:
Lean: ducted: launch together with partner_embraer: launch. open_fan, lobby_emissions and genx stay at hold. RISE stays whole as technology.

Why:
- Additive and paid for the risk. The package is +2.04 in S1, the column the public record supports, and +3.20 in S3. Both clear the $1B margin. The worst column is S2 at -6.00, exactly its bill ($4B of R&D plus $2B of strain), so the downside is bounded. On my provisional weights (S1 .65 / S2 .15 / S3 .20) it is +1.07 against hold.
- Hard rule 3. The trigger is on the record: two rival new NB engines, launched and selected with CFM on the NGSA. It's a defence of our third of a committed airframe. It isn't a bet on orders nobody has placed.
- It's what we said. In 2030 we said we would commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus is committed.
- The Embraer partnership is what makes the Ducted pay. The Ducted alone is +0.07, which buys nothing over its bill. Doctrine, not my record, drives the Embraer call: it flips when the grid shows it positive. It stands or falls with the Ducted.
- Holding gives up $2.04B in S1, above the $2.0B round cap.
- I know my installed-base lens could rationalise a launch, so I'm holding it to the grid row.

Conditions, all needed before I decide:
- Mohamed's 2041 date held internally;
- a cross-functional durability gate signed off, with no open flag;
- my 20% line rebutted on physics;
- Rahul's volumes-first test on Embraer answered on evidence;
- S2 kept below about 25%.

If a safety or durability flag stands, safety wins. I hold and declare the $2.04B gap, and the reason is safety ahead of the number.

Open Fan: no. It's barred by H2, and at $21.01B it is beyond the RISE allowance. I'll say plainly that the 2050 objective is out of reach.

Safran gate:
- Ducted: a defence that keeps CFM competitive on a committed Airbus airframe alongside two launched rival engines. It protects the installed base both partners share 50-50. That is joint practice, so consent is assumed.
- Embraer: CFM serving every airframer, open and not exclusive. Consent assumed (inference).
- Open Fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme.
- Lobby (hold): it serves RISE, and is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- Airbus agreements: price, rate and capacity go to Safran first.

Draft public line: we said we'd commit alongside a committed airframer, and we are. It names no rival, gives no year and no price, never says 'next generation', and leaves RISE's date to the airframers.

Expected column S1. Book expected PV low, at or below -25.03.

Ain't that hard.

tests.name: Item values verified (Culp ask 1)
tests.threshold: Culp's item values must match the round-2 grid rows to within $0.01B
tests.numbers:
All match to the cent.
- Package (Ducted + Embraer) row -25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91, minus hold -27.07 / -38.62 / -34.11: +2.04 / -6.00 / +3.20.
- Ducted row -27.00 / -44.62 / -33.18, minus hold: +0.07 / -6.00 / +0.93.
- Embraer on the Ducted (D+E minus D): +1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27.
- Open Fan row -48.62 / -48.62 / -57.24, minus hold: -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13.
- Ducted + Open Fan + Embraer + Lobby row -46.04 / -53.62 / -53.57, minus the package: -21.01 / -9.00 / -22.66.
- Two more, for the record. Open Fan + Embraer equals Open Fan in every column, so Embraer is 0.00 on an Open Fan alone. Ducted + Open Fan minus Open Fan is -4.00 in every column, so a Ducted beside an Open Fan without Lobby earns nothing over its bill.
- Culp's weights (.65 / .15 / .20) check: package +1.07 (1.066), Embraer +1.73, Ducted alone -0.67. Equal weights: package -0.25.
- Break-even weight on S2: 25.4% with the rest on S1; 30.4% with S1 and S3 even; 27.8% on Culp's S1:S3 mix.

tests.name: Strain reading (Culp ask 1)
tests.threshold: Where an item can gain nothing (S2), its value should equal its bill plus the $2B strain if the 2030 GEnx still counts as a running project
tests.numbers:
Confirmed on two independent rows.
- Ducted alone in S2: -6.00, which is $4B of R&D plus $2B of strain.
- Open Fan alone in S2: -10.00, which is $8B plus $2B. Open Fan + Lobby in S2: -11.00, which is $8B + $1B + $2B.
- Embraer adds no strain: D+E and D are both -6.00 in S2.
So the GEnx counts as running (inference from the grid, matching the Board's), and any launch this round is a second project. The strain costs the Ducted most of its margin: +2.07 in S1 without it, +0.07 with it. I flagged this in 2030.

tests.name: Pays for itself: Ducted + Partner Embraer package (Culp ask 3)
tests.threshold: The row beats hold in the expected column (S1) with its whole bill charged (inference: my price/cost rule in PV form). The Board's margin for a Ducted is more than $1B
tests.numbers:
S1: row -25.03 against hold -27.07, so +2.04. That is $1.04B above the $1B margin. The full $6.00B bill ($4B R&D plus $2B strain) is already in the row.
- Gross value in S1: $8.04B (Ducted 6.07, Embraer 1.97).
- Cost in S1 against hold: nothing net. It adds $2.04B, and the yield goes from 83.1% to 84.4%.
- S3: +3.20.
- S2: -6.00, exactly the bill and never more, so the downside is bounded.

tests.name: Pays for itself: Partner Embraer item
tests.threshold: Above zero in the expected column, net of any strain it triggers
tests.numbers: D+E minus D: +1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27. No board R&D, no added strain, and never below hold in any column. It needs a new CFM engine, so it stands or falls with the Ducted.

tests.name: Pays for itself: Ducted alone (for the record)
tests.threshold: The row beats hold in the expected column (S1)
tests.numbers:
It passes on the letter only.
- S1: -27.00 against -27.07, so +0.07 on a $6B bill, about 1%.
- Weighted: -0.67 on Culp's weights, -0.71 on mine, -1.67 on equal weights.
- It is under the Board's $1B margin in every column (+0.07 / -6.00 / +0.93).
- Against the package it gives up $1.97B in S1.
It is not price/cost positive in any sense I'd defend, so I raise a non-binding objection.

tests.name: Pays for itself: Open Fan and Lobby
tests.threshold: The item beats hold in the expected column net of its bill and strain
tests.numbers:
- Open Fan alone: -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13 against a $10B bill ($8B plus $2B strain). It loses more than its bill in S1 and S3, because of the 35 pp wait penalty.
- The cheapest Open Fan row in S1 (Ducted + Open Fan + Embraer + Lobby) is -21.01 against the package.
- Lobby: Open Fan + Lobby minus Open Fan is -1.00 in every column. It has no effect without a live Open Fan.
- Embraer on an Open Fan alone: 0.00.
All are held in my orders. RISE stays whole as technology (hard rule 5), so this is not a cancel.

tests.name: Volumes first: Ducted
tests.threshold: Judge in the columns consistent with the public record. A Ducted that meets hard rule 3 as mapped passes (inference: my disclosure habit applied as a capital test)
tests.numbers:
S1 is the record's column. The NGSA launched in 2030, enters service in 2037 and carries code 7 (CFM, P&W and RR fitted). GTF2 (ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (ready 2037) are launched and both selected, so the hard-rule-3 trigger is on the record.
- The package is +2.04 in S1, with no selection assumed beyond the record.
- NGSA volumes on the record: Airbus's public plan (NGSA at a rate of about 50 four years after entry, 80 at six and 100 at eight), the Alt plan's A320 tail (82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month), and Airbus's public request for NGSA engines from CFM.
- Condition: work the exact NGSA volume assumptions with Airbus inside the long-term-agreement answer, jointly with Safran, before any number goes out.

tests.name: Volumes first: Partner Embraer (Culp ask 4)
tests.threshold: No capital and no number before the airframer's volumes are agreed (inference: CX-0944 as a capital test); judged in the record's columns

tests.name: No overcapitalization: R&D per year, 70% payout, rating (Culp ask 5)
tests.threshold: New R&D and strain committed this round, spread over development years, at or below about $2.5B a year: what is left after returning more than 70% of about $8.5B of 2028 free cash flow (inference: an analogy from capex at 2-3% of revenue)
tests.numbers:
- Ducted $4B over 6 years is $0.67B a year; strain $2B over 6 years is $0.33B a year; total $1.0B a year. Embraer adds $0.
- That sits against $2.55B (30% of $8.5B), leaving $1.55B of headroom.
- The 70% payout ($5.95B) stays whole.
- Rating: debt $35B against EV $160B (22%). The whole $6B bill is 3.75% of EV. The board shows no rating risk.
- Yields: S1 84.4% (hold 83.1%); S2 72.1% (hold 75.9%).

tests.name: Premium in dollars (Culp ask 6)
tests.threshold: Doctrine plus objective premium at most $2.0B a round and $4.0B a game, against the best plan in the expected column. One RISE allowance up to $15B, declared in full against the best non-RISE plan (company doctrine; inference)
tests.numbers:
Package: $0 in S1, $6.00B in S2, $0 in S3.
Other plans, against the best plan in each column (S1 / S2 / S3):
- Hold: $2.04B / $0 / $3.20B. S1 is above the cap by $0.04B.
- Ducted alone: $1.97B / $6.00B / $2.27B.
- Best Open Fan row: $21.01B / $15.00B / $22.66B against the best non-RISE plan.
- Open Fan alone: $23.59B / $10.00B / $26.33B.
The S1 $21.01B is above the $15B allowance, and above the allowance plus the whole $4.0B game cap ($19B). For the record, the only column where an Open Fan fits the allowance is S2 (Open Fan alone, $10.00B). S2 is not expected, and H2 bars it there too.
Game total: $0 of $4.0B; the RISE allowance is unused.

tests.name: Expected column and weights (Culp ask 2)
tests.threshold: Weights rest on the record, not on early signals (inference: CX-0896)
tests.numbers:
S1 is expected (code 7 is on the record).
- 15% on S2 is fair, not light. Airbus called CFM 'the only maker certain to be ready' and asked for NGSA engines from CFM. S2 needs Airbus to drop two makers it has selected.
- I'd trim S3 to 15%: Boeing says 'not yet' and holds 57 a month with idle slots.
- My weights (.70 / .15 / .15): package +1.01, Embraer +1.72, Ducted alone -0.71. Package row -28.85 against hold -29.86.
- Stress: package +0.61 at 20% on S2 (.65 / .20 / .15) and +0.20 at 25% (.60 / .25 / .15). Break-even is 27.2% on my mix. Equal weights: -0.25.
- Airbus's code is locked after this round (entry 2037, next round 2045), so S2 resolves in this round's sealed orders.

tests.name: What the case leaves out (Culp ask 7)
tests.threshold: Name the worst column for the recommended plan, its gap to the expected column, and the scenarios the expected case ignores
tests.numbers:
Worst column: S2 at -44.62. That is 19.59 below S1 (-25.03) and 6.00 below hold.
- No exit: the Ducted is ready in 2041, before the next round (2045), so it cannot be cancelled. The $6B is committed in full.
(a) An Airbus code change this round (S2). Hold already loses 11.55 there, and nothing buys it back.
(b) A P&W-RR Joint Venture: CFM -10 pp NB. The Ducted's +10 pp still applies, and the loss hits hold too.
(c) An fps on another clock (7-year or via Embraer) or with a code that leaves us out. That is the largest exposure: we are sole source on the 737, and the grid doesn't show it.
(d) A widebody re-engine, UltraFan WB or Trent 1000 upgrade moving the GEnx's 2042 start.
(e) Ready-year slip (money only; dates are Ali's). My rough model puts the cost at $0.32B, $0.71B and $1.16B for one, two and three years, taking the package to +1.72, +1.33 and +0.88 in S1. A three-year slip puts it under the $1B margin. My own volume dates have slipped on suppliers before.
(f) My usual three: a slowdown in airframer delivery schedules (a slower NGSA ramp pushes the gain later), tariff escalation, a global recession.
(g) The grid assumes nobody moves after this round.

tests.name: Dated profit sequence
tests.threshold: For each launch: bill year, ready year, first year of share gain, and payback inside the NB horizon to 2056 (inference: my dated sequences applied to the board)
tests.numbers:
- Ducted: bill in 2035 ($4B plus $2B strain, charged in full). Ready 2041 (launch + 6, Ali's planning date). First gain 2041 on the NGSA (entry 2037), giving 16 years of gain to 2056.
- Embraer: no bill. Counts from 2042 (launch + 7), first gain 2042.
- Rough PV payback (inference). Per-engine value comes from the brief's table: about $6.0M per NB engine in 2026 money. The NGSA is assumed at 50, 80 and 100 a month from 2041, 2043 and 2045. On that basis the package pays back its $6B in about 2051. The Ducted alone pays back only in 2056, the horizon's last year. It's back-end loaded.
- Open Fan: $8B in 2035, ready 2045, no share gain on the board, only the wait penalty from 2037.
- GEnx: running, counts from 2042.

tests.name: No second stack of projects (advice)
tests.threshold: Flag a plan with two or more projects (the $2B strain); each item passes only net of the strain it adds
tests.numbers:
Flagged. The package is a Ducted on the running GEnx, so two projects and the $2B strain are charged. It is positive net of strain in S1 (+2.04) and S3 (+3.20). Embraer adds no strain.
Nothing more this round: an Open Fan on top adds $8B, and the cheapest version is -21.01 in S1.
GE9X losses are not live (past peak a year after its 2026 entry).

tests.name: Terms (Culp ask 8)
tests.threshold: No launch-era pricing, no price concession, and no CFM narrowbody price talk without Safran, in any public statement or other move
tests.numbers: The draft line ('we said we'd commit alongside a committed airframer, and we are') carries no price, concession or terms. The answer to Airbus's request for long-term A320neo and NGSA agreements is made as CFM, jointly with Safran: price, rate and capacity go to Safran first, on standard terms, with nothing in public. The Embraer announcement carries no terms. Advice on top: no volume or rate number in public either. I'll re-check the final text at the veto check.

tests.name: Guide low (Culp ask 9; advice)
tests.threshold: Recommend the low end of the expected column, with no upside before it is confirmed (inference: my guidance habit)
tests.numbers: Recommend expected_pv_b -27.00. That is the package's S1 row (-25.03) less Embraer's +1.97, which rests on a volume no airframer has agreed; it equals the Ducted-alone S1 row. Raise it to -25.03 once an Embraer volume is agreed. No S3 upside (+3.20, which needs a Boeing fps) is booked. Weighted on my weights: -28.85. Worst column: -44.62.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: hold everything with S1 expected and no standing safety or durability flag
vetoes.ground: capex (a premium above the cap, hard rule 9). My veto right is an inference from my price/cost and volumes-first record; under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with evidence. Hold gives up $2.04B against the best S1 plan (-27.07 against -25.03), $0.04B above the $2.0B round cap. If the hold is a safety call (an Ali flag with no cross-functional answer), I do not veto: safety is not my ground and ranks first in the tie-break. The $2.04B must then be declared as a safety exception.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: ducted: launch + partner_embraer: launch with S2 as the expected column
vetoes.ground: capex (pays for itself; premium above the cap). The veto right is an inference that binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. In S2 the Ducted item is -6.00 and Embraer 0.00. Neither beats hold, and the plan gives up $6.00B against hold, the best S2 plan, which is above the $2.0B cap.

vetoes.plan: Conditional: open_fan: launch in any combination (alone, with Ducted, Embraer or Lobby), including Embraer riding on an Open Fan alone
vetoes.ground: capex (pays for itself; premium above the cap and the RISE allowance). The veto right is an inference that binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. Open Fan alone is -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13 against hold. The cheapest Open Fan row gives up $21.01B in S1 and $22.66B in S3 against the best non-RISE plan. That is above the $15B allowance, and above the allowance plus the whole $4.0B game cap. Embraer on an Open Fan alone is 0.00 and does not beat hold. This is not a cancel: RISE stays whole as technology (hard rule 5).

vetoes.plan: Conditional: lobby_emissions: launch with no Open Fan launched or live
vetoes.ground: capex (pays for itself). The veto right is an inference that binds under the team rule unless answered with evidence. Lobby is -1.00 in every column (Open Fan + Lobby minus Open Fan) and has no board effect without an Open Fan.

vetoes.plan: Advice: ducted: launch without partner_embraer
vetoes.ground: Not a binding veto: it passes my test on the letter (+0.07 in S1, a $1.97B premium within the cap). The objection is price/cost in substance: +0.07 on a $6B bill, -0.67 weighted on Culp's weights and -0.71 on mine, under the Board's $1B margin in every column, with payback only in 2056 on my rough model. Take the package or hold.

vetoes.plan: Advice: anything stacked on the package this round; booking Embraer's value before its volume is agreed
vetoes.ground: Not a veto. Stacking: the package already runs two projects under the $2B strain, so add nothing more. Guidance: book -27.00 and not -25.03 until an Embraer volume is agreed, and put out no volume, rate or date number for the NGSA or Embraer before the airframer's volumes are worked jointly with Safran.

vetoes.plan: Standing: any public statement or other move (including the answer to Airbus on long-term A320neo and NGSA agreements and the Embraer announcement) that offers launch-era pricing or a price concession, or talks CFM narrowbody price without Safran
vetoes.ground: terms. The veto right is an inference from my pricing record and the joint-decision rule. It binds under the team rule; on a statement alone the Board reads it as a recommendation. Culp's draft line and other moves pass as described: no price, no concession, price, rate and capacity to Safran first, nothing in public. Any added price or terms language would fail.

cfo.would_change_mind_if:
Seven things would move me.
(1) Airbus signals a move toward P&W only before the code locks, or confirmed data puts S2 above about 27% on my mix (25% with the rest on S1). The package then goes negative weighted and is -6.00 in S2, so I'd recommend hold.
(2) An Ali safety or durability flag stands with no cross-functional answer on evidence. Safety comes first: hold, and declare the $2.04B as a safety exception.
(3) Ali's ready year moves past about 2043 on test evidence. A three-year slip takes the package to about +0.88 in S1, under the $1B margin (my rough model).
(4) Safran declines consent on the Ducted or on the Embraer partnership.
(5) The Embraer partnership turns into real spend (integration or support). That comes back to my capex test.
(6) An Embraer volume is agreed. I'd raise the guide by $1.97B, to -25.03.
(7) A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment on the record would not change the call: the Ducted's +10 pp still holds, and the -10 pp hits hold too.
cfo.memo:
Larry, the money on one page. Your item values check to the cent. So does the strain reading, on two rows: in S2 the Ducted alone is -6.00 and the Open Fan alone -10.00, each its bill plus $2B. As I flagged in 2030, the strain bites: the Ducted alone would be +2.07 without it and is +0.07 with it.

The package pays for itself: +2.04 in S1, the record's column, with the full $6B bill charged. Volumes first passes for the Ducted on the record: code 7, both rival engines selected. Embraer passes on your evidence: no board R&D, no added strain, never below hold. But no Embraer volume is agreed, so no number goes out and I don't book it.

R&D is $1.0B a year against about $2.5B. The 70% payout stays whole, and I see no rating risk. Premium $0 in S1. Holding gives up $2.04B, over the cap.

What the case leaves out: S2 at -44.62, $6.00B below hold, with no exit, since the next round comes after the 2041 ready year. On my rough arithmetic it pays back about 2051. A three-year slip would put it under the $1B margin. Open Fan: $21.01B, beyond any allowance.

Weights: 15% on S2 is fair on Airbus's own words; I'd trim S3 to 15%. That leaves the package at +1.01.

Book -27.00, and raise it by $1.97B once Embraer volumes are agreed. Plenty of work to do, and we are all over it.

tests.name: Turn on, turn off (my date veto): every ready year in options A-D
tests.threshold: No ready year earlier than the board's development time: Ducted at launch + 6; Open Fan at launch + 10 and not before 2045; Embraer counts at launch + 7; GEnx counts at launch + 3, and only from the first re-engine (2042 if there is none). An order whose value depends on an earlier year fails. This is an inference: my test standard applied to the board's development times.
tests.numbers:
Culp's ask (1).
- Ducted: 2035 + 6 = 2041.
- Embraer: 2035 + 7 = 2042. It needs the Ducted.
- Open Fan: max(2035 + 10, 2045) = 2045.
- GEnx upgrade: 2030 + 3 = 2033, but it counts from 2042 because no re-engine is on the record.

Package B values:
- Ducted item (Embraer also at default): +2.04 / -6.00 / +3.20. That is the Ducted + Embraer row (-25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91) minus the hold row (-27.07 / -38.62 / -34.11).
- Embraer on the Ducted: +1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27, against the Ducted row (-27.00 / -44.62 / -33.18).

The rules count the Ducted's +10 pp from its ready year and Embraer from launch + 7. The Ducted alone at +0.07 in S1 is consistent with value counted only from 2041, on a third of a ramping NGSA. I cannot see inside the grid, so I take 2041 and 2042 as its dates. I confirm that no value in B rests on an earlier year.

What test stands behind 2041: none on a ducted product. What we have on test:
- the LEAP-1A fuel-nozzle fix in production by March 2024;
- the HPT hardware certified in December 2024;
- LEAP-1A new-make engines at CFM56 levels by November 2025;
- RISE: over 350 tests, and compact-core HPT dust testing from October 2025.

2041 is the board's date. I hold it as a planning date, kept out of public.

tests.name: Test, not analysis (my date veto): dates in Culp's draft public line and other moves
tests.threshold: Every date in the public statement or other moves must be one a test can back: no Open Fan or RISE entry before 2045, and no ready year before launch plus development years (hard rule 6).

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Ducted + Embraer, 2035 launch (advice)
tests.threshold: Report the gap in years. A defensive Ducted ready after the airframe's entry still earns +10 pp from its ready year once a new narrowbody is in service, so lateness does not fail it. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
Gap to the NGSA and the rival engines:
- Ducted 2041 against the NGSA's 2037 entry into service: 4 years after.
- Against GTF2 (ready 2036): 5 years after. Against UltraFan NB (ready 2037): 4 years after.
- Embraer counts from 2042: 5 years after the NGSA.

In S3, a 10-year fps launched in 2035 enters service in 2045. The Ducted is ready 4 years ahead of it, and Embraer counts 3 years ahead.

The NGSA does not wait for us. It carries code 7, CFM is always available, and our LEAP derivative is fitted from 2037. GTF2 and UltraFan NB are both ready by entry into service, so all three makers are fitted. The grid prices the lateness: the +10 pp starts in 2041. Our NB share on the hold row is 75.8% in 2037, 69.2% in 2040 and 61.6% in 2041.

2041 has no slack built in. On our record the LEAP-1B kit ran about a year late and the RISE demo slipped from mid-decade to 'this decade'. A slip moves the start of the +10 pp later. What that is worth is Ghai's estimate, not mine.

tests.name: Ready no later than the airframe: Open Fan, 2035 launch (advice)
tests.threshold: An Open Fan ready no later than the first new narrowbody's entry into service avoids the 35 pp wait penalty (20 pp with Lobby). Report the gap. Not a veto ground (inference).
tests.numbers:
Culp's ask (4). Ready 2045, 8 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry into service. In S3 the fps also enters in 2045, but the NGSA is first, so the penalty applies.

Open Fan alone against hold: -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13, against an $8B bill plus $2B strain.

The 2045 date itself is correct, so this is not my veto. Hard rule 2 bars the launch. Confirmed: a 2035 launch is ready no earlier than 2045. RISE stays whole as technology.

tests.name: Physics (wording check; Culp's ask 3)
tests.threshold: Call RISE the next generation only at 20% or better. A ducted engine has 'less than half' the gain, so it is never the next generation. That it is a defensive step only is doctrine (hard rule 3), not my words. Inference.

tests.name: Durability first, and the hot-and-harsh gate (Culp's ask 2)
tests.threshold: No plan trades durability or time on wing for fuel burn or schedule. This test applies because Culp's frame makes a durability claim (the gate, and durability not traded). Inference: Culp's line applied to my seat.
tests.numbers:
The gate was set up as the 2030 private readiness work. It is cross-functional and has a test plan. There are no turn-on, turn-off results on ducted hardware, because no ducted hardware exists until a launch funds it. The sign-off I can give is on the gate and its plan, and the cross-functional team makes the call, not one person. It is not a sign-off on results.

The test plan:
(i) Harsh-environment dust and hot-section testing at the earliest point in development, as on the RISE compact core from October 2025.
(ii) Turn on and turn off: reproduce the LEAP harsh-environment failures from 'a small, handful of parts' in test, and show the new design removes them.
(iii) Yardstick: harsh time on wing against the CFM56's 7,000-8,000 cycles, not the LEAP's about 4,800. Benign: 9,882 against about 17,000. Company target: 8,000 harsh and 17,000 neutral.
(iv) Enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make and MRO from the first engine.

The LEAP record:
- LEAP-1A: the nozzle fix in production in March 2024, the HPT hardware certified in December 2024, new-make engines at CFM56 levels by November 2025;
- LEAP-1B kit: certification was due in early 2026. The outcome is not in my evidence.

The plan trades nothing:
- the Ducted claims no 20%, so there is no fuel-burn target to trade against;
- value already counts only from 2041, so there is nothing earlier to chase by compressing tests.

Condition: this is an entry-into-service gate. A failed gate moves the date, not the gate. No safety or durability flag is open on the evidence. Confirmed: durability is not traded for fuel burn.

tests.name: Supply load: Ducted + Embraer as a second project alongside the GEnx (seat doctrine)
tests.threshold: Two or more projects cost $2B of strain and load the same constrained suppliers. Recommend against stacking unless the grid pays more than the strain. Inference: my supply role is in Culp's words only (board strain rule).
tests.numbers:
Strain:
- The board still counts the 2030 GEnx as running. The Ducted alone is -6.00 in S2 = $4B R&D + $2B strain.
- The strain is $2B once for two or more projects, so Embraer adds none.
- Net of strain the package is +2.04 / -6.00 / +3.20. It pays more than the strain in S1 and S3, and not in S2.
- On the shop floor the GEnx upgrade has been ready since 2033, so its development load is behind us. One new programme is in development. The strain is the board's count.

Volumes on the hold row:
- Peak 2,604 in 2036, +2.0% on 2034's 2,553.
- Then 2,592 (2037), 2,342 (2038), 2,225 (2041) and 2,064 (2042).
- The package adds share only on the new types, and only from 2041-42. By then the hold row is 379 and 540 engines below the 2036 peak. Whether the added share stays inside that headroom is an inference from the rules' ramp shape, not a test.

Risk:
- Ducted development hardware in 2035-41 overlaps the 2036 peak and the Alt-plan A320 tail (CFM 60% of A320neo engines, about eight years after NGSA entry into service).

Culp's ask (6), Embraer's load: no board R&D and no strain. In engineering it is the same Ducted, with no new hot section. No Embraer airframe is on the record, so no installation work is defined. No evidence: following Culp and doctrine.

No evidence: following doctrine (the board's strain rule).

tests.name: LEAP supply review on field data (Culp's ask 5; the Board's ask)
tests.threshold: My 2030 condition for lifting the one-commitment advice: OE deliveries meet the airframers' rate on field data, the 9 suppliers at 15 sites are cleared, and shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate, with any rationing call made cross-functionally.
tests.numbers:
Deliveries against rate, 2026-34 (field data): our NB engines were 75.8% of two per aircraft delivered in every year.
- 2034: 1,684 aircraft, 3,368 engines, 2,553 of them ours.
- Airbus ran at its 85 a month (1,020).
- Boeing delivered 664 with 20 MAX slots idle for lack of demand, not supply.
- No aircraft in the record waited on a CFM engine.

The 9 suppliers at 15 sites: the brief has no supplier-level data. I will not certify them cleared on analysis. So my 2030 condition is half met on evidence.

I lift the one-commitment advice for two reasons: one programme is physically in development, and the grid pays the strain in S1 and S3.

Standing conditions:
- shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate, and ahead of Ducted development hardware on the constrained suppliers;
- they are durability work, not spares;
- any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team.

The pass rests on the deliveries data, not on supplier clearance.

tests.name: Fix, don't redesign
tests.threshold: On the widebody, prefer the GEnx upgrade on a proven architecture to a new engine. On the narrowbody, keep RISE technology flowing into LEAP while RISE matures. This does not argue against the Open Fan (inference).
tests.numbers:
GEnx: hold is the only option. The 2030 upgrade is on a proven architecture, ready since 2033 and counting from 2042.

Narrowbody: the LEAP derivative flies the NGSA from 2037. The Ducted, as a defensive LEAP successor, should carry the GE90/GEnx/LEAP hot-section lineage and RISE compact-core technology, not a clean-sheet hot section. Hot-section cycles are the moat. This is an inference.

tests.name: Safety call
tests.threshold: If a problem or an order touches safety or durability, a cross-functional team decides it, never one person.
tests.numbers:
The package touches durability: a new hot section for hot-and-harsh service, and kits against OE rate on shared suppliers. Culp's frame puts both the durability gate and any rationing call to a cross-functional team.

Standing requirement: enhanced inspection of safety-critical parts in new-make shops and MRO from the first Ducted engine.

tests.name: RISE test record for the Open Fan decision (Culp's ask 4; doctrine gate G4)
tests.threshold: RISE test progress reported and no open durability failure before any Open Fan launch.

vetoes.plan:
CONDITIONAL, NOT TRIGGERED. Option B and Culp's draft line do not trip it, and no objection of mine stands against them.

It applies to:
- any order valued on a ready year earlier than launch plus development years: a Ducted before 2041, Embraer counting before 2042, an Open Fan before 2045, or the GEnx counting before 2042 with no re-engine;
- any public statement or other move that gives a Ducted ready year, an Embraer start year, an Open Fan or RISE ground-test, flight-test, ready or entry year, or any other date no test backs.
vetoes.ground:
Dates not backed by real testing, binding grounds 1 and 2: 'if it's not turn on and turn off, I will not believe the outcomes'; 'it's not on the back of a theory. It's not on the back of analysis.'

Inference note: my words date from 2024, when I was VP of Engineering, and concern whether to believe durability-fix results. That they give me a veto over programme dates is an inference. Under the team rule it binds unless Culp answers it with test evidence.

Every value in options A-D rests on the board's development times, so nothing is vetoed now. I will re-check the final orders and the statement at the veto check.

vetoes.plan: open_fan: launch in 2035, alone or in any combination, and lobby_emissions: launch, which is live only with an Open Fan
vetoes.ground:
Advice, not a date veto. The 2045 ready year is correct, but it is 8 years after the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, so the 35 pp wait penalty applies in S1 and S3 (20 pp with Lobby). Open Fan alone is -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13 against hold. Hard rule 2 bars it.

I have no RISE ground-test or flight-test results after October 2025 to put behind any product decision. Keep RISE whole as technology. We failed twice. We got it done.

vetoes.plan: ducted: launch without partner_embraer (option C), or the package with S2 as the expected column
vetoes.ground:
Supply load. This is advice from doctrine, not my record, and money is Ghai's ground. The Ducted alone is +0.07 / -6.00 / +0.93 net of strain: a second project on the constrained suppliers for less than the $1B margin anywhere. With S2 expected, the package is -6.00, its full bill, and the grid does not pay the strain.

No evidence: following doctrine.

vetoes.plan: Wording in the public statement and other moves
Standing conditions on a Ducted + Embraer launch. These are conditions, not a safety or durability flag.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Only test or field data, never analysis.

(1) The Ducted date. A hot-and-harsh test on ducted hardware or the RISE compact core that turns the failure on but cannot turn it off would move 2041 later. I would then raise a durability flag for the Board and report the slip in numbers. A claim of a ready year before 2041 on analysis gets my veto.

(2) Supply. Any of these on field data would turn my supply advice against a second project, and I would advise sequencing it:
- LEAP OE deliveries falling below airframer rate;
- shop-visit material or time-on-wing kits falling behind OE rate;
- the 9 suppliers at 15 sites shown not cleared.

(3) The column. Airbus switching the NGSA to code 2 on the record (S2) means the package pays nothing against its $6B bill. A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment on the record changes the share, not my dates; that is Culp's and Ghai's call.

(4) The LEAP-1B kit. A certification result showing the fix does not turn the harsh-environment failure off would be an installed-fleet durability flag. It would come ahead of any new programme.

(5) The Open Fan. Nothing on this board moves it before 2045. I would need RISE ground-test and flight-test results and compact-core durability turned on and turned off, plus an airframer whose entry into service is 2045 or later.
ops.memo:
Last round's number holds. A Ducted launched in 2035 is ready in 2041: launch plus six. Embraer counts from 2042. An Open Fan is 2045, eight years after the NGSA enters service in 2037. Rivals are ready in 2036 and 2037. We are four years behind the airframe. The grid counts us from 2041, and the NGSA flies our LEAP derivative until then. No value in the package rests on an earlier year. My date test passes.

Precisely: we have never turned a ducted product on and turned it off. 2041 is a planning date. Not public.

Durability. The gate is set, cross-functional, with its test plan. No results on ducted hardware, because there is no ducted hardware. The yardstick is CFM56 in harsh service, 7,000 to 8,000 cycles, not LEAP's 4,800. If the gate fails, the date moves, not the gate. No safety or durability flag is open on evidence.

Physics. Less than half the open fan's gain. Not the next generation.

Supply. Field data: every aircraft delivered 2026-2034 got its engines; 2,553 of ours in 2034. The 9 suppliers at 15 sites are not in my data; I will not certify them. Kits and shop-visit material stay ahead of OE rate. No evidence: following doctrine. The grid pays the strain in S1 and S3, not S2.

RISE results after October 2025 are not in my evidence. I won't invent them.

Embraer, lobbying, timing: No evidence: following Culp. I recommend Ducted plus Embraer, test-gated. No veto on this plan.

other_moves.move: CFM answers Airbus's public request for long-term engine supply (A320neo tail and NGSA), jointly with Safran
other_moves.detail: Made as CFM, jointly with Safran. Price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, on standard terms [CX-0184]. Nothing goes out in public: no price, no concession, no volume, no rate and no delivery year. Ghai's condition applies: the NGSA volume assumptions are worked with Airbus inside this answer before any number goes out. Unpriced on the board.

other_moves.move: Embraer partnership announced as open and not exclusive
other_moves.detail: Announced without terms: no volume, price, start year or exclusivity. No airframer is locked out (H1). It rides on the new CFM engine and adds no board R&D. Any real spend (integration or support) comes back to Ghai's capex test and to the Board before it is committed. Doctrine (profile section 6) drives this call, not my record.

other_moves.move: CFM engines stay on offer to both airframers
other_moves.detail: The LEAP derivative is fitted on the NGSA from its entry into service, and CFM offers its engines on any new single-aisle Boeing launches (H1). No price, terms or dates in public. Any pricing goes to Safran first.

other_moves.move: RISE continues whole as a 50-50 technology programme with Safran
other_moves.detail: Funded as technology and not cancelled for cost (H5). No product launch, and no ground-test, flight-test or entry year in public (H6, Ali's advice). The airframers set the date for the architecture.

other_moves.move: Ducted hot-and-harsh durability gate, run as an entry-into-service gate
LEAP fleet first on the constrained suppliers, plus a supplier-clearance review
other_moves.detail: Shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits stay ahead of OE rate and ahead of Ducted development hardware on the constrained suppliers. They are durability work, not spares [CX-0529]. Any rationing call goes to a cross-functional team. Ali reviews the 9 suppliers at 15 sites on field data [CX-0613, CX-0633] and reports to the Board in the 2045 round. Tripwire: if OE deliveries fall below airframer rate, or kits fall behind OE rate, on field data, the Ducted's development hardware is sequenced behind them.

other_moves.move: Board watch list

decision.public_statement:
Safety, quality, delivery and cost, always in that order. That's how we run this business, and it's how we made this call.

Five years ago we said we'd commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus has committed, and so have we. Together with our partners at Safran, CFM is launching a new single-aisle engine. It builds on the hot section and the durability lessons of the LEAP fleet, and it enters service when the testing says it's ready, not before. The dates and rates for that aircraft are Airbus's to give, not ours.

We're also teaming up with Embraer. It's open, it's not exclusive, and there are no terms to talk about today. CFM's engines stay on offer to every airframer. We don't have a birthright on anybody's next order. We have to earn it.

Here's what we know. Our first job is still the LEAP fleet flying today. We'll keep shop-visit material and time-on-wing kits ahead of the new-engine delivery rate, and we don't trade durability for fuel burn. Airbus has asked for long-term engine supply, and we'll work that through with them, jointly with Safran.

Here's what we don't know: how the next decade's market plays out, or when the airframers will want the next architecture. RISE remains a technology programme we're all in on with Safran, and the airframers will set the date for it.

It's that simple. Ain't that hard.
decision.rationale:
DECISION
- ducted: launch, together with partner_embraer: launch.
- open_fan, lobby_emissions and genx stay at hold. GEnx hold is the only option offered.
- RISE stays whole as technology.
- The expected column is S1.
- No overrides: no colleague's veto is triggered.

WHAT GAME, HOW WE WIN
The game is the installed base, not share for its own sake [CX-0422, CX-0493]. In 2030 Airbus launched the NGSA for a 2037 entry into service with code 7. P&W GTF2 (ready 2036) and RR UltraFan NB (ready 2037) were launched and selected alongside CFM. So we hold a third of a committed airframe, flying a LEAP derivative.
- If nobody moves, we lose $27.07B. That loss comes from the airframers' choices and the share rules, not from anything we order.
- What we control is whether we defend and grow our third. In 2030 we said in public that we would commit a new engine alongside a committed airframer. Airbus has committed.

THE GRID: each Board item against its default (S1 / S2 / S3)
- Ducted: submitted row (Ducted + Embraer) -25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91. Its default row is hold, -27.07 / -38.62 / -34.11, because Embraer needs a new CFM engine and falls with it. Item value +2.04 / -6.00 / +3.20.
- Partner Embraer: submitted row -25.03 / -44.62 / -30.91. Default row (Ducted alone) -27.00 / -44.62 / -33.18. Item value +1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27.
- Ducted alone, for the record: +0.07 / -6.00 / +0.93 against hold. That buys nothing over its bill, so I would not launch it without the partnership.
- Open Fan alone: -21.55 / -10.00 / -23.13.
- Best Open Fan row (Ducted + Open Fan + Embraer + Lobby) against the package: -21.01 / -9.00 / -22.66.
Ghai verified every figure to the cent.

TESTS
(1) Additive and paid for the risk [CX-0301]. The package is the best grid plan in S1 and S3. In S1 it is +2.04 against hold, $1.04B above the Board's $1B margin, with the whole bill charged ($4B R&D plus $2B strain). In S3 it is +3.20.
- What it costs in S1: nothing net. It adds $2.04B, and the yield goes from 83.1% to 84.4%.
- Worst column: S2, at -6.00, which is exactly its bill and never more.
- Weighted on S1 .70 / S2 .15 / S3 .15 (I took Ghai's trim of S3 from my .20): package +1.01, Embraer +1.72, Ducted alone -0.71. The package row is -28.85 against hold at -29.86.
- On this mix the package breaks even at 27.2% on S2. On equal weights it is -0.25, but equal weights ignore the record.
- I know my installed-base lens could rationalise a launch that buys nothing. That is why the Ducted alone stays out: +0.07 does not pay for $6B.

(2) Low case first [CX-0248, CX-0536]. S1 is the public record: code 7, all three makers selected and on track for 2036-37.
- S2 needs Airbus to drop two makers it has selected. Airbus has said in public that multi-source supply "matters to our customers and to the ramp", and it asked CFM for NGSA engines as "the only maker certain to be ready". So 15% on S2 is fair, not light.
- S3 needs a Boeing fps, and Boeing says "the other two aren't there yet" and holds at 57 a month with idle slots. So 15%.

(3) No birthright [CX-0564]. I read S2 as hard as S1. There a rival takes our NGSA slot. Hold already loses 11.55 against S1, and nothing we can order buys it back: the Ducted is -6.00 and Embraer 0.00. That bounded $6B is the risk I'm taking, and at 15% on S2 it is paid for.

(4) Hard rule 3, defence only. The trigger is on the record: GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036) and UltraFan NB (launched 2030, ready 2037), both selected with CFM on the 2037 NGSA (code 7). I invoke it for Ghai's volumes-first test as mapped. The Ducted defends our third of a committed airframer. It is not a bet on orders nobody has placed.

(5) The airframer sets the date (H2) and dates come from tests (H6). Ali's date test passes:
- Ducted 2035 + 6 = 2041; Embraer counts from 2042; no value rests on an earlier year.
- We are four years behind the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, and the grid prices that lateness: the +10 pp starts in 2041.
- The NGSA does not wait for us, because our LEAP derivative is fitted from 2037. Deferring to Airbus's dates makes us late, but late is still positive here.
- 2041 is a planning date and stays internal: we have never turned a ducted product on and off [CX-0009].

(6) My 20% line, rebutted on physics. A next engine needs at least 20% better fuel burn [CX-0217]. A ducted engine gets "less than half" of the open fan's gain [CX-0183], so it cannot meet that line and is not offered as one. It is a defensive LEAP successor, never the next generation, in public or in private. The line keeps binding RISE. Durability is not traded for fuel burn [CX-0208]. The Ducted claims no fuel-burn target, so there is nothing to trade it against.

(7) Durability and safety. Ali signs off the cross-functional hot-and-harsh gate and its test plan as an entry-into-service gate.
- Candidly, there are no results on ducted hardware, because none exists until this launch funds it. A failed gate moves the date, not the gate.
- No safety or durability flag is open on the evidence. Had one stood, safety would have won: I would have held and declared the $2.04B as a safety exception.

(8) Can the suppliers carry it [CX-0613, CX-0633]?
- The grid confirms the strain on two rows (Ducted alone -6.00 and Open Fan alone -10.00 in S2), so the GEnx counts as running and this is a second project. The $2B is charged, and the package pays it in S1 and S3.
- Ali's review on field data: no aircraft in 2026-34 waited on a CFM engine (2,553 engines on 1,684 aircraft in 2034, Airbus at 85 a month).
- The 9 suppliers at 15 sites are not certified, because they are not in his data. So his condition is half met, and I say so.
- Volumes on the hold row fall from the 2036 peak of 2,604 to 2,225 in 2041 and 2,064 in 2042, so the Ducted's share arrives with headroom. That is an inference, not a test.
- I commit with standing conditions and a tripwire (other moves). Ali's supply record is my own description of his job, so I checked it against doctrine (the board's strain rule). Doctrine drove this part.

(9) Partner Embraer. My record has no evidence on it. Company doctrine (profile section 6) drives the call: launch it only with a CFM engine launched and only when the grid shows it additive, and it is (+1.97 / 0.00 / +2.27, no R&D, no added strain, never below hold).
- Ghai's volumes-first test passes on that evidence: its +5 pp is a rule effect of our own order, not an assumed selection.
- Conditions: no volume, price, terms or date in public; its $1.97B kept out of expected_pv_b until an Embraer volume is agreed; any real spend comes back to Ghai.

(10) Open Fan. Hold. H2 bars it: a 2035 launch is ready in 2045, eight years after the NGSA's 2037 entry into service, so the 35 pp wait penalty applies in S1 and S3. Against the best non-RISE plan it costs $21.01B in S1 and $22.66B in S3, above the $15B RISE allowance and above the allowance plus the whole game cap. I won't stretch the allowance. RISE is not cancelled for cost (H5) and stays whole as 50-50 technology.

(11) Lobby. Hold. Doctrine: it does nothing without an Open Fan (-1.00 in every column).

(12) Tie-break. Not needed: the package beats hold by $2.04B, more than the $1B ε. Safety still came first: the decision rested on no open flag.

(13) Money [Ghai]. The Ducted is $4B over six years plus $2B of strain over six, about $1.0B a year, against about $2.55B of headroom. The 70% payout ($5.95B) stays whole [CX-0645]. Debt of $35B against EV of $160B shows no rating risk.
- Payback is about 2051 on Ghai's rough model, so it is back-loaded.
- Ghai's slip estimate (his inference): one, two and three years take S1 to +1.72, +1.33 and +0.88. A three-year slip drops it under the $1B margin but keeps it above hold.
- There is no exit: the 2041 ready year comes before the 2045 round.

SAFRAN GATE (CFM parity rule, H7)
- ducted (launch): a defence that keeps CFM competitive on a committed Airbus airframe alongside two launched rival engines, protecting the installed base both partners share 50-50. That is joint practice, so consent is assumed.
- partner_embraer (launch): CFM serving every airframer, open and not exclusive, with no airframer locked out and no added R&D. Consent assumed (inference; no record of Safran on Embraer).
- open_fan (hold): RISE stays the 50-50 technology programme. We are not asking Safran to fund a product no airframer can take.
- lobby_emissions (hold): it serves RISE and is not proposed without an Open Fan.
- The Airbus long-term-agreement answer is joint: price, rate and capacity go to Safran first [CX-0184].
- genx: GE alone, no gate.

PREMIUM AND OBJECTIVES
- premium_b is $0 against the best S1 plan, which is this plan. The game total is $0 of $4.0B, and the RISE allowance is unused.
- Dominate NB is measured by the GM. On the hold row it is not met (41.0% in 2050). The package adds +10 pp (2041) and +5 pp (2042) on NGSA engines. My rough arithmetic on the public rules (inference, not a grid number) puts 2045 in the mid-50s and 2050 near 50%, too close to call. No PV was given up for it.
- Open Fan launched and ready by 2050: not met. 2035 was the last round in which a launch could have met it, and the NGSA's 2037 entry makes that launch pay the wait penalty. I say so here and to the Board, not in public (Ali's advice; the airframers set RISE's date).

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND
- Airbus moving the NGSA toward a single maker before the code locks.
- A durability gate test that turns a failure on but can't turn it off.
- LEAP OE deliveries or kits falling behind rate on field data.
- Safran declining consent.
- Embraer turning into real spend.
A P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment hits hold too, and it does not change this call.

Guide low: book -27.00.

memo_weighing.cfo:
Ghai's memo carries the money, and I took it nearly whole.
- Every item value and the strain reading check to the cent. Every test passes for the package: pays for itself (+2.04 in S1, above the $1B margin), volumes first (the Ducted on the hard-rule-3 trigger; Embraer answered on evidence), and R&D at $1.0B a year against $2.55B with the payout and rating whole.
- His binding vetoes are all conditional, and none is triggered: S1 is expected, no Open Fan, no Lobby, and no price or terms language in the statement or other moves.
- I adopted his weights (.70 / .15 / .15, trimming S3), his guide-low of -27.00 (Embraer's $1.97B is not booked until a volume is agreed), and his Embraer conditions: no number or terms in public, and real spend returns to his capex test. I also took his advice not to stack anything more this round.
- His payback (about 2051) and slip estimates are his own rough model, so I treat them as inference. On his record his profit calls land and his volume dates slip, so I read the payback timing with a haircut. Even a three-year slip leaves the package above hold.
memo_weighing.ops:
Ali's memo carries dates, physics and durability, and I took it on those grounds.
- His date test passes with no veto triggered: Ducted 2041, Embraer 2042, Open Fan 2045. I keep 2041 internal, as he asks.
- His physics confirms my 20% rebuttal: 'less than half' the open fan's gain, so never the next generation.
- He signs off the cross-functional gate and test plan, not results (there is no ducted hardware yet), and reports no open safety or durability flag. I accept that and record it plainly.
- His record is thin: his own words end in March 2024 and cover engineering only, Medium confidence. On supply his record is my own description of his job [CX-0633], so I checked his supply pass against doctrine (the board's strain rule: $2B charged and paid in S1 and S3).
- He was candid that the 9 suppliers at 15 sites are not certified and that his pass rests on deliveries data. I keep his standing conditions (kits ahead of OE rate and of Ducted development hardware, cross-functional rationing calls, enhanced inspection from the first engine) and add a supplier-clearance review with a tripwire.
- His wording advice is all in the statement: no years, no RISE test year, no 'next generation', and the 2050 objective kept out of public.

decision.expected_scenario: S1, rivals hold. Airbus keeps code 7 on the NGSA (entry into service 2037), with CFM, P&W and RR all fitted. GTF2 is ready in 2036 and UltraFan NB in 2037. No Boeing fps this round, and no P&W-RR Joint Venture commitment. This is the column the public record supports. It does not count on any selection not yet made.
decision.best_grid_plan_in_expected_scenario: Ducted + Partner Embraer: -25.03 in S1 (yield 84.4%), against hold at -27.07. It is also the best plan in S3 (-30.91). Hold is best only in S2 (-38.62).
decision.premium_reason: $0. The submitted plan is the best grid plan in the expected column S1 (-25.03), and also in S3. It would give up $6.00B in S2 against hold, but S2 is not expected (15% weight) and that loss equals the package's bill. No RISE allowance is used: an Open Fan would cost $21.01B against the best non-RISE plan in S1, beyond the $15B allowance, so none is declared. No doctrine or objective premium is paid. Cost and risk. S2 resolves in this round's adjudication, Airbus's last chance to change the NGSA code before its 2037 entry into service. Embraer. Put out no volume, price, terms, exclusivity or date, and take nothing to Embraer before Safran has seen it. Any real spend (integration or support) comes to Ghai's capex test and to the Board before it is committed. Book its $1.97B only once a volume is agreed.

Be candid about RISE. The NGSA is the first new narrowbody and enters service in 2037. So while it does, any Open Fan in this game carries the wait penalty, and the airframer-path test cannot pass in 2045 or 2050. Keep RISE whole as 50-50 technology, never cancelled for cost, and do not stretch the allowance. Bring the RISE results from after October 2025 when they are on the record.

Keep the 70% payout whole. Answer Airbus's request for long-term engine agreements as CFM, jointly with Safran: price, rate and capacity go to the partner first, with no terms in public. The statement passes our disclosure test: no rival named, no blame, no year and no price. Keep it that way.

pratt_whitney.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms, and we will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

Our next-generation geared turbofan, launched in 2030 for the new Airbus single-aisle, is planned to be ready in 2036. Its durability will be proven before it enters service: time on wing ahead of fuel burn, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. If the test data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

Today Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. This adds to our engine on the new Airbus aircraft; it is not a hedge against it. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not done so. The terms are these: risk, investment and revenue shared, and both partners on one new engine. Each partner keeps its own technology. Our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property. What each side brings counts in the share split and is not licensed. Nothing changes in the engine we are certifying.

Our next-generation engine is available to any other new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.

1. Starting point. Eddy proposed hold + commit, and Mitchill recommended the same orders. I start there.

2. Binding vetoes struck.

- No binding veto stands on A, B or C. Mitchill's opposition to C and D is advice on the return gate, outside his four grounds. Eddy's concern on C is advice. Both point the same way as the grid.
- Mitchill lifted his round-1 ground-4 veto on a commit, because the facts changed: code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, the live GTF2 covers our $2B share, and the row is never below hold. He ruled ground 3 a pass. There is no discount and no cash to buy Rolls-Royce in. 'Credit the technology each side brings' is not a price term; it is the core-technology red line, and I hold it in the terms (below).

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- GTF2 is planned ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS on Airbus's record. That is a one-year margin, and it passes the binding readiness test.
- I discount my own operating dates. The GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087], and Eddy's slip prior lands at 2037.5-2038. So the margin is a minimum, not a cushion. The test cell decides it, and no testing is compressed.
- The bad number: Eddy has no 2035 gate data in the brief and invents none. I accept that, and it goes to Governance and Public Policy as it stands.
- If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2, ready in 2036, which is our tested engine and our architecture. Eddy's conditions (4b)-(4d) are written into the terms: no change to the configuration being certified, P&W signs durability only on what it tested, and no Rolls-Royce architecture in GTF2's certification path.
- Parts: Eddy's ground 2 passes. Fleet spares rank ahead of GTF2 installs through the longer A320neo tail.

4. Optimise inside the constraint.

gtf2_solo, hold. 2035 is GTF2's last cancel round, and the question is closed here.
- A cancel writes off $2.00B × 5/6 = $1.67B, booked in 2035, to save $0.33B of final-year cash.
- Against hold it trails in every column: −17.65 / −2.01 / −19.98 / −17.65. That is −14.87 on my weights, −14.87 on Mitchill's and −14.32 on equal weights.
- NGSA is live on code 7, which includes P&W, and GTF2 can be ready by its EIS. A cancel now would be harvesting a programme the customer asked for. I reset programmes that have stopped working [PX-0064]; this one has not. Applying the reset rule to engines is inference.
- After this round GTF2 runs to completion.

jv_with_rr, commit. The lever condition is met: NGSA's live code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- Against hold the commit is worth 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35. It is never negative, and the worst column against hold is 0. It adds $0 of new R&D and has no fold-in write-off, because spend to completion ($2.00B) is within our $2B share.
- Item value: +0.24 on my weights, +0.12 on Mitchill's, +0.59 on equal weights.
- Rolls-Royce's board vetoes a first commit, so if we wait, no Joint Venture forms in any round.
- Doctrine favours `hold` over `commit`. The commit is the order that serves the capitalise objective, and it is never below hold, so the objective's order wins at no premium (objectives.md §6).
- The doctrine pair test (no GTF2 and Joint Venture aimed at one airframer unless the grid favours the pair) is met: B ≥ A in every column, as Mitchill confirms.

5. Bias check, architecture loyalty. The GTF is 'the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]. I commit because GTF2 is the further-along engine that folds in and our gear and core stay ours, not because partnership is a goal. My Joint Venture record is Low. This view is doctrine (profile.md row 12, [P-1233], [P-1875]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.

6. Reading of p(S4). Orders are sealed and simultaneous. Rolls-Royce says it commits 'in the round P&W's commitment is on the public record', and its board vetoes a first commit. I read that as most likely a 2045 match, after this round's bulletin. I keep 0.10 for a same-round reading, against Mitchill's 0.05. The difference does not change the decision, because the item is never below hold.

7. Weights. I moved S2 up to 0.20, taking Mitchill's reading over my framing draft (0.15). Airbus's public line that CFM is 'the only maker certain to be ready' is a readiness signal, and I discount my own dates. I cut S3 to 0.15: Boeing says 'ready on our end', but not the market or the technology. Final weights: S1 .55, S2 .20, S3 .15, S4 .10.

The Board's round-1 discipline stands: a triggered GTF2 is not cancelled while the selecting airframe is live. 2035 is the last round in which GTF2 could be cancelled (it is ready in 2036). A cancel costs between 2.01 and 19.98 against hold in every column. Write that into `rationale` so the question is closed.

Consider `jv_with_rr: commit` this round. The Board cannot order it, but would approve it on the terms stated. On the grid it is a free option: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35 against hold, with $0 of new R&D while GTF2 is live. Rolls-Royce says its board vetoes a first commit, so if P&W waits, no Joint Venture forms in any round. Set out the terms in the commitment itself: risk, investment and revenue shared; each partner keeps its own technology; the gear and the core stay P&W's work-share and IP; and both partners are aligned on one new engine. Ask Mitchill to rule explicitly on ground 4 and ground 3. Because the commitment stands until withdrawn, Finance should review it every round. If a later grid (for example a Rolls-Royce match in 2045, which is off this grid and not booked) shows the formed Joint Venture below hold, withdraw before formation.

Durability gate to the Board. Before EIS, Eddy reports through the Governance and Public Policy Committee: severe-environment endurance data, LLP life at full life at entry into service, and maturity gates against the 2036 ready date, with the bad number first and no testing compressed to hold the date. The margin to the 2037 NGSA EIS is one year. Airbus's public view that CFM is 'the only maker certain to be ready' is the S2 risk (-16.61). The answer to it is evidence from the test cell, not a promise.

Show the return against Do Nothing and against a buyback. Present GTF2's whole-life case to Finance, as UTC's board saw the GTF's NPV every year: ΔPV -0.97 (engine value +1.03 against $2.00B of R&D, charged undiscounted). Show what lifts it to 0 or above: S4, a formed Joint Venture (+1.38), and S3, an fps on code 7 (+1.36). Neither is booked. Show the commit's weighted item value on Mitchill's weights beside equal weights (+0.59).

Disclosure. In the public statement, call GTF2 'planned to be ready in 2036' and say its durability 'will be proven before entry into service'; do not say it is proven unless Eddy's data show it. Name no Airbus or Boeing date. If P&W commits to the Joint Venture, say the Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and claim no Rolls-Royce commitment. Present the commitment as an addition to GTF2 on NGSA, not a hedge against it, and say plainly that our gear and core stay ours. Drop or qualify last round's 'we will launch that same round' line: GTF2 is already launched, and any repeat needs the 'in time for its entry into service' qualifier.

No price concessions. Do not buy the NGSA code against an S2 switch, or an fps selection, with launch-style discounts or free upgrades. A rival's discount never moves the answer. Keep the GTF Advantage kit on standard terms with pass-through pricing, and report progress as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration.

Fleet first, and the dividend and debt path whole. Under Airbus's Alt plan and its LTAs for A320neo engine slots, the GTF tail runs longer while the GTF2 ramp starts in 2036. Eddy's parts result should show fleet spares ranking ahead of GTF2 installs on pacing parts. Mitchill should confirm that GTF2's final-year spend (about $0.33B) and a commit ($0 of new R&D while GTF2 is live) leave the dividend covered and debt on its pre-ASR path, with no envelope stretch.

frame.question:
Control what you can control [PX-0020]. We do not control three things: whether Airbus keeps us on NGSA's code until it enters service, whether Boeing launches fps, and whether Rolls-Royce matches a Joint Venture commitment. We do control three others: whether GTF2 reaches its planned 2036 ready date with durability proven, whether we close the cancel question for good, and whether we put on the record the standing Joint Venture commitment that Rolls-Royce says its own board needs before it will move.

The question this round has two parts.
- Do we keep GTF2 whole (`gtf2_solo: hold`) through its last cancel round?
- Do we make `jv_with_rr: commit`, a public, standing commitment? It adds no new R&D while GTF2 is live and has value only if Rolls-Royce matches. We would make it only on terms that keep our gear and core ours, change nothing in the engine we are certifying, book nothing Rolls-Royce has not done, and leave the dividend and debt path whole.

Applying "miss a cycle" [PX-0071] to engines is inference, because I said it of RTX's businesses in general. It is already answered: GTF2 is launched against visible demand [PX-0109]. This round is about keeping that position, not chasing a new one.
