frame.initial_lean:
My lean is B: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit`, premium $0.00B, subject to Neil's ground-4 and ground-3 rulings and Shane's technical conditions.

**Why hold.** GTF2 is selected, live and planned ready a year inside NGSA's EIS. A cancel is worse than hold in every column (by 2.01 to 19.98) and serves neither objective. I write into the rationale that the cancel question is closed: 2035 is GTF2's last cancel round.

**Why commit.** My own Joint Venture condition is met on the code test: NGSA's live code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- On the grid it is a free option: 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35 against hold, with $0 of new R&D because GTF2 folds into our $2B share.
- Rolls-Royce's board vetoes a first commit, so if we wait, no Joint Venture forms in any round.
- It is the only order besides S3 that can lift us to capitalise (+1.38 in S4). It is never below hold, so the doctrine-favoured `hold` and the objective-serving `commit` cost the same in the worst case. The objective's order wins, and I pay no premium.

**Guarding my own bias.** I also check my architecture loyalty: the GTF is 'the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]. I commit only because GTF2 is the further-along engine that folds in and our gear and core stay ours. Partnership is something we keep under strain [PX-0038][PX-0037], not a reason to give away our technology [P-1233].

**What would change it.**
- Neil vetoing on ground 4 or ground 3.
- Shane finding that formation touches the 2037 certification configuration.
- Terms that pool the gear.
Any of these sends me back to A at a cost of +2.35 × p(S4).

**Draft weights:** S1 .55, S2 .15, S3 .20, S4 .10. The expected column is S1, where hold and hold + commit tie at −0.97. Expected PV is −2.62 under B against −2.85 under A.

**Other moves.**
1. GTF Advantage kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms, progress reported as fleet configuration percentage (public).
2. Fleet-first ranking on pacing parts through the A320neo tail and the GTF2 ramp (internal).
3. The 2035 durability gate to the Board's Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first (internal).
4. Finance reviews the Joint Venture commitment every round, with withdrawal before formation if a later grid turns it negative, 2045 first (internal).

**Proposed disclosure** (public statement, draft): "Control what you can control. The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine. We continue the GTF Advantage hot-section kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms, and we report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. Our next-generation geared turbofan, launched in 2030 for the new Airbus single-aisle, is planned to be ready in 2036. Its durability will be proven before it enters service: time on wing ahead of fuel burn, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. If the test data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF. Today Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. It adds to our engine on the new Airbus aircraft; it is not a hedge against it. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not yet done so. Its terms are these: risk, investment and revenue shared, both partners on one new engine, and each partner keeps its own technology. Our gear and our core stay ours, and nothing changes in the engine we are certifying. Our next-generation engine is available to any other new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours."

If the commit falls away, I drop the Joint Venture paragraph and keep the rest.

Commit to hold, before filing:
- The commitment text or terms pool or hand over the gear or core, or grant Rolls-Royce rights 'to credit the technology each side brings'. That is a company red line, which I flag at the veto check.
- The terms carry any cash payment to Rolls-Royce. That is new cash, not on the grid.
- The public statement claims a Rolls-Royce commitment, a formation date, a 2036 Joint Venture ready date or a share gain. That is ground 4, and binding at the veto check.
- Eddy finds that formation changes the 2037 certification configuration. That is his veto, not mine.

Commit to withdraw in 2045: run the 2045 grid's withdraw row against hold before Rolls-Royce can match.
- GTF2 is ready in 2036, so it may no longer fold in. A 2045 formation could then cost $2B of new Joint Venture R&D, and the equal-share rule could cut our share.
- Withdraw if hold is below withdraw in any column I weight at 0.2 or more, or on weighted value.
- Orders are simultaneous, so a 2045 withdrawal stops formation even if Rolls-Royce commits that round.

Weights:
- p(S4) rises only on a Rolls-Royce commitment on the record.
- p(S2) rises if Airbus changes NGSA's code on the record.
- p(S3) rises on a Boeing fps launch on the record.

Hold against cancel: nothing on this grid moves it, because hold beats cancel in every column, and after 2035 GTF2 cannot be cancelled.

Envelope or dividend view: only if a brief adds spend above about $6B a year.

Off-grid, named and not counted: a formed Joint Venture combined with an S2 code-5 switch. The Joint Venture engine counts as Rolls-Royce's NB engine, and 'P&W and RR then hold equal NB shares'. On the rule text that could narrow the S2 loss, but the size is unknown and it is not on the grid, so I book nothing.
cfo.memo:
Low end first. On my weights (S1 .60, S2 .20, S3 .15, S4 .05), holding GTF2 is worth −3.75, and S2 is the floor at −16.61. Plainly: in 2030 the NGSA trigger column showed +5.59 on code 6. Airbus took all three makers, and we're at −0.97. My first read of Airbus's "only maker certain to be ready" is timing. It's my job to always worry about things, so S2 gets .20.

GTF2: hold. NGSA selected it on code 7, so it isn't an unselected engine. A cancel writes off $1.67B to save $0.33B of 2035 cash, and trails hold in every column, by 2.01 to 19.98. The question closes this round.

Joint Venture: commit. Last round I vetoed it: Rolls-Royce was in no code, and the row showed −2.00 in S7. The costs have moved. Code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, the live GTF2 covers our $2B share, and against hold the row is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35: +0.12 on my weights, since I read Rolls-Royce's "the round they do" as 2045. Ground 4 passes: the value sits only in the order's own condition; we book $0.00B. Ground 3 passes: no discount, no cash to buy Rolls-Royce in, gear and core stay ours.

Cash: $0.33B in 2035, about 5.5% of a $6B envelope, $0 new. Dividend covered, pre-ASR debt path intact.

Written in: in 2045, if GTF2 no longer folds in, the Joint Venture is $2B of new money. Run withdraw against hold before Rolls-Royce can match.

ops.proposal:
PROPOSED ORDERS: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit`. This is Calio's row B. On the grid, row B reads -0.97 / -16.61 / +1.36 / +1.38. Row A (both hold) reads -0.97 / -16.61 / +1.36 / -0.97. The difference is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35, so B is never below hold.

WHY `gtf2_solo: hold`. GTF2 launched in 2030, is selected on NGSA's code 7, and is planned ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS. This is its last cancel round.
- Cancel is legal this round, and my default is hold.
- My cancel check: GTF2 can still be ready by the EIS of a live airframe whose code includes P&W (NGSA, code 7, 2037).
- Against hold, a cancel is -17.65 / -2.01 / -19.98 / -17.65. The write-off is $2B x 5/6 = $1.67B. A cancel leaves no P&W engine ready for NGSA.
- My record says nothing on cancels, so this is Calio's and Mitchill's call. I flag it to both.

WHY `jv_with_rr: commit`. My lever condition is met: a live airframe's code includes Rolls-Royce (NGSA, code 7). On this board the technical conditions pass:
- If the Joint Venture forms in 2035 (S4), its engine is ready in 2036 through the folded GTF2. That is ahead of UltraFan NB's 2037 and of formation + 6 (2041).
- Both solo programmes fold into one engine, so the partners are aligned [P-1875]. That engine is an extended GTF, our architecture.
- While GTF2 is live, a commit adds no engineering and no production.
I clear it technically on the conditions in (4). Whether to commit is Calio's call, through Mitchill's grounds 3 and 4. My record says nothing on a Joint Venture, so this is the seat's doctrine (defend the architecture; partners carry capital) and P-1233.

ANSWERS TO CALIO

(1) As above.

(2) Readiness, bad number first. I cannot give the Board 2035 gate data: severe-environment endurance hours, LLP life at EIS or maturity-gate status. None of it is in my brief, the board does not model it, and I will not invent hours for the Governance and Public Policy Committee.
- On the record: launch 2030 + 6 = ready 2036. The brief (section 1) and the bulletin say "in development; ready 2036" and show no slip.
- Margins: NGSA EIS 2037 leaves one year. An fps 10-yr launched in 2035 (S3) enters service in 2045, nine years after GTF2 is ready.
- Is the one year real? On the board, yes: it passes the binding test. In my judgement it is my minimum, with nothing spare. My Advantage certification went from mid-2024 to 2025 [PX-0128][P-0785]. The company's +1.5 to 2 year prior on 2036 lands at 2037.5-2038, past NGSA's 2037 EIS.
- Airbus calling CFM "the only maker certain to be ready" is a fair read of that risk. We answer it from the test cell.
- What goes to the Governance and Public Policy Committee before EIS: severe-environment endurance (three quarters of the GTF fleet flew in cool climates, which hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122]; the Advantage ran more than double the original endurance testing [P-0779]); all LLPs at full life at EIS [PX-0128]; maturity gates on the weekly drumbeat [PX-0131].
- If the data put 2036 at risk, Airbus and the Board hear it from us first. We do not compress testing to hold the date. The 2037 EIS is Airbus's date, not ours.

(3) Joint Venture readiness.
- Forms in 2035: ready in 2036 through the folded GTF2, the earliest of 2041, 2036 and 2037. Both solo programmes fold into one engine [P-1875], and UltraFan NB stops as a separate engine.
- Forms in 2045 (off-grid; on Rolls-Royce's text, this is the likelier reading): GTF2 would have been in service on NGSA since 2037. The rules do not say whether a ready engine folds in. If it does, Rolls-Royce comes onto our in-service engine, its gear and its core, which is the red line. If it does not, the Joint Venture is a second new engine, ready in 2051 and in development during the GTF2 ramp and the A320neo tail.
- Either way, we need a 2045 test before formation. The answer is withdraw if formation touches the in-service GTF2's gear, core or certified configuration, or starts a second development while the fleet is short of parts. Not booked.

(4) Technical conditions on a commit. All four hold, and none fails ground 1 now.
- (a) The gear and core stay P&W's work-share and IP. Rolls-Royce's "credit the technology each side brings" is acceptable only as a valuation in the share split, never as a licence or rights over the gear or core.
- (b) Formation changes nothing in the configuration being certified for the 2037 EIS. That configuration is frozen. Rolls-Royce content enters only after EIS, as an engineering change with its own test evidence.
- (c) P&W signs durability only on the engine it has tested: GTF2.
- (d) No Rolls-Royce architecture goes into GTF2's certification path.
Ground 1 becomes binding at the veto check if the terms or the statement break (b), (c) or (d). Condition (a) is a company red line [P-1233], which I flag.

(5) Parts and capacity. The brief and bulletin show no live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem, so this passes. The board does not model parts.
- Volumes (brief section 1): P&W NB engines run 816 (2035), 824 (2036) and 820 (2037), dip to 664 (2038), then rise from 699 (2040) to 1,068 (2044). That is +53% in four years, a bigger step than the +40% castings step I reported in 2023 [PX-0125].
- Under Airbus's Alt plan the A320 lines run about eight years past NGSA's EIS (82, 62, 52, 42, then 14 a month). So GTF OE on the A320neo slots in the long-term agreements runs to about 2045, beside the GTF2 ramp (NGSA at rate 50 about 2041, 100 about 2045).
- About 7,300 GTF engines delivered in 2026-36 on this board come into the shops through the same window.
- Ranking on the roughly 30 pacing parts [PX-0123]: first, AOG fleet spares and MRO material; then OE (the A320neo LTA slots and GTF2 installs), decided daily and reviewed weekly. GTF2 installs never take a pacing part from an AOG engine.
- The powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040], so the GTF2 ramp gets supplier quality gates before each rate step.
- Ground 2: pass, no veto.

(6) Engineering load.
- GTF2's last development year costs about $0.33B ($2B / 6): certification and endurance testing through 2036, then NGSA integration to 2037.
- A commit adds $0 of R&D and no second programme while GTF2 is live.
- If the Joint Venture forms in 2035, the integration work (governance, work-share, supply chain, aftermarket) stays outside the certification configuration until after EIS. That keeps it to one programme.
- This board has no strain charge, so this is advice: pass. Flag: a 2045 formation could start a second engine.

(7) Veto rulings.
- A: passes both grounds.
- B: passes both grounds, on conditions (4b) to (4d).
- C: not on my grounds (it puts no engine on an airframe and launches nothing), so not binding. I do not propose it, and I flag that it fails the Board's premature-exit test.
- D: ground 1 binds in its S4 column. GTF2 is cancelled and the Joint Venture forms in 2035 around the folded UltraFan NB, ready in 2037 against a 2037 EIS: zero margin, with P&W signing durability on an engine it did not test. In S1 to S3, D puts no engine on an airframe.

(8) The GTF Advantage kit: yes, as a public other move.
- Standard terms, pass-through pricing, no free upgrade.
- Progress reported as the percentage of the fleet in the latest configuration [PX-0116], not as a dated AOG recovery [PX-0115].
- My last figure is 60% in June 2023, with 90% targeted in 2-3 years. The evidence has no outcome for that target and no 2035 figure, and I have not invented one.
- The kit's hot-section parts are pacing parts too, so fleet first.

STATEMENT CHECK (Calio's draft): it passes on full life.
- "Planned to be ready in 2036" is launch + 6. "Will be proven before it enters service" is a future condition, not a claim.
- It includes LLPs at full life, no compressed testing, and no Airbus date.
- "Nothing changes in the engine we are certifying" matches condition (4b); keep it. Also keep "each partner keeps its own technology" and "our gear and our core stay ours".
- Advice: do not attach an AOG number we do not have to "the GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it".

ops.would_change_mind_if:
(1) Severe-environment endurance data, LLP life or maturity gates show GTF2 cannot be proven by 2036, or would slip past NGSA's 2037 EIS. Then readiness fails on ground 1. Airbus and the Board hear it from us first, we compress no testing, and a Joint Venture commit does not fix it.
(2) The Joint Venture terms or the statement put Rolls-Royce technology into the 2037 certification configuration, make P&W sign durability on an untested engine, or grant rights over the gear or core. Then I propose `jv_with_rr: hold`, or `withdraw` once it is legal.
(3) A brief shows a live P&W fleet, quality or supply problem: rising AOG, an escape, a durability crisis. Then I contain first with a dated recovery, and the fleet beats the GTF2 ramp.
(4) A 2045 formation (off-grid) would fold the in-service GTF2 into shared IP, or start a second engine during the ramp. Then I propose `withdraw` before formation.
(5) Mitchill's ground 3 or 4 veto on the commit. That is not my ground; I would accept hold.
ops.memo:
The bad number first. I can't give the Board 2035 test hours. Severe-environment endurance, LLP life and maturity-gate data are not in my brief, the board doesn't model them, and I won't make them up. On the record: GTF2 planned ready 2036, NGSA EIS 2037. One year. My Advantage certification slipped a year; the company prior is 1.5 to 2. One year is my minimum, not a cushion. Airbus calling CFM "the only maker certain to be ready" reads that risk. We answer it from the test cell, with no testing compressed to hold a date.

I propose `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit`.

Hold: GTF2 is selected on code 7 and can be ready for NGSA. A cancel loses 2.01 to 19.98 in every column.

Commit: if the Joint Venture forms in 2035, its engine is the folded GTF2, ready 2036, ahead of UltraFan's 2037. One engine, both partners on it. My conditions: the gear and core stay ours; nothing changes in the configuration we certify for 2037; we sign durability only on what we tested. The call is Calio's, through Neil's gate.

Parts: no live fleet, quality or supply problem in the brief, so ground 2 passes. The squeeze is 2040-44: 699 to 1,068 engines (+53%), while about 7,300 GTF engines delivered 2026-36 come into the shops. Fleet spares first.

No binding veto on A or B; ground 1 binds on D. My record is one event, June 2023. The Joint Venture view is doctrine.

other_moves.move: GTF Advantage hot-section durability kit across the A320neo fleet
other_moves.detail: We keep fitting the hot-section kit across the in-service A320neo GTF fleet at standard terms with pass-through pricing: no free upgrade and no launch-style discount [PX-0100][PX-0088][PX-0106]. We report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration. We give no dated AOG recovery, because my own dated recoveries have slipped [PX-0098][PX-0104]. We publish no fleet figure we do not have (Eddy's advice). The kit's hot-section parts are pacing parts and are ranked fleet first. It changes no payoff on the board.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment terms, published with the commitment
other_moves.detail: Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. Terms: risk, investment and revenue are shared. Both partners work on one new engine [P-1875]. Each partner keeps its own technology. The gear and the core stay Pratt & Whitney's work-share and intellectual property [P-1233]. What each side brings is recognised only as a valuation in the share split. No licence or rights over our gear or core pass to the partner. No cash payment goes to the partner. Formation changes nothing in the configuration being certified for the new Airbus aircraft; partner content can enter only after entry into service, as an engineering change with its own test evidence. Pratt & Whitney signs durability only on an engine it has tested. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not committed. The commitment stands until withdrawn. We claim no formation date, Joint Venture ready date or share gain.

other_moves.move: Fleet first on pacing parts through the A320neo tail and the GTF2 ramp
other_moves.detail: On the roughly 30 pacing parts, AOG fleet spares and MRO material rank first, then OE: the A320neo long-term-agreement slots under Airbus's Alt plan and GTF2 installs. Allocation is decided daily and reviewed weekly. A GTF2 install never takes a pacing part from an AOG engine [PX-0080][PX-0123]. Supplier quality gates come before each GTF2 rate step, because the powder-metal escape came from a capacity ramp [P-1040]. The squeeze to watch is 2040-44, when P&W narrowbody engines go from 699 to 1,068 (+53%) while about 7,300 GTF engines delivered in 2026-36 come into the shops.

other_moves.move: GTF2 durability gate to the Board's Governance and Public Policy Committee, bad number first
other_moves.detail: Before entry into service, Eddy reports to the committee: severe-environment endurance data (three quarters of the GTF fleet flew in cool climates, which hid the hot-and-sandy shortfall [PX-0122]), all LLPs at full life at entry into service [PX-0128], and maturity gates against the planned 2036 ready date on a weekly drumbeat [PX-0131]. The bad number first: today the committee has no endurance hours, LLP-life figures or gate status, and we will not invent any. The margin to NGSA's entry into service is one year. Eddy's slip prior of +1.5 to 2 years would land past it. No testing is compressed to hold a date. If the data put 2036 at risk, Airbus and the Board hear it from us first.

other_moves.move: Finance reviews the Joint Venture commitment every round; 2045 withdraw test written in
other_moves.detail: The commitment is reviewed by Finance every round. Before Rolls-Royce can match in 2045, Mitchill runs the 2045 grid's withdraw row against hold. We withdraw before formation if hold beats withdraw in any column he weights at 0.2 or more, or on weighted value. We also withdraw if Eddy finds that formation would touch the in-service GTF2's gear, core or certified configuration, or would start a second development while the fleet is short of parts. GTF2 is ready in 2036, so a 2045 formation may not fold it in and could mean $2B of new Joint Venture R&D. Orders are simultaneous, so a 2045 withdrawal stops formation even if Rolls-Royce commits that round. None of this is booked.

decision.public_statement:
Control what you can control. The GTF fleet is still not where our customers need it to be, and we own that. Time on wing and getting aircraft back in the air come first, ahead of any new engine. We are continuing the GTF Advantage hot-section kit across the A320neo fleet at standard terms, and we will report progress as the share of the fleet in the latest configuration.

Our next-generation geared turbofan, launched in 2030 for the new Airbus single-aisle, is planned to be ready in 2036. Its durability will be proven before it enters service: time on wing ahead of fuel burn, life-limited parts at full life at entry into service, and no testing compressed to hold a date. If the test data tell us something we don't like, you will hear it from us first. We have learned our lesson from the industrial gaps on the GTF.

Today Pratt & Whitney commits to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Rolls-Royce. This adds to our engine on the new Airbus aircraft; it is not a hedge against it. The Joint Venture forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not done so. The terms are these: risk, investment and revenue shared, and both partners on one new engine. Each partner keeps its own technology. Our gear and our core stay ours, in work-share and in intellectual property. What each side brings counts in the share split and is not licensed. Nothing changes in the engine we are certifying.

Our next-generation engine is available to any other new single-aisle whose entry into service it can meet, on standard terms, priced for value. We are not in the early entry phase. The dates and rates of any new aircraft are the airframer's to give, not ours.
decision.rationale:
Decision: `gtf2_solo: hold`, `jv_with_rr: commit`. This is row B and Eddy's proposal, unchanged. Premium is $0.00B and `overrides` is empty.

1. Starting point. Eddy proposed hold + commit, and Mitchill recommended the same orders. I start there.

2. Binding vetoes struck.
- Eddy's ground 1 binds on row D (cancel + commit). In S4 the Joint Venture would form around the folded UltraFan NB, ready in 2037 against a 2037 EIS with zero margin, and P&W would sign durability on an engine it did not test. D is struck.
- No binding veto stands on A, B or C. Mitchill's opposition to C and D is advice on the return gate, outside his four grounds. Eddy's concern on C is advice. Both point the same way as the grid.
- Mitchill lifted his round-1 ground-4 veto on a commit, because the facts changed: code 7 includes Rolls-Royce, the live GTF2 covers our $2B share, and the row is never below hold. He ruled ground 3 a pass. There is no discount and no cash to buy Rolls-Royce in. 'Credit the technology each side brings' is not a price term; it is the core-technology red line, and I hold it in the terms (below).

3. Safety and durability constraint first [PX-0035][PX-0073].
- GTF2 is planned ready in 2036 against NGSA's 2037 EIS on Airbus's record. That is a one-year margin, and it passes the binding readiness test.
- I discount my own operating dates. The GTF Advantage was promised for 2024 and certified in 2025 [PX-0017][PX-0087], and Eddy's slip prior lands at 2037.5-2038. So the margin is a minimum, not a cushion. The test cell decides it, and no testing is compressed.
- The bad number: Eddy has no 2035 gate data in the brief and invents none. I accept that, and it goes to Governance and Public Policy as it stands.
- If the Joint Venture forms this round (S4), its engine is the folded GTF2, ready in 2036, which is our tested engine and our architecture. Eddy's conditions (4b)-(4d) are written into the terms: no change to the configuration being certified, P&W signs durability only on what it tested, and no Rolls-Royce architecture in GTF2's certification path.
- Parts: Eddy's ground 2 passes. Fleet spares rank ahead of GTF2 installs through the longer A320neo tail.

4. Optimise inside the constraint.

gtf2_solo, hold. 2035 is GTF2's last cancel round, and the question is closed here.
- A cancel writes off $2.00B × 5/6 = $1.67B, booked in 2035, to save $0.33B of final-year cash.
- Against hold it trails in every column: −17.65 / −2.01 / −19.98 / −17.65. That is −14.87 on my weights, −14.87 on Mitchill's and −14.32 on equal weights.
- NGSA is live on code 7, which includes P&W, and GTF2 can be ready by its EIS. A cancel now would be harvesting a programme the customer asked for. I reset programmes that have stopped working [PX-0064]; this one has not. Applying the reset rule to engines is inference.
- After this round GTF2 runs to completion.

jv_with_rr, commit. The lever condition is met: NGSA's live code 7 includes Rolls-Royce.
- Against hold the commit is worth 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.35. It is never negative, and the worst column against hold is 0. It adds $0 of new R&D and has no fold-in write-off, because spend to completion ($2.00B) is within our $2B share.
- Item value: +0.24 on my weights, +0.12 on Mitchill's, +0.59 on equal weights.
- Rolls-Royce's board vetoes a first commit, so if we wait, no Joint Venture forms in any round.
- Doctrine favours `hold` over `commit`. The commit is the order that serves the capitalise objective, and it is never below hold, so the objective's order wins at no premium (objectives.md §6).
- The doctrine pair test (no GTF2 and Joint Venture aimed at one airframer unless the grid favours the pair) is met: B ≥ A in every column, as Mitchill confirms.

5. Bias check, architecture loyalty. The GTF is 'the architecture of the future' [PX-0014]. I commit because GTF2 is the further-along engine that folds in and our gear and core stay ours, not because partnership is a goal. My Joint Venture record is Low. This view is doctrine (profile.md row 12, [P-1233], [P-1875]) plus Mitchill's cash test and Eddy's technical test.

6. Reading of p(S4). Orders are sealed and simultaneous. Rolls-Royce says it commits 'in the round P&W's commitment is on the public record', and its board vetoes a first commit. I read that as most likely a 2045 match, after this round's bulletin. I keep 0.10 for a same-round reading, against Mitchill's 0.05. The difference does not change the decision, because the item is never below hold.

7. Weights. I moved S2 up to 0.20, taking Mitchill's reading over my framing draft (0.15). Airbus's public line that CFM is 'the only maker certain to be ready' is a readiness signal, and I discount my own dates. I cut S3 to 0.15: Boeing says 'ready on our end', but not the market or the technology. Final weights: S1 .55, S2 .20, S3 .15, S4 .10.

Expected PV by row:

| Row | Expected PV | Worst column |
|---|---:|---|
| A | −3.75 | S2, −16.61 |
| B | −3.51 | S2, −16.61 |
| C | −18.62 | −18.62 in every column |
| D | −16.79 | (vetoed) |

8. Dividend and debt. Ground 1 does not apply because the envelope passes. GTF2's final-year spend is $0.33B, about 5.5% of the ~$6B envelope, and the commit adds $0. The dividend is covered and debt stays on its pre-ASR path. No stretch is needed, and the once-in-the-game stretch is unused.

9. Booked number in S1: $0.00B for the commit. We book no Rolls-Royce commitment, no fps selection, no code change, no Joint Venture ready date and no share gain.

Off-grid, named and not counted:
- A 2045 Rolls-Royce match and formation. The withdraw test is written in.
- A formed Joint Venture combined with an S2 code-5 switch. Under 'P&W and RR then hold equal NB shares', this could narrow the S2 loss, but its size is unknown.

Red lines in force, none breached:
- Durability first.
- Fleet first.
- No cancel of a selected GTF2 while NGSA is live.
- Joint Venture terms share risk, investment and revenue, never the gear or core.
- Dividend, then debt, then buybacks.
- Value, not share: no concession.
- Proof before commitment.
- No airframer dates.
- Narrowbody only.
- Shared source (code 7) and equal Joint Venture shares declared as doctrine relief at $0.00B (inference, franchise defence [PX-0058][P-1292]).

Disclosure changes, per the Board:
- Dropped last round's 'we will launch that same round' line; GTF2 is already launched.
- The offer to other airframes carries the 'whose entry into service it can meet' qualifier.
- 'Planned to be ready in 2036' and 'will be proven'.
- The Joint Venture 'forms only when Rolls-Royce commits, and Rolls-Royce has not done so', presented as an addition, not a hedge.
- 'Industrial gaps' replaces 'prior iterations'.
- No AOG number is attached to the fleet line.

recommendations.text:
Bring the standing commitment back before it can form. The commitment stands until withdrawn, and an all-hold 2045 round never reaches the Board. The ExCo reads Rolls-Royce's 'we commit the round they do' as most likely a 2045 match, which is off this grid. By then GTF2 has been ready since 2036 and may not fold in. A 2045 formation could therefore mean $2B of new Joint Venture R&D, the 'equal NB shares' rule applied to an in-service fleet, and Rolls-Royce on an in-service engine. Before the 2045 orders are sealed, the ExCo should bring the following to the Finance Committee and to the Board:
- Mitchill's withdraw-versus-hold rows on the 2045 grid.
- Eddy's technical check: does formation touch the in-service GTF2's gear, core or certified configuration, or start a second development during the ramp?
- A plain statement of the equal-shares effect.
If withdraw leads, submit `withdraw`; the Board will review it under Premature exit. If hold leads, put the reasons in `rationale`. Today's approval rests on the 2035 columns and does not cover a 2045 formation.

Keep the Joint Venture terms in the definitive agreement exactly as published:
- Risk, investment and revenue shared.
- 'What each side brings' recognised only as a valuation in the share split.
- No licence or rights over the gear or core, and no cash payment to the partner.
- No change to the configuration being certified before EIS; partner content enters afterwards only as an engineering change with its own test evidence.
Any draft that departs from these terms is a significant transaction and comes back through Finance to the full Board before signature.

The durability gate has to report between rounds. GTF2 is ready in 2036 and NGSA enters service in 2037, both before the next round, so the Governance and Public Policy Committee cannot wait for 2045. The Board notes Eddy's bad number: no endurance hours, LLP-life figures or gate status are yet in front of it. Before the 2036 ready date, the committee should receive:
- Severe-environment endurance data.
- Evidence that all LLPs are at full life at EIS.
- Maturity-gate status.
If a slip threatens the 2037 EIS, Airbus and the Board hear it first, and no testing is compressed to hold the date. Also correct the attribution in the internal move: the +1.5 to 2 year slip prior is the company's derivative-entry prior, not Eddy's own record.

The Board endorses `gtf2_solo: hold` (not a Board item) and records the cancel question as closed. A cancel would write off $1.67B and trail hold by 2.01 to 19.98 in every column, while the airframe that selected GTF2 is live. Finance should keep reviewing GTF2's whole-life NPV each year, as UTC's board did:
- Report ΔPV -0.97 (+1.03 engine value against $2.00B of R&D). Mitchill's discounted view (about -0.06) is information only.
- State that S3 and S4 are the only columns that lift it to 0 or above, and book neither.

Keep the balance sheet whole. S2 (-16.61, about 15% of EV) cannot be hedged by any order on the grid, and it is P&W's largest exposure. The dividend comes first, then debt back to its pre-ASR path, then buybacks. The once-in-the-game envelope stretch stays unused. Its use would need Mitchill's memo to show the dividend covered.

Disclosure: the statement passes. In later rounds:
- Claim no Joint Venture formation date, Joint Venture ready date or share gain until each is on the public record.
- Keep 'planned to be ready' and 'will be proven' until Eddy's data prove durability.
- Never present the Joint Venture as a hedge against an S2 code switch.
- Name no airframer date.

Fleet first and value, not share: both endorsed. Keep AOG spares and MRO material ahead of GTF2 installs on pacing parts through the longer A320neo tail. Put supplier quality gates before each rate step in the 2040-44 squeeze (699 to 1,068 engines, +53%). Report the plan to the Governance and Public Policy Committee. The GTF Advantage kit stays at standard terms with pass-through pricing, and no concession is offered to hold NGSA's code.

rolls_royce.rationale:
DECISION. ultrafan_nb_solo: hold. jv_with_pw: commit. ultrafan_wb: hold. t1000_upgrade: hold. This is my framing proposal unchanged. Both memos recommend the same orders, and neither raises a binding veto against them. I checked every figure below against the round-2 brief (§1 grid, §2 objectives) and recomputed the expected values.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
(1) Start from the proposal: hold, commit, hold, hold.
(2) Strike any plan that fails a binding veto.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature, as a binding veto, on t1000_upgrade launch (alone or with the commit) and on ultrafan_wb launch (alone or with the commit). Both stay at hold, so both vetoes are respected.
- She co-signs jv_with_pw: commit and invokes no balance-sheet veto.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. He sets standing conditions for the commit, and the package meets each one: (a) no public text gives an UltraFan NB date earlier than 2037, and none gives a Joint Venture date; (b) the rationale counts on no engine before its ready year; (c) configuration, test plan and certification basis stay frozen to EIS, with shared technology after EIS; (d) the partner-shop support plan is live before 2037 and is carried as a private other move.
(3) Expected scenario: S1 (rivals hold). Best grid plan in S1: hold, tied with hold + commit at +11.77.
(4) Premium: 0. Hold + commit weakly dominates every row on the grid.
(5) Red-line sweep: no breach (see below).
(6) Board: every order that differs from the default (only the commit) goes to the Board, and the commit is on its would-approve list.

WEIGHTS (shown; the brief gives none)
- Mine, S1-S6: 0.55 / 0.15 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05. S2 sits above the Board's 0.10 because Airbus called CFM 'the only maker certain to be ready', a signal against a zero-margin entrant. S3 is low: Boeing says 'the other two aren't there yet'. S4 is 0.10: P&W committed GTF2 Solo and said nothing on the Joint Venture. S5 and S6 are low: Boeing invests in today's 787, and the A350 is Airbus's focus.
- Cross-checks: the Board's set (0.60 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05); an S2 stress (0.45 / 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05); and a low-S4 case (S4 at 0.02).
- Every item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights.

GRID ROWS, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1-S6)
- Position, 'UltraFan NB: hold': +11.77 / −3.87 / +16.14 / +11.77 / +11.68 / +11.68. Expected +9.63 (mine), +10.41 (Board), +7.29 (S2 stress).
- jv_with_pw commit ('hold + commit to JV' against 'hold'): 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights, the Board's and the S2 stress; +0.05 at S4 0.02. Worst column 0, against its own −$4B bill. The same +2.29 holds beside either widebody item. The +2.29 is exactly R&D not spent ($8.00B less $5.71B). Engine value (19.77) is unchanged, and NB share stays 31.3% in 2050. So equal shares with P&W cost nothing on this grid. McCabe confirms.
- t1000_upgrade: −6.03 in S1-S4, −5.87 in S5-S6; expected −6.01. Worst −6.03, beyond its −$2B bill, because the permanent $5B strain is in the row. STRUCK. Grounds: McCabe's binding veto; the red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development, to 2037); a shortfall above the $3B cap; and the widebody test is not triggered.
- ultrafan_wb: −9.00 in S1-S4, −6.96 in S5-S6; expected −8.69. Worst −9.00, beyond its −$4B bill. STRUCK. Grounds: McCabe's binding veto; no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record or announced; the red line (no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo not doubly selected); and a shortfall far above the $1B sub-cap.
- ultrafan_nb_solo cancel: −18.05 / −2.41 / −22.42 / −18.05 / −18.05 / −18.05; expected −15.92. Worst −22.42, beyond its $5.71B write-off. It is worse than hold even in S2. With the commit it is still −4.00 in S4 against hold + commit, because a cancelled Solo cannot fold. STRUCK under cancel discipline (NGSA flies the engine on code 7) and the Board veto.
- Package expected PV: +9.86 (mine), +10.64 (Board), +7.52 (S2 stress), +9.67 (low S4).
- Worst column of the package: −3.87 in S2. That belongs to the position, not to any item.

WHY COMMIT NOW, AND WHY THIS IS DOCTRINE RATHER THAN MY RECORD
- My record has no first-commit decision and no Joint Venture terms (thin; Low confidence). This follows company doctrine and teams.md as mapped by dashboard_game.md §5: partner first, judged once a Solo is live by the Joint Venture row against hold.
- The partner test is met on its second limb: NGSA is live, not yet in service, and its code 7 includes P&W.
- Orders are sealed, and the next round is 2045, after the Solo is ready in 2037. So the fold, and the $2.29B it saves in S4, can only happen if we stand committed this round. Waiting for P&W's commitment to be on the record first means giving up the +2.29.
- My one reservation is that a commitment made first does not make P&W credit the technology we bring [RX-0072]. McCabe names its cost: the $1.71B written off, already netted inside the +2.29. Nothing else is priced on this board. I accept it.
- The tail beyond this round is bounded. If P&W commits only in 2045, the worst plausible case is −$4B, the item's own bill. I control the hedge: a withdrawal ordered in 2045 stops formation in that round (inference from the rules). Watson adds that a Joint Venture formed in 2045 would be ready in 2051 and meet no airframe on the record. So in 2045 I re-test and withdraw unless the commit beats hold. That keeps it from becoming options management [RX-0051].
- The round-1 public note ('the Board vetoes a first commit') is corrected publicly, with the reason, as the Board asked. 'We commit the round they do' is honoured, not reversed. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098].

READINESS AND SAFETY (WATSON; I DISCOUNT MY OWN DATES)
- UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 (2030 + 7) against NGSA's 2037 EIS: zero margin, a pass with a note. I count on no engine before 2037.
- Pacing is not compressed. A certification-readiness gate in 2036 reports to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If the durability evidence is short, we say so publicly and the engine is not fitted. Watson reads that outcome as near the S2 column (inference).
- If the Joint Venture forms this round, the folded engine takes the bulletin's date: 2037 through our Solo, or 2036 if GTF2 counts as further along. Either is by NGSA's EIS, and the grid is the same either way. We never say 2036 for UltraFan.
- A 10-year fps (S3, EIS 2045) has eight years of margin.

RED-LINE SWEEP (FINAL ORDERS)
- No UltraFan launch without an airframe: no new launch is ordered.
- No early date: UltraFan NB is stated only as 'ready in 2037, seven years from launch'; there is no Joint Venture date and nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates.
- Joint Venture only after the partner test: met on the second limb, and the commitment is public at once.
- One big programme at a time: both widebody items are at hold, so strain is $0 in S1-S6.
- Cancel discipline: hold.
- Balance sheet: no equity, leverage unchanged, payout and buyback cadence untouched.
- No colleague flagged a breach against the final orders. Overrides are empty.

CASH (MCCABE)
- The remaining Solo spend is $2.29B over 2035-36, about £0.84bn a year. It has been in plan since 2030 and is funded from operating cash. If the Joint Venture forms, it falls to £0.
- Go-forward hurdle: 24-30% IRR on margin in five columns.
- Full-life lookback: 8-11%, below the hurdle. That is said plainly to the Audit Committee.

OBJECTIVE
- Enter narrowbody: met (28.0% in 2045, 31.3% in 2050).
- Widebody dominance: met (55.2% in every column).
- The $4B line stays breached: $8.0B, or $5.7B if the Joint Venture forms. It cannot return inside $4B.
- Strain: $0 only while both widebody items hold.

'So until I am sure we will deliver, I'm not committing' [RX-0124]: we are delivering what we own, and committing only to what costs nothing unless it saves us money.

Weigh a Joint Venture commit this round. We would approve it, and on balance we recommend it.
- The facts behind our round-1 'partner first' have changed: NGSA now carries P&W and RR together. Sealed orders mean 'we commit the round they do' can only be honoured by a standing commitment.
- Value: never below hold, and +2.29 in S4. A fold saves $2.29B, writes off $1.71B and brings our own narrowbody money to $5.7B.
- The window closes when the Solo is ready in 2037.
- Inference from the public rules: once formed, the equal-share rule would also hedge S2, where Airbus keeps P&W and drops us.
- The round-1 public other move said the Board would veto a first commit. Correct it publicly, with the reason.
- In 2045, re-test the standing commitment and withdraw it if P&W has not joined and its value is below 0.

Hold the widebody items, and keep Trent durability work inside the existing budget as an other move. CFM's GEnx upgrade takes our widebody share from 58% to 55.2% from 2042. That is still at least 50% in every column, so the franchise test is not triggered. As long as UltraFan NB is on record, any board-level widebody programme carries the $5B strain. In the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record, bring UltraFan WB or the upgrade with the strain in the row, against the $1B and $3B caps.

Commercial discipline against S2. Do not buy Airbus's confidence with price concessions, earlier dates or launch-style terms: narrowbody is an option, not a need, and it carries no premium. The response to 'the only maker certain to be ready' is readiness shown in tests.

Public statement:
- Give no Joint Venture EIS date and nothing on NGSA's or the fps's dates. UltraFan NB 'ready 2037' is already public and is launch + 7.
- Word the UltraFan WB line as subject to the Board and to paying after the strain.
- If we commit, say our Joint Venture commitment is on the record and the Joint Venture forms when P&W joins.

Capacity for the ramp. The brief shows 267 narrowbody engines in 2040, 742 in 2042 and 1,132 in 2045. Bring the supplier plan (castings, forgings, gearbox) and ring-fence Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support. A Joint Venture would share the gearbox and MRO load (inference).

frame.question:
So, 2035. The question is the quality of earnings on a programme we already own, not share [RX-0054]. In 2030 NGSA selected us on code 7, so UltraFan NB launched. We have spent $5.71B, $2.29B is still to come, and the engine is ready in 2037 against NGSA's 2037 EIS. Holding it is worth +11.77 in S1 and is negative in only one column (S2, −3.87, where Airbus drops us). Three questions, in this order:
(1) Delivery. Do we bring UltraFan NB in at maturity, with no cancel and no compressed date? A cancel is worse than hold in every column and breaks our own rule while NGSA flies the engine [R-1573].
(2) The Joint Venture. Do we put a standing Joint Venture commitment on the record now? Orders are sealed and the next round is 2045, after the Solo is ready, so this is the only round in which a fold can happen. Against hold the commit is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 / 0. In S4 it saves $2.29B of our own money. 'We commit the round they do' can only be honoured by already standing committed.
(3) Widebody. Does any widebody money move? I say no. With UltraFan NB on the record, both widebody items carry the permanent $5B strain, and no Re-engine is on the record.
"We won't do anything not profitable" [RX-0058].
frame.situation:
PUBLIC RECORD (round 2 bulletin)
- NGSA (Airbus): launched 2030, EIS 2037. Engine code 7 (RR, P&W and CFM). It flies CFM + P&W + RR if nothing changes. Airbus runs the Alt plan (A320 lines kept longer through the ramp).
- P&W GTF2 Solo: launched 2030, ready 2036. P&W says it is durability-first, with no compressed testing, standard terms, and no word on the Joint Venture.
- RR UltraFan NB Solo: launched 2030 (launch_if_selected triggered), ready 2037.
- CFM/GE: GEnx upgrade launched 2030, ready 2033. It takes our widebody share from 58.0% to 55.2% from 2042. CFM offers a LEAP derivative to both airframers, and RISE stays a technology programme.
- No fps: Boeing says it is 'ready on our end' but 'the other two aren't there yet'.
- No 787 or A350 Re-engine. Boeing is investing in today's 787 and Charleston; for Airbus, 'the A350 family ... remains our widebody focus'.
- Airbus, in a public other move, buys NGSA engines from 'CFM, the only maker certain to be ready'. That is a signal against us and against P&W.
- Our own round-1 public line: 'we commit the round they do' on the Joint Venture. Our public other move also said that 'the Board vetoes a first commit'. That is now wrong, because NGSA's code 7 carries P&W.

OUR POSITION (brief §1)
- On hold: ΔPV +11.77 = engine value +19.77 less R&D of 8.00.
- NB engine share: 8.5% (2040), 28.0% (2045), 31.3% (2050). NB engines: 267 (2040), 742 (2042), 1,132 (2045).
- WB engine share: 58.0% to 2041, then 55.2%.

OBJECTIVE STATUS (brief §2)
- Enter NB: MET. 28.0% in 2045 and 31.3% in 2050; 7.2% in 2050 even in S2.
- Keep WB dominance: MET. Worst year 55.2%, in every column.
- Bounded NB risk (≤ $4B): NOT MET. $8.0B now, $5.7B if the Joint Venture forms this round. It cannot be brought back to $4B.
- WB never starved: MET ($0 strain), but only while both widebody items stay at hold.

COLUMNS
- S1: rivals hold.
- S2: Airbus moves NGSA to code 6 (P&W and CFM).
- S3: Boeing launches a 10-year fps on code 5 (EIS 2045).
- S4: P&W commits to the Joint Venture.
- S5: 787 Re-engine.
- S6: 787 and A350 Re-engines.

BOARD GUIDANCE (non-binding; its veto comes after my decision)
- Risk appetite 4 of 5.
- Would approve: jv_with_pw commit (never below hold; partner test passed on its second limb because NGSA's code 7 includes P&W), with McCabe's co-signature, no Civil veto standing and no Joint Venture EIS date disclosed. Holds are never vetoed.
- Would veto: ultrafan_nb_solo cancel; ultrafan_wb launch; t1000_upgrade launch; and a commit without McCabe's co-signature, with a binding ExCo veto unrespected, with a red-line flag unresolved, with non-empty overrides, or with Watson's maturity, early-date or support veto standing.

Ready 2037 against NGSA's EIS of 2037 (zero margin). A cancel writes off $5.71B and is a Board veto item: NGSA flies the engine on code 7.

cfo.memo:
Safety, then the balance sheet, then distributions, then investment. In that order, this round is about delivering what we own.

I confirm Tufan's grid. The Joint Venture commit is 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 / 0 against hold: +0.23 on every weight set, worst column 0 against a $4B bill. The +2.29 is exactly the R&D not spent, $8.0B less $5.71B, with engine value unchanged. I co-sign. The upgrade (−6.01, worst −6.03) and UltraFan WB (−8.69, worst −9.00) lose in every column, beyond their own bills. I withhold my signature on both. A cancel loses $15.9B expected, and even in S2 it is $2.41B worse than hold. Hold the programme.

The Board's hurdle case, plainly. On this board's lifecycle revenue at Civil margins of 17-25%, the full $8B earns about 8-11%, below our mid-to-high teens; folded, 10-13%. That is the miss. Today's decision is the remaining $2.29B, which earns 24-30% in five columns and falls short only in S2. Hold that low: the board's lifecycle multiple is narrower than our aftermarket.

Cash: about £0.84bn a year for 2035-36, 22-23% of FY2026 free cash flow guidance, already in plan. No equity, no new borrowing, payout and buyback cadence unchanged. Narrowbody money stays at $8.0B, or $5.7B if the Joint Venture forms; it cannot return to $4B.

The commitment is time-boxed. In 2045 we re-test it and withdraw it unless it beats hold.

That's how you should hold it. That's our best view at the minute.

tests.name: Ready by EIS
tests.threshold: UltraFan NB ready (launch + 7) no later than the EIS of each live airframe that selects RR. Zero margin against NGSA is a pass with a note, not a fail and not a veto ground. A Joint Venture engine is ready at formation + 6, or earlier only if a folded Solo is further along (the date the bulletin shows). A late engine fails as advice: it is simply not fitted, and McCabe prices the downside.
tests.numbers: (1) UltraFan NB: launched 2030, ready 2037 (2030 + 7). NGSA launched 2030, EIS 2037. Margin 0: a pass, noted. The bulletin shows 'in development; ready 2037'. I hold 2037 as the paced date, not a floor to be beaten. I am sure of it as the date we pace to, never an earlier one. Test pacing: the remaining work for 2035-36 (the $2.29B still to spend) runs to its schedule, with no compression to protect the zero margin. Durability evidence at EIS: the standard is a time-on-wing target written into the specification, endurance and durability testing complete, and life-limited parts cleared to full life at EIS. That matches the public bar P&W has set. Gate: an internal certification-readiness review one year before EIS, reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If the durability evidence is not at standard there, we say publicly that maturity needs longer. The engine is then not fitted at 2037; it is not rushed. A slip that drops us from NGSA would land near the S2 column (−3.87 against +11.77 in S1), because the fitted makers would be the same, CFM and P&W (inference). (8) S3: a 10-year fps launched in 2035 has EIS 2045. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037: 8 years of margin, confirmed. A 7-year fps launched in 2035 (EIS 2042) would have 5 years. (2) Joint Venture: if P&W commits this round (S4), the Joint Venture forms in 2035 and the live Solo folds in. The folded engine takes the date the bulletin shows: 2037 through UltraFan NB, or 2036 if the bulletin counts P&W's GTF2 (launched 2030, ready 2036 at launch + 6) as further along. Either date is at or before NGSA's 2037. Without a fold the date would be formation + 6 = 2041, but a 2035 formation always folds the live Solo. The grid is unchanged by which date applies: 31.3% NB share in 2050 in S4 either way. A Joint Venture formed only in 2045 is ready in 2051 and meets no airframe on the record (NGSA is in service from 2037, and a 2045 fps EIS is earlier). That is a Ready by EIS fail as advice, and the reason to withdraw in 2045 if P&W has not joined.

tests.name: No early date
tests.threshold: No statement, other move or disclosure gives a date earlier than launch + 7 for UltraFan NB (2037), launch + 6 for UltraFan WB, or formation + 6 for the Joint Venture (2041 if formed in 2035), unless the bulletin shows an earlier folded basis. Nothing is said on Airbus's or Boeing's dates.
tests.numbers: (9) The CEO's draft statement, checked word for word. 'UltraFan narrowbody is in development for NGSA, ready in 2037, seven years from launch' gives 2037 = 2030 + 7, already public: pass. It gives no NGSA or fps EIS date: pass. On the Joint Venture, 'our Joint Venture commitment is now on the record. The Joint Venture forms when Pratt & Whitney joins' gives no date: pass. 'Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board in the round a Re-engine is on the record' gives no date: pass. 'If maturity needs longer, we will say so' is the right line, and I keep it. Conditions for the veto check: (a) the public correction of the round-1 note ('the Board vetoes a first commit') gives no Joint Venture date; (b) if P&W joins and the bulletin shows the folded engine at 2036 through GTF2, Rolls-Royce never states 2036 for UltraFan NB, which stays at 2037. If we ever mention the Joint Venture date, it is the bulletin's date with its folded basis, or formation + 6; (c) the rationale counts on no engine before its ready year: UltraFan NB from 2037, the Joint Venture only from the bulletin's date. Advice, not a condition: one line on support would help the S2 defence without a date, such as 'support through partner shops is being built now, in place before entry into service'.

tests.name: Support before EIS
tests.threshold: RR has no narrowbody MRO scale. A support plan through partner shops must be in the package and live before any narrowbody EIS (NGSA 2037; a 2035 fps 2042 or 2045), for the standing Solo and for any Joint Venture commit.
tests.numbers: (3) The round-1 plan has been live since the 2030 trigger, and it must be carried again in this round's package as a private other move, reported against 2037 (two years out). It has three parts. (i) Partner-shop MRO on the Singapore joint-venture model, with repair technology invested in those shops. (ii) A spares and lease-engine pool. (iii) An EIS field team able to respond quickly and intervene in the early years. All three must be in place at EIS. The load the plan must carry comes from the brief's NB engines (my cumulative sums): 7 in 2037, 24 in 2038 and 84 in 2039, so 115 installed by 2039; 382 by 2040, 1,631 by 2042 and 4,704 by 2045. The field team and the spares pool carry 2037-39. Partner-shop capacity has to scale through the early 2040s as the fleet passes about 1,600 engines (2042) and 4,700 (2045). For S3, the same network extends to the fps by 2045. With a Joint Venture, P&W's existing GTF shop network could share the load (inference). I have no evidence on how much, so I put no number on it. Our plan stands without it, and P&W's network is an addition, not a substitute. If the package drops the plan, that is Civil veto ground (c).

tests.name: Engineering load
tests.threshold: Flag the $5B strain, with the years of overlap, whenever an NB project (Solo or Joint Venture) and a WB project (UltraFan WB or upgrade) are both on record. Red lines: no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo unless both are selected; no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development. These are seat and company rules, not my words (inference).
tests.numbers: Recommended orders: UltraFan NB (in development 2030-37) plus a Joint Venture commitment, both NB. No WB project, so the strain is $0 and there is no NB+WB overlap. (5) Confirmed: the brief charges a one-off $5B whenever both kinds are on record, 'whatever their dates and even after one is ready'. Only cancelling one before it is ready removes it. UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 and we will not cancel it, so after 2037 it cannot be cancelled. Any WB item therefore pays $5B whenever we take it, in 2045 or 2050 as much as now; a formed Joint Venture would carry the same charge. The upgrade is not merely deferred: its red line lifts after 2037, but the strain stays. Taken now, the upgrade would run 2035-38 and overlap UltraFan NB development in 2035-37, which breaks the red line; it would be −6.03 in S1-S4 and −5.87 in S5-S6 (expected −6.01). UltraFan WB would run 2035-41 and overlap in 2035-37. It is beside an NB Solo that is not doubly selected, with no Re-engine on the record, so it breaks the red line too: −9.00 in S1-S4, −6.96 in S5-S6 (expected −8.69). Fold advice (inference): one chief engineer and one test plan to EIS, so the management change does not pull engineers off the test programme.

tests.name: Capacity and suppliers
tests.threshold: State RR engines a year from the brief's year table. The board has no capacity limit, so the result is not applicable. A narrowbody ramp is flagged as needing partner MRO and high-performing supplier capacity, as advice.
tests.numbers: (4) RR engines a year (brief §1), NB + WB = total: 2040: 267 + 197 = 464. 2042: 742 + 188 = 930. 2045: 1,132 + 188 = 1,320. 2050: 1,160 + 188 = 1,348. NB peaks at 1,172 in 2051. By 2045, NB volume is 6.0 times the board's WB line and 3-4 times my own midterm OE ramp of 300-350 a year. Shop visits: I use my CMD figures of 1,100-1,200 total a year at the midterm (RX-0279). Helen's 1,400-1,500 (RX-0223) were never reconciled with mine; neither is a board number. Supplier plan (advice): move castings and forgings to high-performing suppliers; size gearbox capacity early (with a Joint Venture, P&W's gearbox capacity could carry part of it, inference); ring-fence Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support while the NB line ramps from 2037.

tests.name: Widebody dominance
tests.threshold: RR widebody engine share of at least 50% in 2040, 2045 and 2050 on the brief's projection. Time on wing is the lever (inference).
tests.numbers: (6) On hold, and with the commit: 58.0% in 2040, then 55.2% in 2045 and 2050 (from 2042, after CFM's GEnx upgrade), in every column S1-S6. Confirmed. With the upgrade it would be 60.0% in 2050; with UltraFan WB, 64.8% in S5 and S6 only (55.2% elsewhere). The 50% line is not at risk anywhere: the worst year is 55.2%, 5.2 points clear. Note: in S5 Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 30.2%, which shrinks the A350 fleet we power alone, though the board's engine share does not move. Trent durability work (HP turbine blades on the Trent 1000 and 7000) continues inside the existing budget for time on wing.

tests.name: Technology pull-through
tests.threshold: An UltraFan in development or idle still feeds the Trent fleet. Noted qualitatively only; no grid adjustment, ever.
tests.numbers: No grid adjustment. UltraFan NB development (2030-37) and the demonstrator's technology keep flowing into today's Trent fleet for time on wing, whether the Solo stays Solo or folds into the Joint Venture.

vetoes.plan: jv_with_pw commit, with the CEO's draft public statement and other moves (standing conditions for the veto check, not invoked now)
vetoes.ground: Not invoked. The Civil grounds are compressed maturity, an early disclosed date and no support plan; none is met by the lean. I would invoke the veto at the veto check if any of these appears: (a) a public text gives an UltraFan NB date earlier than 2037 (including '2036' through a GTF2 fold), or a Joint Venture date earlier than formation + 6 (2041) without the folded basis shown in the bulletin; (b) the rationale counts on an engine entering service before its ready year; (c) the fold merges configurations before EIS while holding 2037, cuts the remaining test programme, or changes the certification basis, which would be compressed maturity; (d) the package carries no partner-shop support plan live before 2037. If invoked, the team rule makes it binding. The ground rests on attributed transcript turns (RX-0296, RX-0284, RX-0283).

vetoes.plan: Zero margin: UltraFan NB ready 2037 against NGSA EIS 2037
vetoes.ground: A note, not a fail and not a veto. We pace to 2037 and never compress. If maturity slips at the certification-readiness gate, we say so publicly and the engine is not fitted; McCabe prices that downside (near the S2 column, inference).

vetoes.plan: t1000_upgrade launch
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not my Civil ground: no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development (overlap 2035-37). It also carries a $5B strain for good while UltraFan NB is on record: −6.03 in S1-S4, −5.87 in S5-S6. The CEO strikes it; the Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_wb launch
vetoes.ground: Red-line breach, not my Civil ground: UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo that is not doubly selected, with no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record (overlap 2035-37). It also carries a $5B strain for good: −9.00 in S1-S4, −6.96 in S5-S6. The CEO strikes it; the Board vetoes it.

vetoes.plan: ultrafan_nb_solo cancel
vetoes.ground: Not a Civil ground. It is advice from the installed-base side: it throws away a programme two years from maturity that NGSA flies on code 7. It is −18.05 / −2.41 / −22.42 / −18.05 / −18.05 / −18.05 against hold. The Board vetoes it under cancel discipline.

ops.would_change_mind_if:
Each of these would change my view:
- Test evidence at the certification-readiness gate shows 2037 cannot be held without compression. We say so publicly and the engine is not fitted. I would veto any statement or plan that holds 2037 by compressing it.
- The fold is proposed as a configuration merge before EIS (for example, P&W's gearbox into UltraFan) while holding 2037, or it cuts the remaining test programme. That is compressed maturity, and I would invoke the Civil veto. If the configuration is frozen to EIS and shared technology follows after EIS, tested on its own, I concur.
- Any public text says 2036 for UltraFan NB, or gives a Joint Venture date earlier than formation + 6 without the bulletin's folded basis. I would invoke the veto.
- The package drops the partner-shop support plan before 2037. I would invoke the veto on ground (c).
- P&W has not joined by 2045. A Joint Venture formed then is ready in 2051 and serves no airframe on the record, so I would advise withdrawal.
- A 787 or A350 Re-engine appears on the record. I would re-test UltraFan WB, or the upgrade, with the $5B strain in the row.
- Named airline wins for UltraFan on NGSA would firm up my confidence. Airbus moving to code 6 would not change the hold, because a cancel is worse even in S2.
ops.memo:
From the operating seat: hold UltraFan NB, commit to the Joint Venture, hold both widebody items. No Civil veto.

Readiness. Launched in 2030, UltraFan NB is ready in 2037, launch plus seven, against NGSA's 2037 EIS. Zero margin is a pass with a note. A 10-year fps in S3 enters service in 2045, eight years of margin. We're pacing that programme properly. The gate is the certification-readiness review a year before EIS, reported to the Committee. If durability evidence isn't there, we say so publicly; the engine isn't fitted rather than rushed.

The fold. If P&W joins this round, the folded engine takes the bulletin's date: 2037 through our Solo, or 2036 if it counts GTF2. Nothing is compressed. My conditions: we state no Joint Venture date, we never say 2036 for UltraFan, configuration and test plan stay frozen to EIS, and shared gearbox technology comes after EIS, tested on its own.

Support. The partner-shop plan is live: Singapore model, spares and lease pool, EIS field team, all in place before 2037. Early load is small: 7 engines in 2037, 115 by 2039, 1,631 by 2042.

Capacity. 267 narrowbody engines in 2040, 742 in 2042, 1,132 in 2045: six times our widebody line. High-performing suppliers, the gearbox sized early, Trent XWB and Trent 7000 ring-fenced.

Widebody. 55.2% from 2042 in every column. Either widebody item breaks a red line and pays $5B for good.

This is hard work for the team, but we're already having an impact.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment on the record, and a correction of the round-1 note
other_moves.detail: Rolls-Royce's commitment to a narrowbody Joint Venture with Pratt & Whitney is on the record from this round. It forms when Pratt & Whitney joins, on terms that credit the technology each side brings [RX-0118, RX-0072]. Correction of our round-1 note ('the Board vetoes a first commit'): our partner test asks for P&W's commitment on the record or a live airframe whose engine selection already includes P&W. NGSA's selection now carries both P&W and Rolls-Royce, so the test is met. Under sealed orders, 'we commit the round they do' can only be honoured by standing committed. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098]. No Joint Venture date of any kind is given.

other_moves.move: Commercial discipline: standard terms through the Investment Committee
other_moves.detail: No price concessions, no earlier dates and no launch-style terms to buy share or an airframer's confidence. Campaigns are priced 'win-win' with value remunerated, and every new contract goes through the Investment Committee [RX-0081, RX-0055, RX-0097]. Our answer to doubts about readiness is maturity shown in tests.

other_moves.move: UltraFan technology and Trent durability continue inside existing R&D
other_moves.detail: UltraFan development and demonstrator technology keep flowing into the in-service Trent fleet for time on wing. Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 HP turbine durability work continues inside the existing durability budget [RX-0123]. This is not the board's t1000_upgrade order and makes no grid adjustment.

other_moves.move: Narrowbody support plan, live against the 2037 EIS (condition of Watson's concurrence)
other_moves.detail: Three parts, all in place before EIS. (i) Partner-shop MRO on the Singapore Joint Venture model, with repair technology invested in those shops [RX-0287]. (ii) A spares and lease-engine pool. (iii) An EIS field team able to intervene quickly in the early years [RX-0283]. Sized for 7 engines in 2037 and 115 installed by 2039, with partner-shop capacity scaling past about 1,600 engines by 2042 and 4,700 by 2045 (Watson's cumulative sums from the brief). If the Joint Venture forms, P&W's network adds to the plan but does not replace it. Reported to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee.

other_moves.move: Certification-readiness gate one year before EIS, with no compression
other_moves.detail: UltraFan NB test pacing runs to 2037 on schedule, with the remaining 2035-36 work uncompressed. Durability standard at EIS: a time-on-wing target in the specification, endurance and durability testing complete, and life-limited parts cleared to full life. Watson holds an internal certification-readiness review in 2036 and reports it to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If the evidence is not at standard, we say publicly that maturity needs longer and the engine is not fitted at 2037. It is not rushed [RX-0296, RX-0284].

other_moves.move: Fold engineering rule, if the Joint Venture forms
other_moves.detail: One chief engineer and one test plan to EIS. The UltraFan NB configuration and certification basis stay frozen to EIS. Shared gearbox technology comes after EIS, tested on its own. No engineers are pulled off the test programme. Rolls-Royce never states 2036 for UltraFan NB. Any Joint Venture date we ever give is the bulletin's date with its folded basis, or formation + 6.

other_moves.move: Supplier and capacity plan for the narrowbody ramp
other_moves.detail: The ramp is 267 NB engines in 2040, 742 in 2042 and 1,132 in 2045, about six times the widebody line. Castings and forgings go to high-performing suppliers. Gearbox capacity is sized early; a formed Joint Venture could share the gearbox load (inference). Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support are ring-fenced while the narrowbody line ramps from 2037 [RX-0284, RX-0286].

other_moves.move: Margin-based hurdle case to the Audit Committee (McCabe)
other_moves.detail: Go-forward case on the remaining $2.29B (2035-36): IRR of 24-30% in S1, S4, S5 and S6 at Civil margins of 16.6-24.9%; 27-33% in S3; 8-12% in S2. Expected NPV at 15% is +2.07 to +4.17. Full-life lookback on the 2030 $8B: 8-11%, below the mid-to-high-teens hurdle, stated plainly as a miss on this board's lifecycle multiple. Funding stays inside the broadly flat gross R&D envelope. Payout and buyback cadence are unchanged [RX-0213, R-1579].

other_moves.move: Maturity evidence for Airbus, without dates or price
other_moves.detail: Through the NGSA programme, share endurance and durability test results and the support-plan build with Airbus. No dates beyond the public 'ready 2037', no price, no launch-style terms.

other_moves.move: Joint Venture commitment re-test in 2045
other_moves.detail: The commitment is time-boxed to NGSA's fold window. In 2045 it is re-tested on that round's grid. If P&W has not joined and the commit row is below hold (for example, a ready Solo charged a fresh $4B share, or a Joint Venture that would be ready in 2051 and meets no airframe), we order jv_with_pw: withdraw. A standing commitment no airframe can use is options management [RX-0051].

decision.public_statement: So, plainly. UltraFan narrowbody is in development for NGSA, ready in 2037, seven years from launch. We pace it to maturity and we don't compress it for anyone. If maturity needs longer, we will say so. Support through partner shops is being built now, in place before entry into service. Partnership is our preference, not our need. NGSA already carries Pratt & Whitney and Rolls-Royce, so our Joint Venture commitment is now on the record. It forms when Pratt & Whitney joins, on terms that credit the technology each side brings. There is no change of strategy. Widebody is our core, and our Trent durability work continues. Any UltraFan widebody or Trent upgrade comes to the Board in the round a Re-engine is on the record, and only if it pays after the cost of running two programmes. We won't do anything not profitable. I will say that categorically.
decision.rationale:
DECISION. ultrafan_nb_solo: hold. jv_with_pw: commit. ultrafan_wb: hold. t1000_upgrade: hold. This is my framing proposal unchanged. Both memos recommend the same orders, and neither raises a binding veto against them. I checked every figure below against the round-2 brief (§1 grid, §2 objectives) and recomputed the expected values.

TEAM RULE, STEP BY STEP
(1) Start from the proposal: hold, commit, hold, hold.
(2) Strike any plan that fails a binding veto.
- McCabe withholds her co-signature, as a binding veto, on t1000_upgrade launch (alone or with the commit) and on ultrafan_wb launch (alone or with the commit). Both stay at hold, so both vetoes are respected.
- She co-signs jv_with_pw: commit and invokes no balance-sheet veto.
- Watson invokes no Civil veto. He sets standing conditions for the commit, and the package meets each one: (a) no public text gives an UltraFan NB date earlier than 2037, and none gives a Joint Venture date; (b) the rationale counts on no engine before its ready year; (c) configuration, test plan and certification basis stay frozen to EIS, with shared technology after EIS; (d) the partner-shop support plan is live before 2037 and is carried as a private other move.
(3) Expected scenario: S1 (rivals hold). Best grid plan in S1: hold, tied with hold + commit at +11.77.
(4) Premium: 0. Hold + commit weakly dominates every row on the grid.
(5) Red-line sweep: no breach (see below).
(6) Board: every order that differs from the default (only the commit) goes to the Board, and the commit is on its would-approve list.

WEIGHTS (shown; the brief gives none)
- Mine, S1-S6: 0.55 / 0.15 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05. S2 sits above the Board's 0.10 because Airbus called CFM 'the only maker certain to be ready', a signal against a zero-margin entrant. S3 is low: Boeing says 'the other two aren't there yet'. S4 is 0.10: P&W committed GTF2 Solo and said nothing on the Joint Venture. S5 and S6 are low: Boeing invests in today's 787, and the A350 is Airbus's focus.
- Cross-checks: the Board's set (0.60 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.10 / 0.05); an S2 stress (0.45 / 0.30 / 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.05 / 0.05); and a low-S4 case (S4 at 0.02).
- Every item has the same sign in every column, so no verdict turns on the weights.

GRID ROWS, EACH ITEM AGAINST THE SAME ROW WITHOUT IT (S1-S6)
- Position, 'UltraFan NB: hold': +11.77 / −3.87 / +16.14 / +11.77 / +11.68 / +11.68. Expected +9.63 (mine), +10.41 (Board), +7.29 (S2 stress).
- jv_with_pw commit ('hold + commit to JV' against 'hold'): 0 / 0 / 0 / +2.29 / 0 / 0. Expected +0.23 on my weights, the Board's and the S2 stress; +0.05 at S4 0.02. Worst column 0, against its own −$4B bill. The same +2.29 holds beside either widebody item. The +2.29 is exactly R&D not spent ($8.00B less $5.71B). Engine value (19.77) is unchanged, and NB share stays 31.3% in 2050. So equal shares with P&W cost nothing on this grid. McCabe confirms.
- t1000_upgrade: −6.03 in S1-S4, −5.87 in S5-S6; expected −6.01. Worst −6.03, beyond its −$2B bill, because the permanent $5B strain is in the row. STRUCK. Grounds: McCabe's binding veto; the red line (no upgrade while an UltraFan is in development, to 2037); a shortfall above the $3B cap; and the widebody test is not triggered.
- ultrafan_wb: −9.00 in S1-S4, −6.96 in S5-S6; expected −8.69. Worst −9.00, beyond its −$4B bill. STRUCK. Grounds: McCabe's binding veto; no 787 or A350 Re-engine on the record or announced; the red line (no UltraFan WB beside an NB Solo not doubly selected); and a shortfall far above the $1B sub-cap.
- ultrafan_nb_solo cancel: −18.05 / −2.41 / −22.42 / −18.05 / −18.05 / −18.05; expected −15.92. Worst −22.42, beyond its $5.71B write-off. It is worse than hold even in S2. With the commit it is still −4.00 in S4 against hold + commit, because a cancelled Solo cannot fold. STRUCK under cancel discipline (NGSA flies the engine on code 7) and the Board veto.
- Package expected PV: +9.86 (mine), +10.64 (Board), +7.52 (S2 stress), +9.67 (low S4).
- Worst column of the package: −3.87 in S2. That belongs to the position, not to any item.

WHY COMMIT NOW, AND WHY THIS IS DOCTRINE RATHER THAN MY RECORD
- My record has no first-commit decision and no Joint Venture terms (thin; Low confidence). This follows company doctrine and teams.md as mapped by dashboard_game.md §5: partner first, judged once a Solo is live by the Joint Venture row against hold.
- The partner test is met on its second limb: NGSA is live, not yet in service, and its code 7 includes P&W.
- Orders are sealed, and the next round is 2045, after the Solo is ready in 2037. So the fold, and the $2.29B it saves in S4, can only happen if we stand committed this round. Waiting for P&W's commitment to be on the record first means giving up the +2.29.
- My one reservation is that a commitment made first does not make P&W credit the technology we bring [RX-0072]. McCabe names its cost: the $1.71B written off, already netted inside the +2.29. Nothing else is priced on this board. I accept it.
- The tail beyond this round is bounded. If P&W commits only in 2045, the worst plausible case is −$4B, the item's own bill. I control the hedge: a withdrawal ordered in 2045 stops formation in that round (inference from the rules). Watson adds that a Joint Venture formed in 2045 would be ready in 2051 and meet no airframe on the record. So in 2045 I re-test and withdraw unless the commit beats hold. That keeps it from becoming options management [RX-0051].
- The round-1 public note ('the Board vetoes a first commit') is corrected publicly, with the reason, as the Board asked. 'We commit the round they do' is honoured, not reversed. There is no change of strategy [RX-0098].

READINESS AND SAFETY (WATSON; I DISCOUNT MY OWN DATES)
- UltraFan NB is ready in 2037 (2030 + 7) against NGSA's 2037 EIS: zero margin, a pass with a note. I count on no engine before 2037.
- Pacing is not compressed. A certification-readiness gate in 2036 reports to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee. If the durability evidence is short, we say so publicly and the engine is not fitted. Watson reads that outcome as near the S2 column (inference).
- If the Joint Venture forms this round, the folded engine takes the bulletin's date: 2037 through our Solo, or 2036 if GTF2 counts as further along. Either is by NGSA's EIS, and the grid is the same either way. We never say 2036 for UltraFan.
- A 10-year fps (S3, EIS 2045) has eight years of margin.

RED-LINE SWEEP (FINAL ORDERS)
- No UltraFan launch without an airframe: no new launch is ordered.
- No early date: UltraFan NB is stated only as 'ready in 2037, seven years from launch'; there is no Joint Venture date and nothing on Airbus's or Boeing's dates.
- Joint Venture only after the partner test: met on the second limb, and the commitment is public at once.
- One big programme at a time: both widebody items are at hold, so strain is $0 in S1-S6.
- Cancel discipline: hold.
- Balance sheet: no equity, leverage unchanged, payout and buyback cadence untouched.
- No colleague flagged a breach against the final orders. Overrides are empty.

CASH (MCCABE)
- The remaining Solo spend is $2.29B over 2035-36, about £0.84bn a year. It has been in plan since 2030 and is funded from operating cash. If the Joint Venture forms, it falls to £0.

recommendations.text:
Product safety first: the zero margin is ours to manage, never to compress.
- Watson's certification-readiness gate in 2036 should report to the Safety, Energy Transition & Tech Committee against a written standard: time on wing in the specification, endurance testing complete, and life-limited parts at full life at EIS.
- If the evidence falls short there, we say so publicly and the engine is not fitted. We endorse that line as written.
- Bring the support plan (Singapore-model partner shops, spares and lease pool, EIS field team) to the Committee as a live programme, sized from 7 engines in 2037 and 115 installed by 2039.
- If the Joint Venture forms, hold the fold rule: one chief engineer, configuration and certification basis frozen to EIS, shared gearbox technology only after EIS, and never '2036' for UltraFan NB.

We hold management to the 2045 re-test of the standing commitment.
- Bring the 2045 commit row against hold, column by column, and order `jv_with_pw: withdraw` in that round's sealed orders if its weighted value is below 0 or no live airframe can use it. A commitment no airframe needs is options management.
- Two points the 2035 grid does not show. First, a formation after the Solo is ready saves no R&D: the spend beyond the $4B share would be written off (inference from the public rules). Its value would then rest on share effects alone.
- Second, the equal-share rule cuts both ways. It would hedge a move by Airbus to code 6, but it would dilute us where we fly on more airframes than P&W, for example an fps that selects RR alongside NGSA.
- That is the IAE lesson on alignment. Test it explicitly before the commitment is left standing again.

The widebody holds are endorsed, and we note what they cost. The $5B strain is now permanent for any widebody item while UltraFan NB is on record. A future upgrade or UltraFan WB therefore carries it in its row, against our $3B cap and the $1B sub-cap for UltraFan WB.
- The franchise holds at 55.2%, 5.2 points above our line, in every column. Watch S5, where Airbus's widebody airframe share falls to 30.2%.
- Keep Trent 1000 and Trent 7000 durability work inside the existing budget.
- Bring a widebody item only in the round a 787 or A350 Re-engine is on the record.

Capital and audit. McCabe's full-life lookback should go to the Audit Committee as written: the 2030 $8B earns 8-11% on Civil margins against a mid-to-high-teens hurdle.
- Lesson for any future `launch_if_selected`: bring a margin-based case before the order, not lifecycle revenue alone.
- The go-forward case on the remaining $2.29B (24-30% in five columns) supports holding the programme, and a cancel is worse in every column.
- Confirm the 30-40% payout and the buyback cadence each quarter while the remaining spend runs.

Commercial discipline against S2. Airbus's 'the only maker certain to be ready' is answered with test evidence, not price, earlier dates or launch-style terms. Narrowbody remains an option the company does not need. Share the maturity data through the NGSA programme without dates beyond the public 'ready 2037'.

Public statement: approved as drafted, and the correction of the round-1 note is honest and properly reasoned.
- In future rounds, keep every forward line conditional on Board approval.
- Any Joint Venture date is formation + 6, or the bulletin's folded basis shown.
- UltraFan NB stays 'ready 2037' and nothing earlier.

Capacity for the ramp. The brief shows 267 narrowbody engines in 2040, 742 in 2042 and 1,132 in 2045, about six times the widebody line by 2045.
- Bring the supplier plan (castings, forgings, gearbox sized early) with the 2036 readiness review.
- Confirm that Trent XWB and Trent 7000 supply and support stay ring-fenced.
